Industry News: How to reduce screen time and improve your digital well-being

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1400 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Calm

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Once a week, your phone sends you a screen time report.
  • Screen time adds up fast when work emails and news alerts share a device with your group chats and favorite highlights.
  • In a recent development, conventional wisdom might say “just put the phone down.” But you don’t have to completely give up screens to feel more in control of how you use them.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, MBA.

Once a week, your phone sends you a screen time report. You wince at the number, then swipe it away with the same thumb you were scrolling with.

Screen time adds up fast when work emails and news alerts share a device with your group chats and favorite highlights. By evening, you can feel worn out even if the day wasn’t particularly busy.

In a recent development, conventional wisdom might say “just put the phone down.” But you don’t have to completely give up screens to feel more in control of how you use them. A few small tweaks to your daily routine are a good place to start. Below, you’ll find some realistic ways to cut back, plus a look at why it can feel so hard to put your phone down.

There's no set amount of time that counts as too much. What matters more is how your screen use affects you. Signs worth noticing include strained eyes, restless sleep, reaching for your phone out of habit, and feeling worse after scrolling. If any of these sound familiar, the tips below may help.

💙 Not sure if this sounds like you? Check out these five signs you might be online too much.

If “one more video” keeps turning into one more hour, you’re in good firm. Many apps are designed to keep you scrolling, so you’ll need more than willpower to cut back. Start with one or two tips that feel doable right now. You can come back to the rest later.

Bright colors can make apps harder to put down, and notification badges and thumbnails are built to draw you in. Switching your screen to black and white takes away some of that appeal, which can make scrolling feel less rewarding.

It has been revealed that try: Search “grayscale” or “color filters” in your phone’s settings. You’ll usually find it under Accessibility or Well-Being.

According to recent reports, grayscale may look odd for a day or two. Some people keep it on all day, and others only turn it on in the evening to wind down. You can turn it off whenever you need to, like when you’re using maps or looking at photos.

Industry observers note that 💙 Listen to the Build Healthier Phone Habits series with Dr. Aditi Nerurkar on Calm.

Time can slip by while you scroll. Set a daily limit on your one or two most-used apps, and your phone will nudge you when you reach it.

It has been revealed that try: Search “app limits” or “app timers” in your phone’s settings. You’ll usually find it under screen time.

In a recent development, start with a limit slightly below how much you use those apps now, then lower it gradually. Smaller steps are often more sustainable than cutting back all at once.

Notifications like news alerts, app promos, social likes, and game reminders mostly add noise. Keep the ones you rely on, such as texts, calls, and reminders, and turn off the rest.

Try: Search “notifications” in your device settings, then toggle off the alerts you don’t need, starting with the apps that send the most.

According to recent reports, constant check-ins can keep you glued to your screens all day. Pick a few set times to go through your messages, emails, and feeds.

Try: Limit your check-ins to lunchtime and after work, and keep your personal devices out of reach in between.

Industry observers note that before you open your phone, take one slow breath and ask yourself why you’re reaching for it. If the answer is just habit, that brief pause may be enough to snap you out of autopilot.

Try: Breathe in for four counts and out for six, then see if you still want to unlock your phone.

💙 Discover 10 types of breathing exercises you can try anytime, anywhere.

According to recent reports, when you feel the urge to pick up your phone, try turning to an offline activity instead. Keep an activity you enjoy within reach, like a book on the couch or a sketchpad on the table.

💙 Want to work on the habit before the urge hits? Explore Tame Your Scrolling Habit with Rose Nisker on Calm.

Choose one or two spots to keep screen-free, such as the dinner table or your bedroom. A clear boundary often works better than a vague promise to use screens less. These zones also give you room to be more present, like during a family meal or your evening wind-down.

Sources indicate that try: Place your phone in a dedicated spot, like a basket by the door. If you share a home, invite everyone to join.

It has been revealed that 💙 Not ready to go phone-free at night? Tune in to Sleeping with Your Phone with Dr. Matthew Walker on Calm.

It has been revealed that pick a cutoff time for all your screens, such as 30 minutes before bed, and stick to it as best you can. Late-night screen use can keep your mind active and make it harder to fall asleep.

If you usually watch a TV show before bed, choose one episode and turn off autoplay.

Try: Schedule a nightly reminder for your cutoff. Swap your screen time for a calming activity, like journaling or a short meditation.

💙 Press play on the Wind Down (for Sleep) meditation on Calm.

A few common app features can keep you hooked:.

Infinite scroll: New posts keep loading, so you never reach a natural stopping point.

Autoplay: The next video or episode starts on its own, which keeps you watching unless you stop it.

Unpredictable notifications: Each message or like feels like a small reward, and not knowing when the next one will pop up keeps you checking.

Industry observers note that your emotions play a part too. A screen can be a quick escape when you’re stressed or putting something off. It can bring relief in the moment, even if you feel more drained afterward.

💙 If your screen time has been weighing on your mood, read our guide on what to do if technology is impacting your mental health.

If you want to cut back on screen time without giving up after a few days, start small. Choose one change, like keeping your phone off the dinner table, and give yourself time to adjust before you make another tweak to your routine. If you slip back into old habits, you can always start again the next day.

To set screen time limits that stick, build them into your routine so you don’t have to rely on willpower in the moment. You could use an app timer or set aside a screen-free time each day, like the first half hour after you wake up.

There isn’t a daily screen time limit that works for every adult. If you’d like to use screens less, a good starting point is a limit slightly below your current daily average, and you can lower that limit gradually as you get used to it.

How you spend your screen time matters just as much. An hour on a video call with a friend often leaves you feeling better than an hour of doomscrolling.

Recent findings suggest that you can reduce your screen time at night by setting a cutoff time before bed and charging your phone across the room. Swap your late-night scroll for a book or a short meditation to help you relax before sleep.

It has been revealed that to help your family reduce screen time together, make it a shared strategy. You could agree on screen-free times, such as during meals or the first hour after school or work. Try leading by example, rather than telling your kids or partner what to do.

Industry observers note that no, you don’t have to quit screens completely to feel better. Technology connects you to the people and things you care about. You can cut back on the screen use that leaves you feeling worse, like aimless scrolling, and keep what you value.

In a recent development, mental health is hard. Getting support doesn't have to be. The Calm app puts the tools to feel better in your back pocket, with personalized content to manage stress and anxiety, get better sleep, and feel more present in your life.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Water and diet drinks went head to head in a two-year trial.

Water and diet drinks went head to head in a two-year trial.

People who drink diet soft drinks can keep weight off for two years about as well as those who drink water.

Among those who completed the trial, average weight loss was 4.8 kg in the diet drink group and 3.7 kg in the water group (which was not a statistically significant difference).

Both groups took part in a weight management programme and remained lighter a year after regular support ended.

They also reported similar changes in hunger, despite the difference in how sweet their drinks tasted.

Almost 500 adults with overweight or obesity began the trial after being randomly assigned to drink water or commercially available diet drinks each day.

The study included regular diet drink consumers alongside those who rarely or never chose them.

Everyone began with 12 weeks of active weight loss, followed by 40 weeks of support to help them maintain their progress.

Sugar intake fell by similar amounts in both groups.

One theory is that people learn to expect energy when they taste something sweet.

If the expected calories fail to arrive, the theory goes, that mismatch might affect hunger and lead people to make up the difference by eating more later.

Comparing water with a diet soft drink allows researchers to ask whether sweet taste matters during weight management, since both drinks provide little or no energy.

By the end of the trial, hunger ratings had risen slightly in both groups, and the change was similar whether participants drank water or diet drinks.

Professor Joanne Harrold, the study’s first author, noted:.

“These latest findings show that concerns about sweeteners disrupting appetite or causing weight gain are not supported when tested in a rigorous, long-term randomised trial.”.

When water or a diet drink replaces a sugary soft drink, the swap also cuts the calories in that serving.

A review of 17 randomised trials found small reductions in body weight when people replaced sugary drinks with low- or no-calorie sweetened alternatives, with results broadly similar to those for water (McGlynn et al., 2022).

The two-year trial adds a longer view of what happens when people keep the sweet taste in their drinks while working to maintain weight loss.

The study was published in the British Journal of Nutrition (Harrold et al., 2026).

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Body changes can raise disturbing feelings, such as looking in a mirror and seeing a reflection that may feel spiritually empty, unproductive, ugly, or weak.

Sources indicate that unpleasant sensations such as pain, pins and needles, soreness coursing through limbs, and an inexplicable fog filling the head are a reminder that this body is not the same you anymore, prompting us to wish there was a way to get back there. It may feel impossible to live well unless you do.

This is the disillusionment that most of the population will face at some point in life, through aging, chronic pain, or invisible illness (a disease or health problem that cannot be externally seen, including autoimmune diseases, chronic pain and fatigue, and recently, long COVID).

Recent findings suggest that recent global estimates suggest one in five people are currently experiencing chronic pain. The most prevalent chronic pain reported by adults ages 75 and over includes low back pain and migraine, while tension-type headaches are more often experienced by younger adults. Chronic illness (diabetes, heart disease, and other mid-to-late-life diagnoses) affects about three-quarters of the world population.

Sources indicate that despite how common chronic illness is worldwide, the nuances of navigating a changing body are not often discussed. It’s time for an honest, evidence-based conversation about what it means to navigate chronic pain and illness, aging and transforming identity post-diagnosis, and how to grieve this loss and maintain meaning through these changes.

Research suggest that those with internalized stigma of chronic illness are more preoccupied with how their illness detracts from their view of themselves, and also have a greater tendency to overlook positive aspects of life with a chronic illness.

Psychologists have observed how preoccupation with illness or pain is often accompanied by other grief behaviors. A 2025 study explored how Danish chronic illness patients navigated loss and growth. The study found that many with chronic illness find themselves mourning the life that they thought they would have, often leading to loss of motivation and joy in everyday life.

The perception of losing the life they had once envisioned is often accompanied by a focus on getting back to the “before illness” version of themselves as people struggle to accept how their body has changed, perhaps in how it looks but definitely in how it feels.

It has been revealed that these changes and associated feelings of loss often permeate a person’s sense of identity, as well as their perceived roles within social relationships. Many report a fear of burdening others, especially loved ones, often describing feelings of guilt that “others have it worse than I do.” This is where internalized stigma festers.

It has been revealed that some people have also described feelings of anger, isolation, shame, and exhaustion accompanying sadness. Meanwhile, others have expressed frustration over a gradual loss rather than a “clean break,” accompanied by the inability to find closure.

Sources indicate that first, it’s notable to understand why accepting this continuous loss feels so impossible. Theories of control in psychology state that humans desire control or the ability to achieve a desired outcome according to our own standards.

The best and most enduring of our articles, podcasts, and videos about getting older.

When that ability is seen as stripped away, people are more likely to experience negative mental health symptoms, like anxiety, depression, and even grief. Specifically, feelings of diminished perceived control (subjective belief about our ability to achieve desired outcomes) occur when we face continuous roadblocks to living our desired life because of chronic illness.

Sources indicate that one of the major consequences of loss and major life change is that it can disrupt meaning and challenge identity, purpose, and assumptions about the future. At a time when people feel there is little they can control, psychologist Robert Neimeyer’s Meaning Reconstruction Theory poses the questions: “How do I move forward?” and “What matters most?”.

While the original theory was proposed as an approach to coping with the loss of a loved one, the process is somewhat similar to grieving the close ally that is your body. This theory approaches grief by making sense of the loss and finding ways to rebuild a sense of purpose in a changed life (and body).

To answer relevant questions about how to move forward with chronic illness, two ongoing approaches are needed: integrating the loss and recentering purpose and meaning.

Integrating the loss may look like processing significant bodily losses in therapy, finding trusted loved ones to talk about the loss with, and focusing on being realistic about your current body without judgment.

In a recent development, second, recentering purpose during this major life change involves understanding your why: why is this loss so significant to you, why does it hurt? Maybe it’s because you love hiking in the mountains and a new diagnosis with arthritis feels like the end of this joy. Part of rebuilding meaning is finding new approaches to fulfilling this purpose—perhaps hiking may look different, but nature can be accessed and loved with chronic illness present.

In a recent development, rebuilding meaning might also look like making meaning from this loss: What has this change taught you about yourself, about the impact you can make? Approaching present and future with this perspective helps process grief in a more protective way.

In a recent development, living with chronic pain, illness, and the changes that come with aging often involves grieving physical loss, but also shifts in purpose, relationships, identity, and future plans. While these changes challenge our perceived control and purpose, the Meaning Reconstruction Theory suggests that acceptance and growth comes with integrating loss and rebuilding purpose alongside these changes.

Although the present is different than anticipated, fulfillment is still possible with your current body.

How cognitive behavioral therapy works to treat OCD

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2263 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Calm

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that clinically reviewed by Dr.
  • Obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) can look different from one person to the next.
  • It has been revealed that what unites these scenarios is the OCD loop: there’s an unwanted thought or fear, and you do something to make it stop.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, MBA.

Obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) can look different from one person to the next. For some people, it’s checking the locks again and again, even when they know the door is shut. For others, it’s washing their hands until they feel clean, counting steps or objects, arranging things until they feel just right, or getting stuck on an unwanted thought.

It has been revealed that what unites these scenarios is the OCD loop: there’s an unwanted thought or fear, and you do something to make it stop. But the relief doesn’t last and you end up back at the anxious thought, triggering the process again. For people living with OCD, this cycle can be exhausting.

According to recent reports, cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) is one of the most studied ways to break the OCD cycle, and one type in particular, called exposure and response prevention (ERP), has the strongest research support of any talk therapy for OCD. Here’s a look at what CBT for OCD involves, how ERP works, and what a session can feel like.

CBT is a structured, evidence-based form of talk therapy. It looks at how your thoughts, feelings, and actions feed each other, and it focuses on the present rather than digging through your past. Most versions help you notice unhelpful thoughts and respond to them in newly introduced ways.

CBT for OCD works a little differently. With something like anxiety or low mood, a therapist might help you question a worried thought and look for more balanced evidence. With OCD, that technique can backfire. Trying to argue with an intrusive thought, or prove it wrong, can become a mental compulsion, which keeps the cycle going.

So OCD-focused CBT spends less time debating the content of your thoughts and more time changing how you respond to them. The main tool for that is ERP, a type of CBT that focuses on behavior.

If you've ever been told to "just stop worrying," you may know that advice doesn’t work for OCD. The cycle doesn’t respond to willpower alone.

Here's how the loop tends to run:.

You get an intrusive thought or fear you don’t want (the obsession).

To get relief, you do something to make the feeling go away (the compulsion), like checking, washing, asking for reassurance, or going over events in your mind.

You feel better, but only for a short while.

Each compulsion can teach your brain that the thought was a true threat and that the ritual kept you safe. So the thought tends to return.

Say you’re leaving for work. A thought pops up: What if I left the stove on? Your anxiety spikes, so you go back and check. The stove is off, and you feel relief. But on your way to the car, the doubt returns, along with the urge to check again.

That's why OCD can feel impossible to overcome. The very thing that calms you in the moment is what feeds the cycle.

It has been revealed that ERP involves gradually facing the things that trigger your fears, while holding off on the compulsion. It can sound intimidating, but it’s planned and step by step, and you and your therapist agree on each move together. Here’s what it tends to look like.

It has been revealed that A lot of questions up front: Early sessions are mostly about getting clear on what's happening. Expect to talk through your intrusive thoughts, the compulsions they trigger, and the situations you avoid.

According to recent reports, building a fear ladder: Your triggers get ranked from mild to most distressing, and you start near the bottom. You won't be asked to face your worst fear on day one.

Facing triggers on purpose: You'll meet a fear instead of dodging it, whether that's touching a doorknob, writing down a feared word, or sitting with an uncertain thought.

Not doing the compulsion: Expect to resist the response you'd normally reach for, even something subtle like seeking reassurance.

Sitting with the discomfort: At first the fear climbs, which can feel like proof it won't stop. Over time, many people find the fear eases, and they learn they can cope with it.

Homework between sessions: Practice between sessions is a significant part of progress, so expect to take exposures home and work on them in your daily life.

In a recent development, ERP with a trained therapist is the core of OCD treatment, and nothing below replaces it. But the stretches between sessions can be long, and a few grounding habits may make them easier to deal with.

Mindfulness and meditation can help you practice noticing a thought, letting it pass, and not acting on it or trying to prove it wrong. That fits well with ERP, where you also learn to let urges be present without giving in. A few minutes a day can be a gentle place to start.

In a recent development, one caution: if you catch yourself meditating to “cancel out” a bad thought, that’s the compulsion sneaking back in. The aim is to let thoughts come and go, not to get rid of them.

💙 Practice noticing a thought and letting it pass with Chibs Okereke’s short Working With Thoughts meditation.

Sources indicate that when you’re struggling with anxiety or a racing heart, slow breathing can help your body settle. Box breathing is one option, since the even count gives your mind something simple to hold onto.

Use it for everyday stress, like after a tough commute or before bed. During an exposure, or when you’re trying to make a thought go away, it can work against ERP, because the point is to practice facing the discomfort. Ask your therapist when it’s okay to use it alongside your ERP practice.

💙 For a tense, jittery day, Panic SOS with Kirat Randhawa uses sight, sound, and touch to help your body settle.

Recent findings suggest that poor sleep and OCD symptoms often go hand in hand. Research links poor sleep to more intrusive thoughts and harder-to-manage symptoms. Rest may also make it easier to do your ERP practice.

A steady routine can help. Go to bed and wake up at about the same time each day, and dim the lights and put screens away 30 minutes or so before bed. A warm shower, gentle stretching, or a sleep meditation can help you unwind, and limiting caffeine later in the day may make it easier to fall asleep.

Bedtime can be a hard time for those of us with OCD, as quiet moments can leave room for intrusive thoughts, checking, or reassurance-seeking. If rituals are keeping you up, mention it to your therapist.

💙 Give your mind permission to power down with this Wind Down (for Sleep) session on Calm.

Putting your obsessions, compulsions, and triggers on paper may help you and your therapist spot patterns you’d otherwise miss. Many people find it easiest to jot down a few quick notes each time the loop highlights up: what set it off, what thought or fear came up, what you did in response, and how you felt afterward. Over time, you may notice that certain places, times of day, or moods make the cycle more likely.

While you’re mapping the loop, try not to judge yourself or over-analyze your entries.

💙 If you’re struggling to get started, journaling prompts can help.

According to recent reports, A walk around the block, a stretch, or a few minutes of dancing in your kitchen can help ease stress and give your body a reset. Pick something that feels possible even on a hard day, and tie it to something you already do, like a few minutes of movement while your coffee brews or after you hang up a call. Doing it at about the same time each day can also help it stick.

One thing to watch for: if movement starts to feel like a ritual, like needing to take a certain number of steps or repeat a routine until it feels “just right,” mention it to your therapist.

💙 Tamara Levitt’s Mindful Walking series turns a short stroll into a chance to notice what’s around you.

In a recent development, OCD can be isolating. Talking with a friend or family member you trust can remind you that you’re more than your symptoms. If a loved one wants to help, ask your therapist how. Well-meaning support, like answering the same reassurance question again and again, can accidentally keep the cycle going, and a therapist can guide you both.

Industry observers note that A peer support group can also help. Reputable OCD organizations run groups where you can meet people doing the same work.

Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) is one of the most effective treatments for OCD, especially a type called exposure and response prevention (ERP). Research highlights it can reduce symptoms for many people.

CBT helps by targeting the anxiety cycle that keeps OCD going. Depending on how severe symptoms are, it's used on its own or alongside medication.

Exposure and response prevention (ERP) is the best-studied therapy for OCD, but it isn’t the only option. Other approaches include cognitive therapy, acceptance and commitment therapy (ACT), and inference-based CBT (I-CBT). Cognitive therapy helps you examine the beliefs that make intrusive thoughts feel threatening. ACT focuses on making room for uncomfortable thoughts rather than fighting them. I-CBT targets the reasoning that makes an obsession feel believable. Medication, usually a type of antidepressant called an SSRI, is a separate treatment that can lower the intensity of symptoms. It’s often combined with therapy. A clinician can help you weigh which mix fits your situation.

In a recent development, ERP, or exposure and response prevention, is a type of CBT where you gradually face your triggers while resisting the urge to do a compulsion. It's a first-line treatment for OCD.

Industry observers note that each time you sit with a fear and resist the ritual, your brain gets evidence that the feared outcome doesn't arrive and that the distress is survivable. That learning is what loosens OCD's grip. A therapist structures the exposures so they stay challenging without tipping into overwhelming.

In a recent development, the main difference is what each approach targets. Regular CBT often focuses on changing unhelpful thoughts, such as questioning a worry and replacing it with a more balanced one. CBT for OCD focuses on the compulsion.

It has been revealed that that’s because, with OCD, the compulsion is what keeps the cycle going. Each time you do the ritual, or try to prove the fear wrong, your brain learns that the thought was a real threat and the ritual kept you safe. In ERP, you face the trigger and hold off on the compulsion. Over time, your brain learns that the feared outcome doesn’t happen and that you can cope with the anxiety without the ritual. Some therapists also work on the beliefs that make intrusive thoughts feel so threatening, but ERP is the main tool.

Cognitive distortions are unhelpful thinking patterns, and in OCD they often show up as beliefs that make ordinary doubts feel dangerous. Common examples include:.

Feeling responsible for preventing harm, even when it’s unlikely.

Overestimating how likely something bad is to happen.

Thought-action fusion, or believing a thought is as bad as an action.

Struggling with not knowing for sure (intolerance of uncertainty).

Assuming a thought must matter because you had it.

In a recent development, these patterns are common in OCD, and they can fuel the urge to do compulsions. Therapy can help you spot them and loosen their grip.

💙 Find out more about cognitive distortions and how to reframe negative thoughts.

Many people see meaningful improvement from ERP within about 12–20 sessions, which is often three to four months with weekly visits (intensive programs can be faster). Some notice shifts with fewer sessions, especially with regular practice in between.

Timelines vary with symptom severity, how often you practice, and whether medication is part of the initiative. OCD treatment is usually designed to be relatively short-term and skills-based, not open-ended.

You can do some ERP on your own, and self-help books and apps exist for it, but working with a trained therapist is strongly recommended, especially for moderate to severe OCD.

Self-directed ERP can be tricky to get right. It can be easy to accidentally turn an exposure into a subtle compulsion, or to skip the exposures that matter most. A therapist keeps the initiative honest and adjusts it as you go. If therapy isn't available right now, guided self-help from a reputable OCD organization is a safer starting point than going it fully alone.

Mindfulness can support OCD treatment, but it isn't a standalone fix. Research on mindfulness for OCD is promising but mixed, and ERP remains the first-line treatment.

According to recent reports, on its own, mindfulness won't switch off intrusive thoughts, and expecting it to can backfire. Its real value is helping you relate to those thoughts differently, which is why it pairs with therapy rather than replacing it. A clinician can point you toward using it in a way that helps.

💙 If you’d like to try it, these tips for practicing mindfulness meditation are a gentle place to start.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Across the Western world, young men and boys face a changing economy, with fewer manual labor jobs and factory floors that used to give a swathe of working-class men purpose and value. This leaves a large portion of recent generations feeling left behind and forgotten—and vulnerable to exploitation.

A profitable industry of influencers who misframe evolutionary science to justify their narratives have taken advantage of the addictive nature of social media to hook into this vacuum and light up phone screens every night with the same vitriolic messages: “Reclaim your manhood”; “You are being feminized”; “The world is making you soft.”.

But this narrative conflicts with the biological reality. Across species—from fungal networks trading nutrients underground to astronauts sharing the role of emptying the latrine on the International Space Station—every organism must strike some balance between competing and cooperating. Lessons from the animal kingdom, from my research and others, show that cooperation doesn’t diminish masculinity.

Recent findings suggest that indeed, dominant primates use their power judiciously, and male friendship forms the foundation of cooperation in a variety of species, with affectionate touch, caring, and vulnerability playing crucial roles in male relationships. The simple picture painted for these boys is built on sand. Once we observe the reality of sex, behavior, and connection in the natural world around us, it washes away.

Human males stand to improve their relationships, benefit from a broader base of emotional and social support, and enhance their well-being with these friendship lessons from our closest cousins in the animal kingdom.

Recent findings suggest that one term at the core of the manosphere is the notion of alpha males. Life coaches and politicians push this construct without understanding the true function of hierarchy in the natural world. They believe that to get ahead you must take advantage of others, and that the weak get left behind. In reality, dominant male primates care for relationships and wield their power judiciously.

Sources indicate that it’s true that male chimpanzees form typically linear dominance relationships, where one submits to another, all the way to the top. They compete, and those competitions can spill into physical altercations. Higher-ranking males do tend to sire more offspring.

Sources indicate that but these broad truths hide the nuance of layered cooperation, care, nurturing touch, and love among male chimps. Day after day, most of that competitive pressure never turns into a fight at all. What holds chimpanzee communities together is less the male at the top and more the alliances underneath him. Males groom each other for hours at a time. They embrace after conflicts and kiss the arms and shoulders of their allies before potential competition, to resolve any tension. Before risky boundary patrols, when they might encounter rival groups, they even hold each other’s genitals—a sign of deep trust. Data spanning nearly three decades from Gombe show that males with strong ties to the alpha sired more offspring than those without, and so did males with wider networks of close allies, whether or not they ever rose in rank at all. Those who look out for each other and contribute to a strong community end up thriving.

You can see the value of those alliances when a hierarchy is disrupted. At Taï National Park in Côte d’Ivoire, Anna Preis and her colleagues measured urinary cortisol in wild males across stable and unstable dominance periods. Stress rose in every male during the unstable stretches, regardless of rank. Aggression went the other way, rising when things were calm and the group faced less risk of destabilization. When the risk of escalation was greatest, males backed off. Stability has its own payoff; a group tearing itself apart can’t defend a territory.

Industry observers note that indeed, even in its origins, the term “alpha” contained more nuance than broadly understood. The term rose out of research during the mid-20th century on captive wolves who were thrown together into crowded spaces without room to escape. Such an arrangement would produce a tense, despotic dynamic in any species, including our own. Once biologists began studying wild wolf packs, it became apparent that they are, well, families. They comprise a breeding pair and their grown offspring. L. David Mech, the biologist who popularized the alpha wolf in the first place, has spent more than two decades asking people to retire the term in order to accurately reflect natural communities. Despite its inaccuracy, the idea still perpetuates on podcasts and social media.

The role of vulnerability and comfort in the natural world provides another powerful lesson for humanity. At a wildlife sanctuary in Zambia, I’ve come to know a longstanding alpha male chimpanzee named Doug over many years. One day, during my first field season observing his group, he was separated from his community for routine husbandry purposes, alongside a slightly younger rival and the rival’s paternal ally. During this separation, the rival pair ambushed him, leaving him incredibly shaken. I had known Doug as a strong leader who never broke composure, and I felt shocked to see him cowering and screaming, nothing like the composed figurehead his group had respected.

In a recent development, A low-ranking male, whom Doug had rarely paid attention to, approached first, offering himself in a gesture of submission. What followed drew in most of the roughly 40 other chimpanzees in the group. They embraced, touched, and kissed him; exchanged genital contact; placed their hands in his mouth; and invited him to mount them. This scale of collective reassurance directed toward a single individual is something I’ve never seen since, and is likely only sparked by moments of genuine crisis. The whole group responded to Doug’s distress with an outpouring of comfort and what to humans would appear to be love.

According to recent reports, the main aim of this project was to study consolation: how chimpanzees, and their sister species bonobos, comfort each other after fights. But we kept noticing similar intense, friendly contacts occurring in the absence of conflicts, often in the anticipation of competition. To better understand this, we conducted a feeding task with a five-minute window before the food arrived, filming 116 apes across five groups at two sanctuaries. We found that those who exchanged more reassuring contact beforehand went on to spend significantly more time feeding peacefully alongside others. In chimpanzees, males exhibited most of this behavior, but primarily in Doug’s more tolerant group. In a more despotic group where resources were less evenly distributed, the male-male relationships were markedly weaker. Simply put, friendship and reassuring behaviors among males helped these chimps peacefully put aside competing interests, which may lay the groundwork for collective harmony.

According to recent reports, some of these behaviors require remarkable trust. Placing a finger, or even a whole hand, inside another male’s mouth or pressing your own mouth to someone’s body after they’ve just been attacked may be misinterpreted as having aggressive intent and could spark a latest conflict. Chimpanzees have a reputation for amputating the extremities of others, and that, along with the size of their canines, makes these behaviors exceptionally risky during such turbulent times. Our hypothesis: That could be the point. You only offer that kind of vulnerability to someone you trust not to use it against you, and doing so signals something about the relationship that a show of strength can’t. Again, we noticed that these behaviors were particularly amplified in Doug’s group compared to the one with a less benevolent leader.

Sources indicate that doug remains alpha to this day, and from our research, his tenureship seems to be thanks to the bonds he continues to invest in and the support he reveals for his peers. He’s flawed and sometimes lashes out as any male chimpanzee might do, but throughout the seven years we’ve studied him, no challenges have managed to displace him. Doug looks out for others, and in turn they look out for him. Over my time studying many groups of chimpanzees, it seems the most tolerant social environments emerge from the leadership of strong, stable, and generally fair alphas who allow others access to resources and who keep tight bonds with their closest allies.

Humans can also learn from the way male chimpanzees can be tender in other contexts. At Taï National Park in Côte d’Ivoire, researchers recorded wild chimpanzees adopting orphaned infants, more than half of them taken in by males with no obvious kinship reason to bother. One adult male, Porthos, adopted an unrelated infant female named Gia and carried her on his back for years, sharing food with her long after any potential social debt to her deceased mother had lapsed. Later analysis found that what predicted whether a male took on that role was not the infant’s sex, and not relatedness, but the strength of the grooming bond he’d shared with the mother before she died.

According to recent reports, touch carries power in humans, as well. Research across five European cultures found that the area of the body you’ll let someone touch maps almost directly onto the strength of your emotional bond with them. There is cultural variation. British people are notably more guarded about casual contact than many of their European neighbours, and touch between men in many Western contexts carries particular social weight. Touch conveys intimacy and trust. Yet holding someone’s hand or shoulder can also be used to intimidate or harass. We could learn from primates to stop withholding touch where it would help most and back down from reaching for it where it shouldn’t be used at all.

One key area where more touch helps is sports. A study of all 30 NBA teams during the 2008–09 season found that the teams who touched more early in the season, through fist bumps, chest bumps, hugs, and high fives, went on to perform better and play more cooperatively later, even after controlling for player salaries and pre-season expectations. In women’s college basketball, players who received more physical contact from teammates after missing their first free throw were more likely to convert the second. After five straight shootout losses, England’s governing body in football, the FA, spent 18 months rebuilding England’s approach to penalties under Gareth Southgate, not just the technical side. Players were coached on how to treat each other after a miss. They learned to place an arm around the shoulder rather than leaving each other isolated. Celebrating wildly after a scored kick became a deliberate technique for steadying whoever was up next. Locker-room culture has never been shy about physical contact between teammates. Now we know that the contact might be doing real work.

To be sure, humans show exceptional diversity in our cultures and behavior, for better and worse. But when humans are violent or cruel, people call it primal, or animalistic. We emphasize our altruism as unique to our species. That’s unfair to animals. Humans have bullied others until they took their own lives. We’ve wiped out entire tribes and cultures. And beyond targeting other people, even now, humans are removing protections for endangered keystone species that ecosystems depend upon to thrive. But we don’t need to accept the drive to dominate as inevitable. If the apes show anything, it’s how much of that drive gets managed and set aside day to day, and how much depends on the community you find yourself in. We are a part of the natural world like all other animals, needing to balance our cooperative and competitive urges. And the evidence suggests we sit at the better end of that range far more often than we might think.

Industry observers note that now that we know how central touch and cooperation are to primates and human nature, I hope we can stop being pessimistic when we predict others’ behavior and motives. A study published in Science this June, covering 125 countries and over 100,000 people, found that 69% of us cooperate with a stranger when given the choice. Asked to guess, people put it at 47%. That pessimism demonstrated up in 124 of the 125 countries surveyed. This matters in the grander scheme of things because those of us who expect others to cooperate are far more likely to cooperate also. When researchers simply told participants that most people worldwide see climate change as a threat, belief in others’ willingness to cooperate ticked up, and actual cooperation followed it, slightly, but in the right direction.

Building on the lessons of primate relationships is easier than it seems.

Sources indicate that seek simple interactions. One of the main ways our primate cousins build affiliative relationships is spending time sitting in close proximity. They may groom, or play, or even sit in contact. More often than not they just like to hang out near their close partners. Just being close to one another is meaningful.

Sources indicate that try a car journey or a five-a-side game. Build trust and relationship through activities where nobody has to look anyone in the eye. If a mate isn’t much of a talker, doing something alongside him might get further than sitting him down and asking how he’s doing.

Reach out before a crisis, not after. Great apes exchange most of their reassurance in the tense minutes before competition, not the wreckage afterward. Reconciliation and comforting are commonplace in humans and primates, but it’s much easier to prevent escalation than it is to smooth things over after a fight.

This piece is part of a three-year GGSC project to explore love's role in promoting social well-being, bridging divides, and contributing to a good, meaningful life.

Don’t wait to be the one who’s approached. That 22-point gap between how we actually cooperate and what we think everyone else will do shows the power of offering an invitation to relationship. Most of us are waiting for someone else to go first.

Industry observers note that influencers selling young men and boys on their primal nature fly in the face of the science and what nature actually looks like. Force and competition are real parts of biology, and something we humans have to manage in our everyday lives. But, if there’s one thing I’ve learned from my many years studying our closest relatives, it’s that touch, care, cooperation, and even love are the most instinctive natural components of being part of the primate family.

Jake Brooker, Ph.D., is an NWO Veni scholar based at Utrecht University, The Netherlands, who studies social cognition and socio-emotional behavior in great apes. He completed doctoral and postdoctoral work at Durham University, U.K.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, MBA.

Maybe you’ve had the experience where you’ve opened a gift that didn’t quite land… Another candle, another kitchen gadget, another book you probably won’t read.

Recent findings suggest that when life can feel increasingly materialistic, receiving the gift of an experience can feel like an extra special treat. A coffee date, a class you could take together, or a simple invitation to step away from your routine for a few hours. Gifting experiences is becoming more common as people increasingly value things to do rather than things to have. Experiences create memories, prolonged joy, and ways to connect and bond with your loved ones.

Let’s explore why this trend is becoming a thoughtful option for many, and how to choose the right option for the people in your life.

In a recent development, gifting an experience means offering someone the chance to do or enjoy something, rather than giving them a physical item. It could be a short outing, a shared class, a small adventure, or even a moment of relaxation. The focus is on creating a meaningful interaction or memory.

Industry observers note that at its core, an experience gift acknowledges who someone is and what matters to them — comfort, curiosity, connection, or rest. It’s a way of saying, I see what brings you joy or ease, and building a shared experience around that. This can feel especially supportive for people whose lives are busy or emotionally stretched.

Sources indicate that because these gifts are flexible, they work across relationships and budgets. They can be shared or solo, active or restful, planned or open-ended. They offer a moment that feels nourishing and special for someone you care about.

💙 If relaxation is what they need, a Calm gift card gives them access to sleep support, meditation, and stress tools.

While research on experience gifting is still growing, studies highlight how shared time and supportive interactions can strengthen relationships and help people feel more connected.

And for the giver, choosing an experience can relieve some of the pressure to pick the “perfect” item. Plus, you get to be a bit more creative since experiences can be catered to the person in question more accurately than a fresh sweater or scented bath salts.

It has been revealed that these gifts also tend to linger in memory. A walk through a newly introduced neighborhood, a class where you learned something together, or an afternoon spent doing something familiar but intentional can shape how people feel long after the moment ends. The emotional takeaway is often stronger than anything wrapped.

Choosing an experience gift doesn’t need to feel complicated. A few gentle questions can help you find something that feels both thoughtful and doable:.

What feels realistic for them right now?

What genuinely matches their interests?

Will this support connection in a way that feels natural?

It has been revealed that these considerations keep the focus on care rather than wow-factor. The most memorable experience gifts are often the ones that feel easy to say yes to.

According to recent reports, related read: What is the receiving gifts love language? Plus, 10 examples.

Experience gifts don’t have to be big, expensive, or Instagram-ready. The most meaningful ones usually feel simple, personal, and easy to follow through on. Below are ideas for different people in your life, with concrete examples and small tweaks to make each one feel low-pressure yet purposeful.

1. Slow morning together: Gift a “no-alarm morning” where you initiative nothing except being together. This could look like making breakfast at home, wandering to a café, or staying in pajamas with a movie. You can write it as a simple coupon: “One slow morning: no chores, no plans, just us.” This works well for tired partners who crave rest more than busy plans.

2. A shared learning experience: Choose a class or workshop that feels fun. Cooking, pottery, a dance class, a cocktail-making session, or even a virtual class from home. The goal is to play, not create a new skill. Pick a time that fits your usual schedule, and make it clear there’s no pressure to be good at it. You’re just trying it out.

It has been revealed that 3. A “memory lane” date: Revisit places that matter to your relationship: where you met, a favorite early date spot, or a park you love. You can build a simple route and add tiny prompts, like sharing a favorite memory at each stop. This turns a regular outing into something personal without costing much.

According to recent reports, 4. At-home retreat night: Create a mini retreat without leaving the house. That might mean takeout, candles, phones off for a few hours, and a shared activity like a puzzle, show, or playlist swap. You can include options on a card so they can choose: a massage, a movie, a board game, or just some quiet time together.

Recent findings suggest that 5. Surprise “care afternoon”: Block off a few hours for them where you take on a task they’ve been dreading—organizing a small space, handling an errand, or taking something off their mental load—and then follow it with something relaxing, like a walk or coffee. The experience is both practical support and quality time.

It has been revealed that 6. Future adventure fund: If money is tight or schedules are messy, create a “future adventure” envelope. Add a small amount of money, a short list of possible outings (day trip, concert, special restaurant), and a promise to choose an option together when life settles a bit. The gift is the intention and shared planning, not just the event itself.

According to recent reports, 1. Family game or movie night: Blueprint a night with a few easy games or a movie everyone can enjoy. Add snacks, cozy blankets, and a pause on chores for a few hours. You can give the night a “ticket” and let family members vote on the game or film. Keep it simple so no one has to host a perfect event.

In a recent development, 2. Seasonal outing: Choose something tied to the time of year: apple picking, a beach afternoon, a holiday light walk, or a picnic in the park. The key is to keep expectations reasonable. Pick something close by, flexible with the weather, and not too long. Add a warm drink stop or simple treat to make it feel special.

3. Family photo walk: Go for a walk through a neighborhood, park, or favorite spot and take casual photos of each other and everyday moments. This isn’t about staged portraits. It’s about capturing small, real pieces of your life together. Later, you can print a few favorites as a follow-up surprise.

Recent findings suggest that 4. Shared creative project: Start something you can all contribute to: a family recipe book, a small garden, a scrapbook, or a shared playlist for car rides. The “gift” is the first session to begin the project, plus a blueprint to keep it going at a relaxed pace.

Industry observers note that 5. Story or memory night: For older family members, gift a relaxed evening where you ask about their stories — childhood, early jobs, favorite memories. You can record audio or write things down if they’re comfortable. This can feel especially meaningful for grandparents or relatives who don’t often get to share their history.

6. Chore-free experience swap: Offer to trade time: you handle childcare, yard work, or a big errand so another family member can enjoy their own experience like a class, a nap, a solo walk, or quiet time at a café. The experience you’re gifting is space and freedom, which many busy adults crave more than objects.

1. Friendship field trip: Pick a spot you’ve both wanted to visit, maybe a fresh café, nearby town, market, bookstore, or trail. Make it simple: transportation, one planned stop, and room to wander. You can name it something fun on the card, like “Field Trip Day: You + Me + Snacks.”.

Industry observers note that 2. Theme night at home: Instead of going out, bring the theme to your living room. Taco night, cozy soup night, DIY spa night, or favorite childhood snacks night. The gift is that you blueprint the details so your friend just indicates up and relaxes. This works well for introverts or friends on a budget.

Sources indicate that 3. Shared creative time: Gift a “creative hang” where you both bring whatever you want to work on like, drawing, writing, knitting, music, or even organizing photos. Add music, snacks, and low-pressure conversation. For friends who feel guilty about not making time for hobbies, this can feel like a gentle permission slip.

4. Local class or workshop together: Check out low-stakes options like pottery, candle making, painting, or a casual fitness class. Pick something that doesn’t require special gear or skills and frame it as an experiment, not a performance: “We’ll probably be bad at this, and that’s half the fun.”.

According to recent reports, 5. Walk-and-talk ritual: Offer a series of scheduled or flexible walk-and-talks. Maybe once a month, every other week, or whenever you both can manage. The experience is regular emotional check-ins built into movement and fresh air. If walking isn’t accessible, this can be a sit-and-sip ritual at a park or café.

1. One-on-one “date” with you: Plan a simple outing centered around their interests like ice cream, a playground, a comic shop, the library, or a favorite café. The crucial part is your undivided attention — no multitasking, no rushing. You can make a small “VIP pass” with their name and the activity.

2. Activity day pass: Gift a trip to a kid-friendly place: zoo, aquarium, children’s museum, climbing gym, trampoline park, or mini golf. To keep expectations realistic, include what’s covered (entry, one snack) and how long you’ll stay. That clarity helps avoid meltdowns.

4. Backyard or park adventure: Create a small “explorer kit” experience. Maybe that’s a printed map, a simple scavenger hunt, or nature bingo. Then take them to a nearby park or backyard to complete it together. The kit can be as simple as a folded paper with things to look for: birds, leaves, colors, shapes.

5. Choose-your-own-activity coupon book: Instead of one massive outing, make a few small coupons they can redeem over time: “Stay up 30 minutes late,” “Pick tonight’s dinner,” “Board game together,” “Extra story at bedtime.” This spreads the experience out and gives them a sense of choice.

6. Screen-time with purpose: If screens are part of your life (for most families, they are), turn it into an intentional experience. A planned movie night with popcorn and cozy blankets, or a co-op video game session where you play alongside them. The shift is from “background screen” to “shared screen time.”.

7. Skill-building mini lesson: Offer to teach them something they’ve shown interest in, like basic cooking, drawing, sewing, photography, or music. Keep it short and fun — 30 to 60 minutes with lots of breaks. The experience is meant to help them feel capable and supported, not pushed to master something.

Good experience gifts feel easy to enjoy and don’t add pressure. Simple outings like a coffee date, museum visit, or nature walk work well, as do classes or small day trips.

If you’re unsure, think about what the person already loves—quiet spaces, creativity, movement, or social time—and choose something that gently supports those interests.

Budget-friendly experience gifts often center on time or support rather than cost. A homemade coupon for help with errands, a movie night at home, or a walk together can feel more meaningful than anything store-bought.

You can also offer a few options, like a baked treat, a playlist walk, or a shared hour of connection, so the gift feels personal without being expensive.

Recent findings suggest that experience gifts ease the pressure of traditional gifting and help strengthen connections. They don’t create clutter and often require less guesswork than choosing an item.

Sources indicate that because they create memories, they can feel more lasting and emotionally meaningful. Early research also suggests shared time and supportive interactions may help people feel more connected.

In a recent development, examples include classes, tours, local events, shared meals, creative workshops, or simple nature outings. They can also be quieter moments like helping with a task or planning a cozy night in.

Recent findings suggest that even small gestures—like sharing a playlist—count. The impact comes from the feeling the experience creates, not the size of the activity.

Sources indicate that if you’re unsure, offer a few choices rather than picking one activity. Options like a coffee outing, nature walk, or game night let the person choose what fits their energy. A flexible gift card to a café, movie theater, or class platform also works. Choice keeps the gift from feeling like an obligation.

Families often enjoy simple, low-pressure activities that include everyone. Seasonal outings, game nights, and local events work well because they’re easy to initiative.

In a recent development, shared projects—like cooking or gardening—or gifts of time, such as taking on chores so someone can rest, can also be meaningful. The best family gifts support connection without adding stress.

Friends tend to appreciate experiences that feel connecting and relaxed. This might be a field trip to a fresh café, a creative class, a cozy night in, or a shared walk.

Sources indicate that some friends enjoy active outings, while others prefer crafting or volunteering together. The goal is to match their energy and make time together feel restorative.

Experience gifts can feel better for some people because they avoid clutter, reduce pressure, and often feel more meaningful. They shift the focus toward presence and memory-making rather than buying things.

While not everyone prefers experiences, they offer a gentle alternative for people who value connection or feel overwhelmed by physical items.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • What draws someone to another person when they’re already in a committed relationship?
  • What draws someone to another person when they’re already in a committed relationship?
  • Both positive and dark personality traits are linked to becoming infatuated with someone outside a committed relationship.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

What draws someone to another person when they’re already in a committed relationship?

What draws someone to another person when they’re already in a committed relationship?

Both positive and dark personality traits are linked to becoming infatuated with someone outside a committed relationship.

The clearest link among the dark traits is with psychopathy, which includes impulsivity and a lack of empathy.

Yet a more positive trait, the tendency to see value in other people and admire their qualities, is also linked to stronger infatuation once other differences are taken into account.

The researchers suggest that impulsivity may make a new attraction more rewarding, while an appreciation of other people may make it easier to form an emotional connection with them.

People who are more open to casual sex or less satisfied with their relationship also report stronger feelings for someone else.

The study involved just over 300 adults in Romania who were in committed relationships.

They completed questionnaires about their personality, their attitudes and experiences around casual sex, and how satisfied they were with their relationship.

The researchers also asked about the thoughts, feelings and desires people had towards someone other than their partner.

Psychologists call this extradyadic infatuation, a preoccupation that can involve repeatedly thinking about someone and feeling unable to tell your partner how strongly you feel.

People who scored higher on humanism, the tendency to value and admire others, generally reported less infatuation outside their relationship.

Of all the factors the researchers examined, openness to casual sex had the strongest link to infatuation after the others were taken into account.

The researchers suggest that people high in humanism may be more receptive to forming a close connection with someone new.

Faith in humanity, which reflects a belief in other people’s goodwill, indicated a different pattern and remained linked to less infatuation.

People who expect others to be dependable may also see their existing relationship as more secure and feel less drawn to alternatives, the researchers suggest.

Machiavellianism, a tendency to approach relationships strategically and manipulate others for personal gain, also highlighted a reversal.

It was linked to stronger infatuation when examined on its own and to weaker infatuation once the other factors were considered.

The researchers suggest that someone who takes a calculating approach to relationships may be wary of an outside attachment that demands sustained emotional investment.

Psychopathic traits, by comparison, were linked to stronger infatuation in both analyses.

When the researchers compared all the factors together, openness to casual sex had the strongest link to infatuation.

Dissatisfaction with an existing relationship may also make an alternative partner seem more appealing, although the survey leaves open whether dissatisfaction precedes the infatuation or follows it.

The study was published in the journal Psychological Reports (Huţanu & Holman, 2026).

Psychologist, Jeremy Dean, PhD is the founder and author of PsyBlog. He holds a doctorate in psychology from University College London and two other advanced degrees in psychology. He has been writing about scientific research on PsyBlog since 2004. View all posts by Dr Jeremy Dean.

12 common physical symptoms of anxiety (and how to ease them)

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2109 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Calm

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that anxiety doesn’t only impact your brain.
  • This is what the physical symptoms of anxiety feel like.
  • Below we’ll look at the most common physical symptoms of anxiety, why they happen, and some ways to ease them.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, MBA.

Sources indicate that anxiety doesn’t only impact your brain. Sometimes the first sign is your heart pounding for no clear reason, or a wave of nausea before a big conversation. You might feel dizzy, short of breath, or like there’s a knot in your stomach. You’re not in immediate danger, but your body is reacting as if you are.

This is what the physical symptoms of anxiety feel like. They can be alarming, especially if you don’t recognize them as anxiety right away. But your body responds this way for a reason, and understanding it can take some of the fear out of the experience.

Below we’ll look at the most common physical symptoms of anxiety, why they happen, and some ways to ease them.

Anxiety can affect your body before you've consciously registered that you're anxious at all. These are among the most common physical symptoms.

According to recent reports, 1. Racing or pounding heart (palpitations): A fast-beating or fluttering heart is one of the most recognized signs of anxiety. When your body senses a threat, it releases adrenaline, which speeds up your heart rate to pump blood to your muscles faster. This is useful when you actually need to run. Less so when you’re just checking your inbox.

2. Shortness of breath: Anxiety can make you feel like you can’t get a full breath, or like you’re slightly suffocating. Anxious breathing tends to be shallow and fast, which can lower carbon dioxide levels in the blood. This can feel scary, and anxiety is a common cause.

Industry observers note that 3. Chest tightness or pain: Muscle tension is a core part of the anxiety response and can be most noticeable in your chest, where you might feel tightness, pressure, or even mild pain. Seek emergency care if you feel sudden or severe chest pain, pain with shortness of breath or sweating, or pain spreading to the arm or jaw.

Industry observers note that 4. Dizziness or lightheadedness: Fast, shallow breathing can also leave you feeling faint or spaced out.

Recent findings suggest that 5. Tingling or numbness: Lower carbon dioxide levels in the blood can affect nerve signals and cause tingling or a pins-and-needles feeling in the hands, feet, or face. It can feel unsettling, but it’s usually short-lived. Numbness on one side of the body, sudden weakness, or trouble speaking needs urgent care.

It has been revealed that 6. Sweating: Sweating is part of the fight-flight-freeze-fawn response. Anxiety and stress can switch on your sweat glands even when you’re not hot, especially on your palms, underarms, and face.

According to recent reports, 7. Nausea or upset stomach: Your gut and brain are closely connected through the vagus nerve. When anxiety activates the stress response, digestion can slow or become disrupted. That can cause stomach upset, nausea, cramping, or an urgent need to use the bathroom.

8. Dry mouth: The stress response can slow saliva production, so many people notice a dry or sticky mouth when they’re anxious. It’s common and usually temporary, though it can make speaking feel harder than usual.

Industry observers note that 9. Muscle tension, aching, or trembling: Anxiety hormones prime your muscles to act quickly. Sustained tension without a chance to release can cause aching, stiffness, or subtle trembling, particularly in the hands, legs, or jaw.

Recent findings suggest that 10. Headaches: Tension headaches often appear with anxiety and stress. They’re typically felt as a band of pressure around your head or tension in the neck and shoulders.

11. Difficulty sleeping: Anxiety and sleep tend to make each other worse. Anxious thoughts and a body that’s physically on alert make it hard to fall or stay asleep. Poor sleep, in turn, can heighten anxiety the next day, which is how the cycle keeps going.

Industry observers note that 12. Fatigue: Anxiety takes energy because running the stress response tires the body, and poor sleep or constant tension can add to it. Ongoing anxiety can leave people feeling exhausted even without much physical effort.

It has been revealed that note: Some of the above symptoms can also point to a medical condition. If you have chest pain, trouble breathing, or symptoms that are upcoming, severe, or don’t feel like your usual anxiety, it’s best to seek medical care.

Anxiety triggers the fight-flight-freeze-fawn response (also known as the stress response). When your brain senses a threat, it activates the sympathetic nervous system and releases hormones like adrenaline and cortisol. These hormones prepare your body to respond to danger. Your heart rate increases, your breathing quickens, your muscles tense, and non-essential systems like digestion temporarily slow down.

Sources indicate that this response is useful when the threat is physical. The challenge is that your nervous system doesn’t always tell the difference between real danger and everyday stress. A tense conversation can trigger a milder version of fight-or-flight. The result is a body primed for action in situations that don’t call for it.

For most people these symptoms rise and fall with the stressful moment. When anxiety is ongoing, the symptoms can stick around longer.

There’s no instant off switch for anxiety, but these approaches can help ease physical symptoms, both in the moment and over time.

Sources indicate that controlled breathing can help calm the nervous system, and research suggests slow breathing helps many people feel calmer. Slow, gentle breathing, especially with a longer exhale, can shift your body toward the rest-and-digest (parasympathetic) system, which counteracts the stress response.

It has been revealed that try: Breathe in through your nose for four counts and out slowly for six. Repeat for a few minutes. You could also try box breathing, where you rhythmically hold your breath between inhales and exhales.

💙 When your body needs help slowing down, we have a short, breath-focused session for you: Breathe to Calm Down with Chibs Okereke.

Grounding techniques can help pull your attention out of anxious thoughts and back to the present moment. The 5–4–3–2–1 technique is a popular choice. To try it, notice:.

💙 If anxiety is pulling you out of your body, try Tamara Levitt's Grounding session on Calm, which guides you back to solid earth.

Industry observers note that exercise is well-known for easing tension, and you might find that even a short walk can take the edge off. Science agrees, with research suggesting regular exercise can help reduce anxiety symptoms over time.

Industry observers note that 💙 Not sure where to start? Try this Mindful Movement session with Mel Mah on Calm to bring gentle, non-judgmental awareness to your body as it moves.

According to recent reports, progressive muscle relaxation involves intentionally tensing and releasing muscle groups throughout the body. It’s designed to help you relax by encouraging each muscle to unclench. It doesn’t take long, with typical sessions lasting just 10 to 20 minutes.

According to recent reports, try: Start with your feet. Tense the muscles for five seconds, then release completely. Work your way up through your calves, thighs, abdomen, hands, arms, shoulders, and face. Skip tensing any area that’s injured or painful.

According to recent reports, 💙 Not keen on the tensing? This guided Body Scan Meditation moves your attention gently through the body, one area at a time, no clenching required.

Mindfulness practices train your attention to rest on the present moment rather than looping through worries about what might happen.

Recent findings suggest that mindfulness is something you build with regular practice. Over time, it can lower how strongly your body reacts to stress, which means the physical symptoms of anxiety may appear less often, or feel less intense when they do.

💙 Work through Calm’s Letting Go of Anxiety series, which is designed to help you sit with anxious feelings instead of spiraling.

Caffeine is a stimulant that can raise your heart rate and cause jitteriness, which may feel like anxiety or make it stronger.

Alcohol may feel calming at first, but it can disrupt your sleep and may make anxiety worse.

Cutting back on both is worth considering if you’re dealing with anxiety symptoms frequently.

Sources indicate that if physical symptoms of anxiety are frequent, severe, or getting in the way of daily life, talking with a doctor or mental health professional is a good next step. Effective treatments exist, including cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) and medication when appropriate. You don’t have to manage this on your own.

According to recent reports, physical symptoms are a common part of anxiety. Anxiety activates the body’s stress response, which causes real changes like a faster heart rate, muscle tension, and altered breathing. Many people with anxiety notice at least some physical symptoms alongside the mental ones. If they’re frequent or getting in the way of daily life, it’s worth talking with a doctor or mental health professional.

According to recent reports, “Anxiety attack” isn’t a clinical term, but people use it to describe anxiety that builds until it feels overwhelming, usually in response to a stressor like a looming deadline or a tense situation. The physical symptoms can include a rapid heartbeat, shortness of breath, muscle tension, trembling, dry mouth, dizziness, and nausea. These sensations can be distressing, but they tend to ease as the stressful situation passes or your anxiety settles.

💙 If you’ve experienced the symptoms of an anxiety attack, here’s how to recover and take care of yourself.

In a recent development, some anxiety symptoms feel strange because the stress response affects many parts of the body at once. For example, fast breathing can cause tingling in your hands. Or you might have a feeling of unreality or disconnection (called dissociation). Muscle tension might make it feel like your throat is closing. These varied symptoms can all have anxiety as the common cause. Of course, if they’re fresh, intense, or don’t fit your usual anxiety symptoms, it’s best to check in with a doctor.

💙 Explore lesser-known symptoms of anxiety (some might surprise you!).

When symptoms hit, the quickest relief usually comes through your breath. Make your out-breath longer than your in-breath—for example, breathing in for a count of four and out for six—and repeat for a minute or two. A longer exhale nudges your body out of the stress response and toward its rest-and-digest state.

Sources indicate that grounding works too. The 5–4–3–2–1 method has you name what you can see, touch, hear, smell, and taste, which pulls your focus out of anxious thoughts and back to the room around you.

In a recent development, anxiety can affect the body as well as the mind, and for some people the physical side is what dominates, with few or no obvious worries attached. Your stress response can switch on faster than your conscious mind registers what set it off, so a racing heart or churning stomach can come before, or even without, any clear anxious thought.

These physical symptoms are still part of anxiety, and the same tools, like slow breathing and grounding, can help calm them. If they’re new or unexplained, see a doctor to rule out other causes, such as thyroid problems, heart rhythm changes, or the effects of caffeine or medication.

Recent findings suggest that it’s worth speaking with a doctor if your anxiety symptoms are new and unexplained, severe or getting worse, or affecting your day-to-day life. Some symptoms, like chest pain, shortness of breath, and heart palpitations, should be evaluated medically to rule out other causes, even if you suspect anxiety. A doctor can also refer you to a mental health professional if that would help.

If you’re experiencing sudden or severe chest pain, or chest pain with sweating, shortness of breath, or pain spreading to the arm or jaw, seek emergency care.

Sources indicate that A worry loop is a cycle where anxiety feeds on itself. One anxious thought leads to another, and the more attention it gets, the stronger it grows.

Recent findings suggest that for example, an anxious thought sets off a physical sensation, that sensation becomes the focus of fresh worry (“Why is my heart racing? What’s wrong with me?”), and the worry drives more symptoms.

Breaking the loop usually means addressing both the mind and the body. You can calm the body directly with breathing and grounding, or use cognitive approaches like CBT to interrupt the thought patterns that keep the cycle going.

Tech Report: 17 Ideas From Educators to Start the School Year With Joy
