⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • What a beautiful way to start the school year, not only because it feels good, but also because science reveals that joy is linked closely to learning, as well as individual and collective flourishing.
  • We asked Greater Good Education newsletter readers to share a favorite strategy for bringing joy into their school or classroom at the beginning of the year.
  • According to recent reports, laura M.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Joy! What a beautiful way to start the school year, not only because it feels good, but also because science reveals that joy is linked closely to learning, as well as individual and collective flourishing.

We asked Greater Good Education newsletter readers to share a favorite strategy for bringing joy into their school or classroom at the beginning of the year. The responses did not disappoint! Here are a few that span ages, time commitments, and subject areas.

According to recent reports, laura M. (Newark, DE): “Dancing it out” is a strategy that has been shown to reduce stress, release held feelings, and encourage kids to be in the moment. Providing time for activities like dancing is often seen as an “extra.” Building this activity into our weekly schedule has become a favorite stress-relieving activity—adding tremendous joy and connection between children and children and children and teachers.

Related Greater Good in Education (GGiE) practices: The World Is a Dance; Getting to Know Each Other Through Dance; We Are Better Dancing Together.

Josh (New Haven, CT): Every Monday morning meeting, students greet each other by asking, “What brought you joy (made you smile/laugh) over the weekend?”.

It has been revealed that laura H.: At the end of the day, with second graders, we share the activity from our day that brought the most joy. If I wasn’t there for it (i.e., recess, music, art, PE), I ask them to include details.

Related GGiE practices: Noticing Kindness; Giving Thanks; Looking for Gratitude in School; Sharing Gratitude Stories.

Emi (Lobitos, Peru): Identifying forms of enchantment—I use this approach in our Women & Water Program. It’s an all-girls (ages 3–16) surf, science, and storytelling program based in Lobitos, a tiny fishing village in Northern Peru. We use “enchantment” as a way for young girls to foster their curiosity, creativity, and care for themselves, peers, community, and the coastal environment. We do this through photography (taking “macro” photos of small, wondrous things found in their environment, like a flower petal, a beetle, etc.). Or we do this in surfing—the girls notice the “awe” of riding the energy of a leftover storm until it crashes into the sand. These girls also made this song after an oil spill that rocked our community about two years ago.

Related GGiE practices: Meaningful Photos for Students; Mindfully Finding Awe in Nature.

Recent findings suggest that angela (Pleasant Hill, CA): I am a school counselor and with my students who experience anxiety we use sidewalk chalk to write positive welcoming messages and pictures in front of our school. It makes others feel welcomed and helps my students feel connected to our school. They even told me it helps get them to school the first couple of days knowing they would see their chalk messages.

Related GGiE practices: Designing the Classroom to Promote Kindness; Kindness Buddy; Awe-Inspiring Affirmations.

Lorien (St. Louis, MO): Have a “Would you rather…?” question on the whiteboard at the start of class—the funnier the better. Students put a checkmark next to their choice. It’s a fun way to welcome the “whole student self” into the classroom, not just their “learner selves.” Sometimes we talk about it, but often, we don’t.

Related GGiE practice: Superstar.

Recent findings suggest that pam (Muscogee County, GA): To kick off the year, my eighth graders design and build a cardboard maze that guides three different rolling spheres from start to finish. Working in teams of four, students sketch a plan, build it with cardboard and hot glue, test it, and revise their design. Nothing works perfectly the first time. Students swiftly discover that failure is a useful part of the design process. By the end of the week, teams are cheering when a ping pong ball, golf ball, or rubber ball finally makes it all the way through, and that joy comes from earning it through real trial and error. It sets the tone for the whole year: Engineering is a process of building, testing, and improving.

Kimberly (Williamsport, PA): Something that I introduce during the first week of classes is our 3 Good Things or 3 Little Wins Padlet. Each week students post about three good things or little wins they had during the week. Before the first post, we discuss why it is key to celebrate these things, no matter how small (e.g., a good cup of coffee!). We also discuss the impact that reflecting on these things has on our physical and psychological well-being. Each week I also post my wins for the week and comment on student posts as well. It creates a wonderful community!

Related GGIE practices: Three Good Things for Students; Gratitude Journals.

Jonah (Duxbury, VT): As a high school English teacher, the first writing assignment I give to students asks them to choose a (clean) song that represents them and tell me why they feel connected to this song. I then make a playlist including all the students’ songs, and play it during work times or use it to play students’ walk-up song on special days like birthdays.

Related GGiE practices: Creating Musical Playlists for the Classroom; Prosocial Music Hub (13 practices to bring music into the classroom).

It has been revealed that joe (Bridgeport, CT): Students interact with each other as they navigate around the crowded classroom, connected only by cake-pop sticks balanced between each other using only their index finger. Fosters concentration, cooperation, joyful failures, interconnectedness, and intimacy without actually touching one another.

Related GGiE practice: 1-2-3 Clap.

Sources indicate that david (San Antonio, TX): For my introductory geology class, I work with the students to develop rules for a “rock-rock-rock” (igneous-sedimentary-metamorphic) version of “rock-paper-scissors.” Students develop the necessary hand signals and the action verbs that say what beats what. Once we have the rules established, the students engage in a best two out of three to crown the class champion. Branded university swag is available for the winners, and everyone gets a candy treat for participating.

Related GGiE practice: Making Science Meaningful.

Susan (St. Paul, MN): I ask students to tell the rest of the class their name and a ridiculous lie about themselves—the more absurd the better. There’s always good-natured laughter and encouragement.

Related GGiE practice: Truth or Tale.

Industry observers note that harry (Hailey, ID): I work to end every “session” (class, administration meeting, faculty meeting, etc.) with laughter, whether incited by me or coming from someone else. That moment becomes the punctuation.

Related GGiE practices: Share a Laugh; The SEL 3 Signature Practices.

Paige (Seattle, WA): About the second or third week of classes (graduate and undergraduate students) we begin doing this ritual that we do a few times during the semester: “The joy of contribution…I see this in you!” Students take turns identifying something they have genuinely observed in another student in the cohort/class: “One leadership capacity I see developing in you is________, because I watched you ________.” The BECAUSE matters.

Explore compassion, self-compassion, and awe with educators around the world.

Examples I have heard from pre-certified teachers and principals: “I see courage building in you because I have watched you ask questions the rest of us were afraid to ask.” OR, “I see you really owning belongingness as you consistently notice who is outside the conversation and what is happening around us as you read the room.”.

Related GGiE practices: I See You. Everyone Matters; Behind Your Back.

Industry observers note that lorien (St. Louis, MO): I use a guided visualization to prompt students to think about what joyful teaching, joyful learning, and joyful interactions look like, sound like, and feel like. It makes what we’re doing much more explicit, and it helps me know what they want from me and vice versa.

Related GGiE practice: Designing the Classroom to Promote Kindness.

Angela (McMinnville, OR): A non-dominant hand drawing activity that gets us all out of our “perfection” thinking and into being learners…and laughing.

Related GGiE practice: Drawing as a Way to Manage Emotions.

Milton (San Diego, CA): As the associate principal, I stand out in front of the school in the morning with a MAJOR SMILE sign on and greet the students with a “Good morning & have a great day!” Some students like a fist bump or handshake as well.

Related GGiE practice: Making Families Feel Welcome.

Donna (Arkansas): “JOY” is the grounding rhythm that closes every day, honoring the joyful moments that JUST happened, recognizing community attunement through something an OTHER person did, and celebrating internal self-efficacy via something YOU did. Each person is free to select whichever letter resonates with them to share. We pass a rainstick around the circle; once it is turned to let its gentle cascade settle into silence, the person holding it speaks. This tactile ritual and quiet sound not only brings a profound sense of calm to the transition from classroom to home, but it also serves as a gentle reminder to carry those reflections outward.

Related GGiE practices: Inspiring Virtue With Moral Beauty; Stories of Moral Beauty; Noticing Kindness; Nurturing Students’ Wonder and Curiosity.

In a recent development, thank you to all of the educators in the Greater Good community who shared activities for bringing joy into schools and classrooms. We received many, many more than we could share here. Even in the face of incredible challenges, you are bringing so much joy to your students and their families, your colleagues, and yourself. May you all have a joyful start to the new school year!

In a recent development, we look forward to our next post in the From Our Readers series that will focus on building community through connection and belonging. Want to share an activity? Fill out this quick form! Not only will you strengthen our community, you’ll be entered into a drawing for a free self-paced course or a spot in our Flourishing Spring community of practice!

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Emiglia brand identity by Another Collective: a hand-cut red wordmark, script lettering and windowed packs for a Porto pasta maker and bar.

In a recent development, the rebrand unifies two sides of one business, the Pasta Fresca factory and the Pasta Bar, under a single voice. The studio kept the illustrations that were already part of the brand and built a stronger typographic layer around them, so tradition reads as confidence rather than nostalgia. Red does most of the work, a warm tomato red against cream, with deep burgundy as the second voice. The pasta itself reveals up everywhere, nests on steel trays, boxes with windows, trays stacked in the fridge, and the identity treats that craft as the subject, not the backdrop.

The wordmark is the whole idea in one gesture. Chunky, rounded letters with soft terminals and slightly uneven edges, the kind of letterforms that look cut by hand rather than drawn on screen. It sits huge and flat, filling the width of posters and packs, with the round counter of the A and the arched legs of the M giving it a warmth no geometric sans could carry.

Sources indicate that under it, a loose handwritten script spells out Pasta Fresca or Pasta Bar, and a small typewriter-style caps line carries the facts: massas, molhos, refeiÃ§Ãµes prontas, kits. The order never changes. Wordmark first, script second, small caps last, and the same order repeats on boxes, menus, bags and tees.

The packaging puts the pasta on display. Red boxes carry a clear window so the shapes inside do the talking, with a small illustrated label on each box. Foil trays stack in the fridge under bold red labels, and the same red runs across paper bags, sauce jars and the weekly menu posters.

In the bar, the system turns physical. Menus in red and burgundy sit on steel counters, plates carry a thin red rim with the name set small, and the staff tees carry the house line, Thereâs No Cream In Carbonara, flanked by two small Emiglia badges. From packaging to signage to menus, every piece pulls in the same direction.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • In a recent development, just five of the 56 lots offered Thursday night failed to sell, for a slim buy-in rate of 9%.
  • Roy Lichtenstein, Small Wall Explosion, 1965 Courtesy Christie's Images Ltd.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that wrapping up this autumn’s week of marquee evening sales in Upcoming York, Christie’s 21st-century auction on Thursday (19 November) proved rather lacklustre, bringing in $117.7m ($145.9m with fees). That tally fell short of Christie’s pre-sale expectations, which do not account for fees, and projected a total take in the range of $126m to $192m. It was also a lower result compared to the auction house’s last two equivalent sales in New York—namely the $132m ($162.6m with fees) generated across 42 lots last May, and the $99.5m ($123.5m with fees) brought by 45 lots one year ago.

In a recent development, just five of the 56 lots offered Thursday night failed to sell, for a slim buy-in rate of 9%. Two lots were withdrawn at the last moment, including a Jeff Koons sculpture estimated to bring between $3m and $5m. Twenty-four lots were backed by third-party guarantees and nine were backed fully by house guarantees, representing around 59% of all the works offered. Auction records for three artists were broken over the course of the night.

Roy Lichtenstein, Small Wall Explosion, 1965 Courtesy Christie's Images Ltd.

Business began with a bang at Christie’s Rockefeller Center salesroom: the first lot was Roy Lichtenstein’s Small Wall Explosion (1965), executed in porcelain enamel on steel and perforated steel relief to mimic the Ben-Day dot style from his paintings. It sold to a telephone bidder for $625,000 ($800,000 with fees). From an edition of six, it hailed from the collection of Antonio Homem Sonnabend, the adopted son of the late and legendary dealer and collector Ileana Sonnabend (1914-2007) and who ran his mother’s namesake gallery in its waning years. Antonio Homem died earlier this year, at age 86.

Another of the 19 Sonnabend lots from Sonnabend, Ashley Bickerton’s expansive wall relief Commercial Piece #3 (1990), covered with gallery and fashion-house logos and comprised of anodised aluminium, wood, leather, acrylic and rubber, sold for $120,000 ($153,600 with fees). Both the Lichtenstein and the Bickerton were backed by third-party guarantees.

Andy Warhol, Campbell's Soup Can (Turkey Noodle), 1962 Courtesy Christie's Images Ltd.

Sources indicate that price points for the Sonnabend trove zoomed higher with Andy Warhol’s iconicand hand painted Campbell’s Soup Can (Turkey Noodle) (1962), which sold for $7.3m ($9m with fees) against an estimate of $6m to $8m. Another Lichtenstein, the painting Large Spool (1963)—a razor-sharp depiction of the titular object that has been featured in multiple gallery and museum exhibitions—squeaked by on the tails of a third-party guarantee at $7m ($8.6m with fees) against an ambitious estimate of $10m to $15m.

Still in the Sonnabend lots, Jeff Koons’s toy-like Hulk (Friends) (2004-12), in polychromed bronze and standing nearly 6ft tall, found a fresh home for $3.3m ($4.1m with fees). And another Warhol, redolent with Hollywood celebrity, The Kiss (Bela Lugosi) (1963) in silkscreen ink on white paper, sold to another telephone bidder for $3.3m ($4.6m with fees).

A petite Jasper Johns oil painting on cardboard, Numbers (1957), measuring just 8.5in by 6in and rich in shades of grey, made $2.6m ($3.2m with fees). It was featured in the artist’s first solo exhibition at the Leo Castelli Gallery in 1958. Ileana Sonnabend acquired it from the Castelli Gallery in 1959, the same year of her divorce from Leo Castelli.

The Sonnabend group of 19 lots, including three examples of key 20th-century French decorative art—among them a Jean Prouvé Trapéze table from around 1956 that hit $1.3m ($1.6m with fees)—all in tallied $33.3m ($41.9m with fees), compared to Christie’s pre-sale expectations for the group of $35m to $55m.

Illustrious consignor names continued with works from the collection of the late Museum of Modern Art trustee and patron Agnes Gund sold to benefit the Gund Art Foundation. They included Robert Ryman’s immaculate, small, square all-over white composition Untitled (1961), which brought $2.9m ($3.6m with fees). Vija Celmins’s photorealist oil painting Untitled (Ocean) (1990), which featured in the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art’s traveling retrospective in 2018-2020, went for $5.7m ($7.1m with fees) against an estimate of $6m to $8m. It also was backed by a third-party guarantee.

Vija Celmins, Untitled (Ocean), 1990 Courtesy Christie's Images Ltd.

Industry observers note that gund acquired Alexander Calder’s hanging metal mobile The Eye in the Black (1963) from the Perls Galleries in Fresh York in in 1967. On Thursday night it went to an online bidder for $2.8m ($3.5m with fees). Cindy Sherman’s Untitled Film Still #5 (1977), also widely exhibited and written about by major critics, sold for $320,000 ($409,6000 with fees). Gund had acquired it at Sotheby’s New York in November 2000 for a hammer price of $75,000.

Gund’s contemporary taste bordered on the encyclopaedic, as evidenced by an early Robert Rauschenberg work, Untitled (Gold Painting) (1953), in gold leaf on fabric and paper collage on canvas. The diminutive work, at 8in by 8in, fetched a sizeable sum, $1.7m ($2.1m with fees). Gund acquired it at Sotheby’s in New York in May 1994 for a $55,000 hammer price.

A modestly scaled Lichtenstein work on paper in coloured pencil, graphite and paper collage, Artist’s Studio with Model (Study) (1974), sold to the art adviser Ralph DeLuca for $950,000 ($1.2m with fees).

Jim Nutt, Loom, 1999 Courtesy Christie's Images Ltd.

According to recent reports, A standout from the Gund trove, a work she described as “my Mona Lisa”, was another modestly-scaled work, by Jim Nutt, founder of Chicago’s Hairy Who group. Titled Loom (1999) and measuring 15in by 14in, the portrait of a woman with a penetrating gaze set a new auction record for Nutt’s work when it more than doubled its high estimate of $350,000 and ultimately sold for $850,000 ($1m with fees). The ten lots sold to benefit Gund’s charitable foundation tallied $20.3m ($25.7m with fees), squarely within Christie’s pre-sale estimate of $16m to $24m.

In a recent development, though not part of the Gund Art Foundation offerings, Alice Neel’s double portrait David and Catherine Saalfield (1982) hailed from Agnes Gund’s family and brought $1.6m ($2m with fees). Gund acquired it directly from the artist the year it was painted—not surprising since the sitters were her young adult children.

Alice Neel, David and Catherine Saalfield, 1982 Courtesy Christie's Images Ltd.

The appeal of buying a piece of the legacy of storied dealers and collectors did not fare so well for a work that had belonged to the late gallerist Marian Goodman. Bidding on Gerhard Richter’s Abstraktes Bild (1990) stalled at $5.7m, against an estimate of $6m to $8m, and the lot failed to sell. As Richter’s longtime Upcoming York dealer, Goodman acquired the lushly surfaced squeegee painting directly from the artist and exhibited the painting in a gallery group show the year it was made. (A second Richter from another consignor fared better, with that somewhat larger Abstraktes Bild from 1991 bringing $7.6m, or $9.4m with fees.).

Among the works from more anonymous consignors, Richard Prince’s famous Nurse series made a splash when Everglade Nurse (2003), executed in acrylic and inkjet print on canvas, sold for $3.1m ($3.9m with fees). It last sold at Sotheby’s New York in November 2008 for $3.4m with fees, a rather flat return after 18 years.

Sources indicate that large-scale paintings destined to test living room wall space were also in evidence with Christopher Wool’s untitled black-and-white abstraction from 2009, measuring more than 8ft tall. It brought $2m ($2.5m with fees). George Condo’s more than 9ft-wide Double Heads in Blue and Silver (2014), realised $2.4m ($3m with fees). The Condo hailed from the collection of Stefan Edlis and his wife Gael Neeson, who donated 44 works cumulatively valued at more than $400m to the Art Institute of Chicago in 2015.

The top lot of the evening, unsurprisingly, was Jean-Michel Basquiat’s quirky and text-rich composition, Untitled (Leonardo and his Five Grotesque Heads) (1983), which hammered to another anonymous telephone bidder for $28m ($32.8m with fees) against a sky-high estimate of $30m to $50m.

Jean-Michel Basquiat, Untitled (Leonardo and His Five Grotesque Heads), 1983 Courtesy Christie's Images Ltd.

Evidently inspired by Leonardo da Vinci’s 1493 pen-and-ink drawing on paper A man tricked by Gypsies (also known as Five grotesque heads), from the Royal Collection Trust at Windsor Castle in London, Basquiat’s freestyle interpretation in oil stick and acrylic against a burnt orange background crackles with the artist’s terse way with wordplay and actually features eight heads in all.

Industry observers note that measuring 80in by 80in, the painting has no exhibition history, at least none acknowledged in Christie’s online catalogue entry—though it was included in the Whitney Museum of American Art’s 1992 Basquiat retrospective. The catalogue entry for the Whitney exhibition listed the owner as Zurich’s Bruno Bischofberger, an early and notable champion of the artist. It last sold at auction at Sotheby’s London in October 2005, when it was the top lot at £736,000 ($1.3m) including fees against an estimate of £400,000 to £600,000. Sotheby’s at the time identified the buyer as “US Trade” and the current consignor acquired it from that entity in 2006.

Julia Jo, One Fell Swoop, 2026 Courtesy Christie's Images Ltd.

In a recent development, the evening ended on a sweet note with Julia Jo’s large-scale abstraction One Fell Swoop (2026), donated to benefit the Fresh York-based Coalition for the Homeless. It set a new auction record for Jo’s work, fetching $320,000 ($409,600 with fees). (The night’s other new auction record was for the work of the Spanish artist Antonio Santín.).

Sources indicate that apart from that feeling, the outlook was not as rosy. “It’s been a very long week, with a lot of art, and I think people are tired,” DeLuca remarked. “The theme of the week is that estimates are a little aspirational.”.

The long week’s last burst of activity will be a pair of day sales at Christie’s on Friday (20 November), after which the US art industry will mark a pause to observe Thanksgiving before migrating south for Art Basel Miami Beach.

  • Sources indicate that when winter hits, it’s no surprise that many of us ditch our workout routines and reach for the hot cocoa instead.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, MBA.

Ah winter. It’s dark out, cold, and there’s a biting wind whistling down the street. Wanna grab your running shoes and start pounding the pavement? We didn’t think so.

Sources indicate that when winter hits, it’s no surprise that many of us ditch our workout routines and reach for the hot cocoa instead. And while it’s normal to feel a little unmotivated as the weather shifts, winter exercise doesn’t just help us stay fit, it can help us manage stress and keep our energy levels up. Exercising during the winter can also boost your mood — which can be super important if the cold temps and long nights get you down.

Staying active during the colder months doesn’t have to mean pushing yourself to the max or braving harsh conditions if that’s not your thing. There are plenty of ways to make winter workouts more fun and enjoyable. With a few small adjustments, you could soon start to notice how much better you feel during this time of year.

Winter can feel tough on our bodies and minds, with shorter days, less sunlight, and colder temperatures. These changes can make us feel more tired, sluggish, or even a little down. This is especially true if you get the “winter blues” or seasonal affective disorder (SAD), where the lack of sunlight means your mood and energy levels take a dive. (Currently in a funk? These nine tips can help shift a low mood.).

Exercise can play a big role in managing these wintertime challenges because moving your body can trigger the release of natural mood-boosting chemicals, fight stress and help you to think more clearly.

Getting active in the winter can also improve sleep and help regulate your sleep-wake cycle, so even if you’re feeling thrown off by the longer nights and early darkness, exercise can help you get the rest you need to start your mornings on the right foot. Cue a good mood and steady energy throughout the day too!

Finding the right workouts for winter doesn’t mean you have to head out into the cold — but you can if you want to!

Recent findings suggest that there are so many options you can enjoy indoors—even on the chilliest days—depending on what feels best for you. These are ten great winter workouts that’ll keep your body moving, boost your energy, and help you feel your best.

According to recent reports, ideal for warming up stiff muscles and relieving stress, plus, you don’t need much space or equipment — just a mat or a soft carpet. Check out online classes and videos for beginner to expert workouts.

It has been revealed that use dumbbells, resistance bands, or your body weight — or grab a can of tomatoes from your cupboard! Try exercises like lunges, squats, and push-ups indoors, so you can maintain or build muscle without braving the cold.

If you have access to equipment, enjoy cardio without the cold. These machines let you set a steady pace, so you can up your fitness without overdoing things.

Dancing is great fun, but it’s also a fantastic cardio workout. Try a virtual dance class or follow a YouTube tutorial for a quick, energetic session to get your heart pumping and your face smiling. You can even invite your friends over for an 80s aerobic dance party and dress the part too!

💙 Only have five minutes? Add Mel Mah’s Dance Break to your routine.

In a recent development, if you’re up for some fresh air, bundle up and head out for a winter hike. It’s a great way to explore nature, and the cold will likely feel refreshing once you start moving. Just be sure to dress in layers and check the weather before heading out.

It has been revealed that ice skating might look effortless, but it’s a solid workout for your legs and core. Many local rinks are open during the winter, and even if you’re a beginner, it can help you stay active and try something fresh. Make it social and see if your coworkers want to join you for a weekly session after work to help keep you motivated.

With the right winter gear, running outside can be invigorating. Layer up in moisture-wicking clothes to keep comfortable, and watch for icy spots to stay safe.

💙 Try Mel Mah’s Mindful Run to experience 20 minutes of running with intention.

If you have snow where you live, give cross-country skiing a try. It’s a full-body workout that’s low impact, making it gentle on the joints and awesome for the eyes. It’s the perfect way to soak in the beautiful scenery and the fresh air of a winter wonderland.

According to recent reports, pilates strengthens core muscles and improves flexibility, and like yoga, it doesn’t need much space or equipment. Follow an online session to get a workout that supports your whole body, or practice some basic moves on your own.

Combine bursts of high-intensity exercise with rest intervals to get a lot of action in a short space of time. These workouts can be easy to do at home and don’t require any equipment, just a little space for a few dynamic moves.

Recent findings suggest that once you've picked a few workouts, the next hurdle is getting yourself to do them. We get it. These six tips may help you stay motivated and safe while you exercise in colder weather.

Start by setting small, achievable goals that feel right for the season. Winter can be more about maintaining your fitness and feeling good rather than pushing for big gains or intense goals.

Decide on manageable goals like working out three times a week or moving for 20 minutes a day so they feel achievable, and don’t forget to leave room for flexibility.

And when you’re really struggling, aim to just get started. Once you’ve got your sneakers on, you might find it easier to begin that workout. Be gentle with yourself and listen to what feels best for your body and mind — some days might feel easier than others, and that’s completely normal. These seven tips can help you push through a workout mentally.

In a recent development, decide on a time that suits your energy levels and lifestyle—like in the morning, during lunch, or in the evening—and stay consistent. When you make exercise a regular part of your day, you’re less likely to have to force yourself to do it.

And remember, it’s okay if some days don’t go as planned — just get back to your routine the next day.

If you plan to workout outside, layer up your clothing to stay comfortable and dry as it can make winter exercise much more enjoyable.

Sources indicate that start with a breathable, moisture-wicking base layer, add a mid-layer for insulation, and finish with a wind-proof, waterproof outer for protection from the elements. Add gloves, a hat, and warm socks to keep your fingers and toes cozy and safe, too.

Even if you’re just heading out to a studio down the street, make sure to dress warmly so that once you’re done sweating, you don’t catch a cold.

Cold weather makes muscles tighter, which can increase your risk of injury. To help prevent this, start every workout with a warm-up, especially if you’re outside. Spend 5–10 minutes doing dynamic stretches or gentle movements like walking in place, jumping jacks, or arm circles to get your blood flowing and prepare your muscles.

A good warm-up loosens up your body, reduces stiffness, and gets you ready for the main part of your workout.

When you venture out for your exercise, see if a friend wants to join you so you can catch up while you work out or grab a coffee after a class. The shared experience can boost your mood and keep you going, even on days when it’s tough to get moving.

Sources indicate that no real-life takers? Look for online fitness classes, join a virtual exercise challenge, or check if a friend wants to work out “together” by video call. Virtual communities can create accountability, which can help you stick to your goals. And who knows, you might even make a new friend out of it, too!

Sources indicate that staying active in winter deserves a celebration! Treat yourself when you hit small milestones — have a seasonal-spiced herbal tea after a workout, click “buy” on that upcoming piece of workout gear you’ve been eyeing for months now, or become your own DJ and make a fun, feel-good playlist to exercise to.

Industry observers note that rewards can make the experience more enjoyable and give you something to look forward to. Even simple treats, like watching an episode of a favorite show or getting into comfy clothes post-workout, can help you recognize your efforts and build positive vibes around your winter workouts.

It can be tempting to start your outdoor exercise at a sprint because it’s so cold out, but that might risk stiffness and injury in cold muscles.

You’ll need to warm up first, so begin with 5–10 minutes of dynamic movements to gradually increase your heart rate and warm up your muscles.

If stepping out in sub-freezing temperatures to do your gentle movements doesn’t sound appealing (and we don’t blame you,) warm up inside before you head outdoors.

During colder months, there are lots of ways you can stay in shape and boost your mood by getting active:.

Stay warm by working out indoors.

Whether you venture down the block to the gym or stay at home, these indoor exercises need minimal space and equipment.

Brave the cold and get outdoors.

It might be chilly, but there’s still joy and beauty in the winter — and exercise options available whether you’re close to nature or city-based. Make sure you’ve got proper gear and choose safe paths.

To prevent winter injuries, a few simple but key steps can help you take care of yourself.

Dress warmly in layered, moisture-wicking clothes to keep muscles warm and flexible. Make sure you warm up with gentle cardio or dynamic stretching to get blood flowing, as cold muscles are prone to strain.

Recent findings suggest that when outdoors, avoid icy or uneven surfaces and use footwear with a good grip for stability. Most importantly, listen to your body — if something feels off, don't push through it. Instead, adapt to your needs and take it day by day.

Recent findings suggest that strangely, we tend to feel less thirsty in winter, even when we’re losing water during exercise. So stay aware and follow these easy tips to maintain hydration and support your body's performance and recovery.

According to recent reports, keep a water bottle handy and take small sips throughout your workout. You might even set reminders to drink water before, during, and after exercise. Also, if cold water is unappealing, opt for warm drinks like herbal tea or water with lemon to stay hydrated and warm.

If you’re feeling low because of the dark days and winter weather, you can combat winter blues with exercise, even if it’s just a little bit of movement. That’s because getting active can boost your mood and energy by releasing natural feel-good chemicals.

Set yourself a routine to get out for a walk in the fresh air (and sunshine, when the sun shows its face) and gather your friends or family to make it a fun, social occasion, too — which can also help you stay accountable.

It has been revealed that prefer to stay indoors? Counteract shorter days by sitting near a window or using light therapy to lift your mood, and join a virtual fitness class for encouragement and connection. Be kind to yourself — every bit of self-care can help make winter brighter and healthier. (Take a look at these 20 self-care practices for inspo).

💡 Key Takeaways

  • It has been revealed that so many of us live with jam-packed daily schedules, constantly juggling our responsibilities to work, family, and friends.
  • World Meditation Day, a day dedicated to uplifting the power of meditation and promoting regular acts of self-care, is the perfect opportunity to shift your focus back onto your mental well-being by prioritizing meditation and connecting with yourself through the hustle and bustle of everyday life.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, CDCES, MBA.

It has been revealed that so many of us live with jam-packed daily schedules, constantly juggling our responsibilities to work, family, and friends. The never-ending to-do lists can wear us down, and any remaining free time we may have is spent zoning out in front of the TV or scrolling on our phones. Taking time to pause, breathe, and connect with ourselves may feel impossible, so sometimes we need an extra push.

World Meditation Day, a day dedicated to uplifting the power of meditation and promoting regular acts of self-care, is the perfect opportunity to shift your focus back onto your mental well-being by prioritizing meditation and connecting with yourself through the hustle and bustle of everyday life.

World Meditation Day is held each year on December 21. It’s dedicated to the practice of meditation, a technique that’s been used for centuries to nurture a sense of calm and inner peace. The day is designed to promote awareness about the benefits of meditation and encourage people to bring the practice into their daily lives to restore a sense of balance and clarity.

It has been revealed that originating in India around 1500 B.C., meditation initially combined spirituality with the religious and philosophical life of Hindu and Buddhist traditions. The aim was to cultivate mindfulness and a deep, inward connection to the divine — or the inner self.

Meditation practices spread across Asia and to the Western world, where techniques were adapted to make them relevant to the unique spiritual, therapeutic, and practical needs of each culture.

During World Meditation Day on December 21, people around the world acknowledge and celebrate the rich history and evolution of meditation. The day reminds us of meditation's ancient roots and its wide-ranging health and well-being benefits.

In December 2024, meditation got its own spot on the global calendar when the United Nations General Assembly adopted a resolution proclaiming December 21 as World Meditation Day. The resolution invites people everywhere to observe the day in a way that suits them and to help raise awareness of the benefits of meditation.

Despite a long history, meditation is becoming more and more important in the modern world.

Stress reduction: Regular meditation may help decrease our level of stress hormones, like cortisol, helping to reduce stress and leading to improved mental health and decreased risk of stress-related diseases.

It has been revealed that enhanced concentration: Meditation can help train the brain to focus for longer periods, which can enhance productivity at work. This improved attention span can be extremely beneficial when we’re constantly bombarded with distractions and information.

Promotion of overall well-being: Meditation has been linked with many physical health benefits, including lowered blood pressure, reduced anxiety, and better immune system response.

Sources indicate that contribution to global harmony: By cultivating personal peace and mindfulness, meditation can encourage positive interactions. In this way, World Meditation Day helps promote unity across different cultures and communities.

Whether you’re an experienced meditator or fresh to the practice, taking part in World Meditation Day can be a fulfilling, enriching experience.

Many organizations host global meditation sessions on World Meditation Day. Connect with thousands of others around the world who are practicing meditation. This can be a powerful experience, emphasizing the unity and collective energy of the human experience.

Seek out workshops, either in-person or online, which can expose you to different meditation techniques and enhance your personal practice.

Plan or attend a group meditation session at a local park, community center, or virtually. Group meditations can help build a sense of community and shared purpose, making the practice more enjoyable and impactful.

In a recent development, if you prefer solitude, dedicate specific time on World Meditation Day for your personal meditation practice. Create a special session where you focus on your intentions, gratitude, or personal peace, allowing you to connect with yourself on a deeper level.

According to recent reports, it’s always nice to share the positives in life, so why not spread the love by sharing your meditation experience on social media? Use the hashtag #WorldMeditationDay to join the trend. This can help spread awareness about the day and encourage others to get involved.

Here are a few ways you can enhance and deepen your own meditation practice in honor of World Meditation Day.

In a recent development, if you’re latest to meditation or prefer a structured approach, guided meditations can be helpful. An experienced practitioner directs you through spoken instructions, often accompanied by calming music or natural sounds. Try a guided meditation to help you focus, explore different techniques, or maintain meditation discipline.

💙 Add the Daily Calm to your meditation routine, for a new 10-minute guided meditation each day.

Establishing a specific area in your home for meditation can significantly improve the quality of your practice and be a reminder to pause and reconnect with yourself. Make your space quiet, comfortable, and free from distractions. You can even personalize it with items that promote relaxation and peace such as cushions, candles, incense, or soothing artwork.

Recent findings suggest that explore different styles of meditation to help keep your practice fresh and engaging. Beyond the commonly known mindfulness and transcendental meditation, you might try types like zen, vipassana, or heart-centered meditation, which offer their own benefits.

💙 Dive into Practices: Meditation for Beginners, a 7-day guided meditation series, to expand your practice.

Meditation doesn't always have to be a separate part of your day. Add mindfulness techniques into daily activities like walking, eating, or even during breaks at work to help you stay present throughout the day.

💙 Explore how meditation can be practiced during your 9-5 with the Mindfulness at Work series.

Recent findings suggest that engaging with fellow meditators can provide support, motivation, and deeper insight into your practice. Look for online forums and local groups that offer meetings, discussions, and shared meditation sessions, which can be particularly enriching.

💙 Join the Daily Calm Community on Facebook to engage with other meditators and share questions and experiences from your practice.

Sources indicate that while meditation has been around for centuries, the origin of World Meditation Day isn’t clear. World Meditation Day has been observed for many years and has grown in popularity across the globe in recent years as more people have embraced the practices and recognized their benefits.

Industry observers note that we celebrate World Meditation Day to recognize and promote the many benefits of meditation. These benefits can include reducing stress, improving concentration, enhancing emotional health, and building a sense of peace and community. The day encourages newly introduced and seasoned meditators to dedicate time to their meditation practices and to positively impact personal and global well-being.

If you’re organizing a meditation event in your community, a few simple steps can help make your event a success.

Start by choosing a suitable location such as a community center, park, or an online platform.

Next, decide on the format of the event — for example, a guided meditation, silent meditation, or a workshop with a knowledgeable instructor.

Promote the event through local community boards, social media, and word of mouth.

Provide clear instructions about what participants should bring (such as mats or cushions) and what they should expect from the event.

It has been revealed that there are many virtual meditation resources available to help guide your practice. Explore Calm’s variety of guided meditations, which are suitable for all sorts of different levels and goals, such as stress reduction, better sleep, or increased focus. There’s even a handy beginner series to help you get started, and blog posts on how to meditate if you need a few tips. These resources can make it easy to bring meditation into your daily routine, no matter where in the world you are or how experienced you are.

#160759. How to Build a Habit by Starting Ridiculously Small

📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1327 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Berkeley ↗ Open Full Page

How to Build a Habit by Starting Ridiculously Small

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1327 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Berkeley

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In 75 minutes a week, I can reap the benefits of listening to uplifting music, getting out in nature, and getting morning outdoor light, all while exercising my dogs and getting enough cardio to measurably improve my health, happiness, and longevity.
  • It has been revealed that then, in 2020, I got into a real running habit.
  • Then the Orange Theory studio down the street from me closed.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I love the idea of being a runner.

In 75 minutes a week, I can reap the benefits of listening to uplifting music, getting out in nature, and getting morning outdoor light, all while exercising my dogs and getting enough cardio to measurably improve my health, happiness, and longevity.

It has been revealed that then, in 2020, I got into a real running habit. I’ve told the longer version of this story on a TED stage, so I won’t repeat it here, but suffice it to say that I did it by doing very, very little running. When I started going to Orange Theory classes, I kept running. I sustained this exercise habit for six years, through breast cancer and many other difficult life events.

Then the Orange Theory studio down the street from me closed. I tried other studios, but the classes I like are impossible to get into.

So I embraced working out on my own and getting back to running outside with my dogs. I bought very heavy dumbbells and set up a home gym on our covered porch. I spent an inordinate amount of time choosing a destination race, enlisting my adult children to join me. I set up a training schedule on my Garmin watch, and when I didn’t stick to it, I used Nike Run Club. I made a running playlist. I bought a double running leash.

Friends, I have done four runs in three weeks.

According to recent reports, I know what I need to do. It’s so wildly unambitious that I’m embarrassed to tell you. I just need to get dressed to run first thing in the morning, put my dogs on their double leash, put on my playlist, and walk out the door, down the driveway, and to the mailbox. That’s it.

I know that most days, I’ll get a walk in, and once that walk is familiar, I’ll sometimes run a little. Some days I might run more, without even deciding to. But even when I don’t feel like doing more, the morning light I get while retrieving the mail and the walk back up our steep driveway are both good for me and genuinely enjoyable. It’s way better than nothing.

The mistake I make again and again is assuming that the size of my plan and the odds of my success are related: the more inspiring the goal and the more elaborate the plan, the better my results will be.

Ambition and results are related, of course, but not in the direction you think.

Industry observers note that creating a habit takes energy and focus, and we’ve only got so much of either, which is why ambitious prepares produce a brilliant week and then…nothing. It takes between 18 and 254 days for a behavior to become automatic, and what predicts faster adoption isn’t ambition, self-discipline, or willpower; it’s repetition.

Industry observers note that repetition in a consistent context drives habit formation. Not just effort, intensity, or how badly someone wants it. Doing the thing, in the same place at about the same time, again and again, has the most impact.

Eli Susman, Ph.D., joins me in a webinar in a few weeks to talk about his book Micropractice.

Microhabits: The Science of Habits So Small They Actually Stick.

According to recent reports, success is motivating. Doing what you mentioned you’d do, even something absurdly small, builds the belief that you can do it. Failing repeatedly does the opposite; that’s a major part of why I spent my 40s making elaborate plans but not running.

Small behaviors make repetition more likely. What separates an actual habit from a nice couple of weeks is whether it holds up when you’re stressed, tired, busy, or not feeling 100%.

Missing a single day doesn’t meaningfully set most people back. We don’t need to be perfect here, folks. What won’t survive is a plan so ambitious that the off days outnumber the on days.

Recent findings suggest that micropractices, as researcher Eli Susman calls them, are very small behaviors that also have their own benefits; a tiny practice isn’t just a placeholder for a “real” one. Susman found that 20 seconds of self-compassionate touch (for example, sending kindness to yourself while placing your hand on your heart) per day improved mental health and lowered stress compared with a placebo finger tapping practice.

Across 280,000 meditation sessions in 103 countries, how consistently people meditated predicted their mood and resilience better than how long they sat. Similarly, a meta-analysis combining the results of many studies found that the benefits of practicing breathwork for stress didn’t depend on how long the session were. And breaking up six hours of sitting with brief bouts of walking improves energy, mood, and food cravings more than doing 30 minutes of walking all at once.

In short: How often beats how long.

In a recent development, I hate the idea of abandoning my substantial intends. But the truth is that I am not choosing between the ambitious version and the tiny version. I am choosing between the tiny version and nothing.

It has been revealed that break the core behavior central to your habit down into something you can do in under five minutes, start to finish. Under a minute is even better. This isn’t the version that would impress your doctor or your neighbors; it’s the version you can do while exhausted, while traveling, while a little bit sick, and when you want nothing more than to stay on the couch.

Then, check it for resistance. If you feel any reluctance when you imagine doing it, it isn’t small enough yet. Cut it in half. Most people need to start with a micropractice: putting on your walking shoes and stepping out the front door, doing one pushup or 30 seconds of breathing, eating a single leaf of romaine, which, for the record, contains actual fiber and actual nutrients.

Do just that for a while. Resist the urge to do more. This is hard, but the moment you’re no longer willing to be unambitious is the moment you put the whole thing at risk. That’s when difficulty enters, and negotiation with yourself, and the possibility of failure. Your tiny habit doesn’t depend on motivation, which is precisely what makes it survive the days when you have none.

According to recent reports, expand only when you’re itching to, and only in absurdly small increments. Go one more minute, not 10.

Every time you repeat a behavior, your brain physically strengthens the connections that produce it, the way feet crossing a meadow gradually wear a path. Repeat it enough and the path becomes a groove your brain follows on its own, no willpower required. You’re carving a neural pathway for your habit, and everything you want is downstream from that.

Sources indicate that at some point, it will become uncomfortable not to do this new behavior. You’ll do it without deciding to, without trying to. That’s the whole goal: repetition until the thing runs itself.

In a recent development, it’s hard to abandon our grand aims and great ambitions for something embarrassingly small. But, paradoxically, it is only in that tiny step that some of our grand plans are truly born.

In a recent development, use the 30-day test: if you have wanted to quit for fewer than 30 consecutive days, it is likely a temporary frustration. If the feeling has persisted — or intensified — for 30+ days, it is a pattern worth taking seriously.

How you leave a job matters as much as why you leave. Your professional reputation follows you for your entire career, and the people you work with today may be the hiring managers, clients, or references of tomorrow.

Two weeks notice: This is the minimum professional standard in the United States. For senior roles, three to four weeks is more appropriate. Check your employment contract — some roles require 30, 60, or 90 days notice.

I want to thank you for [specific positive thing], and I am committed to making the transition as smooth as possible. My last day would be [date].".

Recent findings suggest that the transition strategy: Document your ongoing projects, key contacts, passwords, and processes. Offer to train your replacement. Complete as much outstanding work as possible. A strong exit creates goodwill that pays dividends for years.

The FI community has a saying: financial independence is not about quitting your job — it is about having the freedom to choose whether to keep it. Every dollar you save and invest is a vote for your future autonomy. When you have 12-24 months of expenses saved, you negotiate from strength. When you reach Coast FI or beyond, a bad job becomes a choice, not a trap. Build your FI runway and the question changes from "Can I afford to quit?" to "Does this role still serve my goals?".

Work through these steps before making your decision.

Industry observers note that have you consistently wanted to leave for 30+ days? If no, wait. Temporary frustration is not a reason to upend your career. If yes, proceed to step two.

Sources indicate that pro tip: Keep a brief daily journal noting your satisfaction level 1-10. Data beats feelings for decision-making.

Is the glitch your boss, your role, your compensation, the culture, or the industry? Some problems follow you to the next job. A bad manager is fixable by transferring. An industry you hate requires a bigger change.

Verify your emergency fund, health insurance options, debt situation, and FI runway. If you are not financially ready, keep working while you build your safety net and search for alternatives.

Before quitting, have you requested a transfer, a raise, a role change, or a conversation with HR? Many solvable problems go unaddressed because employees assume the answer will be no.

Pro tip: A direct conversation with your manager about your concerns resolves the concern 40% of the time.

If you decide to leave, secure your next opportunity (if possible), give appropriate notice, document your work for your successor, and maintain every professional relationship.

Pro tip: Never burn bridges. The colleague you leave today may be the hiring manager at your dream firm in three years.

At minimum, 3-6 months of essential expenses in a liquid savings account. If you are quitting without another job lined up, aim for 6-12 months. The FI community recommends having your emergency fund fully funded, health insurance secured, and ideally some progress toward financial independence to provide a psychological safety net.

Industry observers note that if your job is causing persistent anxiety, depression, or physical health symptoms that do not improve with coping strategies, therapy, or workplace changes — yes, your health must come first. But do it strategically: secure health insurance, build your financial runway, and consult a therapist or career coach before making the leap. Never make a permanent career decision during a temporary emotional crisis.

Generally, quitting gives you more control over the narrative, timing, and terms. Being fired can qualify you for unemployment benefits (quitting usually does not), but it can also create a negative reference. If you sense a termination is coming, consider whether negotiating a mutual separation with severance is an option. Document everything and consult an employment attorney if you believe the termination may be discriminatory or retaliatory.

Even partial FI — having 2-5 years of expenses invested — means you can quit a toxic job, take time to find the right next role, or transition to lower-paying but more fulfilling work. Higher productivity: In a randomized study, employees who worked from home performed about 13% better than those in the office.

Risk of isolation: In a large 2026 study in Science, remote work was linked to about a third of the rise in isolation and mental distress.

Blurred boundaries: Without a commute or an office door, your workday can stretch into evenings and weekends.

Higher burnout rates: In a review of 44 studies from the pandemic years, remote workers often reported burnout.

A dedicated spot: Pick one place to work, such as the corner of a room or one end of the table. Your brain may start to associate that spot with work.

According to recent reports, natural light: Set up near a window if you can. Morning daylight may help you feel alert during the day and sleep better at night. If you don’t have a window, a warm desk lamp paired with a bright overhead light may ease eye strain.

It has been revealed that physical comfort: Choose a supportive seat and raise your screen to eye level, so discomfort doesn’t pull your attention away. A cushion behind your lower back or a firm pillow under you can stand in for a special chair. If sitting for long stretches is hard on your body, switch positions throughout the day or ask your doctor about seating options that fit your needs.

Industry observers note that fewer distractions: Clear your work surface of anything you don’t need for the task at hand. Close extra browser tabs and silence phone notifications, since digital clutter may pull at your focus in the same way physical clutter does.

Recent findings suggest that sounds for focus: Some people work best in silence, while others prefer instrumental music or ambient sound in the background. In a noisy home, headphones or earplugs can muffle the commotion. If those don’t work for you, a closed door or a “focus time” sign can let the people you live with know you’re concentrating.

In a recent development, working from home takes away some of the structure an office provides, but a solid routine can bring a bit of it back. Here are a few ideas worth trying:.

It has been revealed that A morning anchor: Pick one or two consistent habits for the first hour of your day, like making coffee or journaling. A familiar rhythm can help you feel grounded before the day’s demands roll in.

A work-mode transition: Without a commute, there’s often little time between rolling out of bed and starting work. Mark the start of your workday with a quick ritual, such as changing out of your loungewear.

Sources indicate that protected focus time: Block a window in your day for your most demanding tasks, ideally when your energy tends to be highest. Share those hours with anyone you live with, so they know when to give you space.

Sources indicate that movement breaks: At home, your day may include less movement than in an office. Use your breaks to stretch or take a short walk.

Recent findings suggest that small, regular contact tends to help with isolation more than the occasional big effort. Put one social proposal on your calendar the way you would a meeting, such as a standing coffee chat with a colleague or a coworking session. On busier days, or if you work on your own, a midday text or a voice note to a friend counts too.

If these linger for weeks, consider reaching out to a doctor or mental health professional. Some employers offer free counseling through an employee assistance program. If you’re self-employed, a primary care provider can refer you to options.

According to recent reports, low motivation while working from home is often tied to missing structure. Without coworkers nearby or a set schedule, you may miss the built-in cues an office provides, such as a colleague stopping by your desk to check in. Try building a light routine and dividing work into smaller tasks.

If you’re a remote worker, you can start a morning routine with one or two small anchor habits before work begins. That could be a gentle stretch or a few pages of a book. Keep it short, and give yourself time to adjust.

It’s normal to feel lonely when you work from home. If you feel disconnected, contact with friends or colleagues may help, even if it’s a quick call or message.

According to recent reports, to lower your risk of burnout, aim to set firm boundaries between work and rest. Choose an end time for your work day and take regular breaks. Those limits can help keep your work from spilling into evenings and weekends.

Sources indicate that the best way to stay focused over a long day is to work in blocks and take pauses between them. Work on your most demanding tasks when your energy is highest, reduce visible distractions, and listen to instrumental music or ambient sound if it helps you concentrate.

Low vitamin D and higher BMI can both occur alongside increased inflammation, which could help explain why the three measures were related.

For example, a teenager who regularly misses outdoor activities because of headaches may get less sun.

Diet is another possibility, since vitamin D can come from foods as well as sunlight.

The survey gave researchers a snapshot, so it could not show whether lower vitamin D preceded the headaches or followed them.

In a recent development, though Djurdja Padejski was raised in communist Yugoslavia, her life there felt stable and uneventful for a long time. In the 1980s, under Yugoslavia’s “soft” one-party government, Padejski and her friends read Western literature, watched Hollywood movies, and listened to the BBC.

“We grew up in a very comfortable, naive environment,” Padejski indicates.

Industry observers note that that changed in the 1990s when Yugoslavia split into several republics. Civil war broke out, and a virulent strain of nationalism took hold in Serbia, the Yugoslavian state where Padejski lived. Firebrand leader Slobodan Milošević ascended to power and began meddling in elections, targeting opposition leaders, and igniting ethnic cleansing campaigns.

According to recent reports, “He captured the entire society and his party,” Padejski remembers. “Very soon I found myself on the streets protesting.” Padejski’s activism against repressive Serbian regimes would continue until 2011, when she and her husband, investigative journalist Djordje Padejski, left the country after people threatened to kill them.

It has been revealed that the Padejskis arrived in the U.S. with hard-won knowledge of how to outlast repression over the long haul. In recent years, they’ve tapped back into that knowledge and shared it with those around them as they witness here in America the illegal destruction of government agencies, election tampering, and warrantless arrests of citizens and non-citizens. This isn’t just true in the United States—around the world, democracy is declining.

How can we go on defying rising authoritarianism when no clear endpoint is in sight? Psychology and motivation research complement the experience of people like the Padejskis by addressing how to conserve energy and sustain commitment to your ideals in challenging conditions.

“The goal of the authoritarian regime is to desensitize us to extremes, to things we should never agree with or consider normal,” claims Djurdja Padejski, now a language and culture researcher (and doctoral candidate) at Arizona State University.

It has been revealed that surviving repression depends on rejecting this presumed “normality” and refusing to let your inner state mirror extremes imposed from above. To that end, here are seven research-backed ways to subsist under indefinite duress.

Life under repression feels exhausting due to the colossal scale of so much of what is happening: attacks on the free press, denial of life-saving aid to millions overseas, ongoing ICE killings on the streets and in detention facilities. Reading about such developments understandably triggers feelings of overwhelm. Research finds that these feelings can drive people to shut down their emotions, dampening their motivation to help in concrete ways.

Djurdja Padejski has come to recognize that to avoid that trap, she has to face her human limits squarely without drowning in self-recrimination. As a young adult under Milošević’s rule, she learned early that worrying about what she couldn’t do was a waste of time and energy.

Recent findings suggest that “It is very vital not to get stuck in that moment, not to be clutching your pearls,” she claims. “We have to be strategic to preserve our resources.”.

Sources indicate that admitting your own lack of control over the big picture can be a necessary prelude to taking the actions still available to you, Padejski notes. “We have to see [the situation] for what it is, so we can focus our efforts on keeping our minds, our bodies, and our communities as healthy as possible under the circumstances.”.

Industry observers note that once you’ve gotten clear about what is within your power to control, you can get granular by carrying out regular acts of “micro-resistance.” These acts of defiance do not require you to upend your daily rhythms or put your life on the line. They can be as simple as attending a march, supporting a neighbor at an immigration court visit, or wearing a shirt with a resistance slogan.

Micro-resistance acts—such as creating protest art and continuing to study even when their department was banned from the university—helped sustain both Padejskis through years of repression, reminding them of the power they had despite limits imposed from on high.

According to recent reports, “These micro-level actions add up,” Djordje Padejski writes. “Even small acts of defiance can maintain your sense of agency.”.

Self-described “small-time” lawyer Daniel Suitor excels at this kind of micro-resistance. During ICE raids in his hometown of Minneapolis, he channeled his overwhelm by signing up for a course on how to file legal paperwork to free unjustly detained Twin Cities residents.

Recent findings suggest that after Suitor filed his first case, he found out surprisingly rapidly that he’d won and that the man he was representing would be freed. That proof-of-concept case spurred him to file another legal petition, then several more in quick succession. And he wasn’t alone in his commitment: To date, Minnesota lawyers have filed more than 1,000 cases challenging unjust detentions.

Recent findings suggest that acts of micro-resistance can also help prime us for future courageous action. When people perform smaller acts of selflessness and service, large-scale heroism becomes easier to contemplate, explains Medical College of Wisconsin heroism researcher Zeno Franco. Concrete practice can make you more adept at translating abstract ideals into action.

“You need to understand beyond theory,” Djurdja Padejski indicates. “We actually, as humans, can’t imagine how concepts work in [the] real world unless we experience them hands-on.”.

For the Padejskis, one of the most stifling aspects of life under Serbian autocracy was not knowing when the repression would lift, if at all.

Recent findings suggest that periods of confinement, literal or figurative, are more bearable when a clear endpoint is in sight, and indefinite periods of repression feel uniquely oppressive. A third or more of incarcerated people with open-ended sentences suffer from depression. Others feel rooted to the present moment, severed from any potential future.

Recent findings suggest that “I simply try to live in the here and now and not to proposal,” one prisoner told the University of Bern researcher Irene Marti, who studies open-ended confinement. “Because I don’t have any future or only one that is very far away.”.

When the endpoint of repression is uncertain, or when a challenging situation has no clear natural limit, creating your own intermediate endpoints can help you stay committed to your goals and values.

In a recent goal-setting study, when people broke an annual community service goal into granular sub-goals (say, four hours of service a week, or eight every two weeks), they volunteered more hours in the long run than people without intermediate goals.

Industry observers note that in the same way, committed resisters can pledge to put in a set number of hours each week, or carry out a set number of clearly defined actions. According to self-determination theory, choosing and pursuing your own accessible goals boosts your well-being and motivation—internal changes that persist even when the larger crisis remains ongoing.

Sources indicate that as governments around the world curtail freedom of speech and movement, it’s hard not to feel the noose tightening. One way to create more existential breathing room is to consider how this moment fits into the longer arc of history.

In a recent development, this helps you subsist in the present by reminding you of parallel past moments (whether decades or centuries ago), how they came to a head, and what ultimately resolved them. Research finds that when people take a long-term perspective, reflecting on recent stressful events as though they happened far in the past, they report less emotional distress in the moment.

Djurdja Padejski found solace in doing this during Milošević’s reign. “I survived that period mostly by reading the columns in the newspapers,” she notes. One column in particular, by Serbian anthropologist Ivan Čolović, examined the regime’s activities from a broader historical and social perspective.

“He was offering a vocabulary and a theoretical apparatus to help us deal with the horrors of civil war. The news about it was the most severely censored, the propaganda was relentless, and all of it was upcoming for many of us who were children when the fallout of our world began,” Padejski indicates. “That’s how I survived with my sanity intact, because it helped me to recognize what is happening to society.”.

Among the most potent present-day energy drains is the social media industrial complex that feeds on people’s rage and frustration, serving up extreme viewpoints that deepen entrenched social divides as they rack up likes and views.

Sources indicate that “Social media and internet platforms—they’re amplifying what is also a typical quality of authoritarian regimes. They’re all about grandiosity,” indicates Djurdja Padejski, who studies the linguistic mechanisms of propaganda. “Algorithms grab people’s attention by intensifying the language and the visuals and the overall framing.” That’s a big reason why frequent social media use saps your cognitive resources and motivation, making it harder to subsist under repression.

Plugging this energy drain requires not just limiting your time online, but redirecting more of that time to the in-person, small-group exchange to which humans are uniquely suited.

When you engage with people face to face, it’s much harder to reduce them to a stereotype or particular viewpoint. And by getting to know them in all their messiness, contradiction, and complexity, you bond with them in ways that lighten the mental and practical load for everyone involved.

“To resist this reduction of our existence to, ‘What are you for or against?’ means embracing creativity, art, friends, communal projects, protests, walks,” Padejski states. “These 10 years of resistance [in Serbia]—I honestly remember it as a series of walks. Sometimes that meant running away together from Milošević‘s militias or the official police, or from water cannons, or rubber bullets. But what is left is our conversations on ideas, on creations.”.

Though exchanges like these may not further resistance directly, they form the edifice that sustains it. Within bonded human-scale communities, members have a clear sense of not just their own energetic capacity, but that of others in the group. That means they can pinch-hit for one another: When someone needs help, they can fill in on the spot—or, like relay racers, take up the baton when someone needs to withdraw. This shared flexibility and responsiveness help all group members to stay committed for the long haul.

For the Padejskis, subsisting under Serbian repression meant homing in on the values that were most important to them, and upholding those values even if it meant sacrificing convenience or comfort. When Djordje Padejski needed a lifesaving drug, a relative told him he could work his connections to obtain the medicine, but only if Padejski joined the Serbian dictator’s political party. Padejski refused, knowing that doing so put his health at risk.

Sources indicate that the couple have continued that tradition in the U.S., though in somewhat less life-altering ways. After Elon Musk unleashed an apparent Nazi salute at a Trump post-inauguration event, the Padejskis gave up their Tesla. “I drive a Subaru now,” Djurdja Padejski indicates. “I really don’t like it compared to Tesla, but I don’t regret it.”.

According to recent reports, some people write off such moral stands as more symbolic than substantive. But symbol, it turns out, shapes substance: What you stand for predicts and influences what you’ll do down the road, for good or ill. When people have a clear, consistent moral identity, studies find, they’re more likely to take real-world action aligned with that identity.

On the other hand, when you’re willing to cave on something that seems minor, like supporting a complicit business, “you are detached from your inner beliefs, from what you know is real and good and safe,” Djurdja Padejski states. “Once you’re there, you are ready to compromise a lot of values that you think you are really one with.”.

Recent findings suggest that one unexpected thing the Padejskis learned, under Milošević and afterward, was the importance of not swinging into action every time a devastating piece of news hit. Overcommitment amounted to self-sabotage, sapping energy and resources they’d need later on.

Industry observers note that military commanders have long known the importance of “keeping their powder dry,” Zeno Franco points out, holding back so they can act at the moment of maximum impact. In the same way, the best long-distance runners often hang back throughout a course to conserve energy, then uncork a burst of speed in the race’s final minutes.

It has been revealed that djurdja Padejski followed this principle to great effect under Milošević. She bided her time leading up to the critical elections of 2000, then worked tirelessly as an election volunteer to monitor for irregularities and make sure no one was falsifying results. All the while, ruling party members with guns lurked in the background.

Sources indicate that “This guy started opening his gun and checking the bullets, and we didn’t cave. We just ignored him,” Padejski says. “We knew we were risking our lives, but we really believed it’s now or never.” Serbia’s democratic opposition party ultimately won that election, causing Milošević’s downfall.

Sources indicate that padejski hopes democratic activists around the world will take a similar approach as crucial elections near. Under repressive conditions, keeping your powder dry “is not an instruction to put off action as long as possible, but rather the wisdom to know that being prepared to act at just the right moment may require careful guarding of resources and energy,” Franco notes. “Biding your time is not the same as surrender.”.

It has been revealed that elizabeth Svoboda is the author of What Makes a Hero?: The Surprising Science of Selflessness. Her upcoming book, The Art of Pacing, is about setting a sustainable pace in a speed-obsessed world.
