How to Make Better Decisions in the Age of AI

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2068 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Berkeley

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Artificial intelligence can summarize research, generate ideas, and analyze enormous amounts of data in seconds.
  • In a recent development, AI has the power to enhance decision-making—or to overwhelm it.
  • According to recent reports, she argues that the rise of AI actually makes certain human qualities like reflection, empathy, values, and moral judgment even more important.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Artificial intelligence can summarize research, generate ideas, and analyze enormous amounts of data in seconds. The power of that little “Ask anything” AI prompt box is immense, but can it help us make wiser decisions? Cheryl Strauss Einhorn, author of The Human Edge: Smarter Decisions in the Age of AI, writes:.

In a recent development, AI has the power to enhance decision-making—or to overwhelm it. It can illuminate pathways we might not have seen or narrow our choices in ways we do not fully recognize. As AI systems become more integrated into our lives, the challenge is no longer simply about harnessing their power but about leading them with clarity, discernment, and commitment to human agency.

According to recent reports, she argues that the rise of AI actually makes certain human qualities like reflection, empathy, values, and moral judgment even more important. We spoke with her about why human judgment is a competitive advantage, how to engage our values when we prompt AI, and how AI can help us clarify our thinking.

Kia Afcari: You argue that AI makes human judgment more, not less, vital. How can we make sure that the values of kindness and care are reflected when we use AI to help us make decisions?

Sources indicate that cheryl Strauss Einhorn: AI has no values. It has biases and influences by those who have designed it, and from whatever information has been fed into it. So to be sure that prosocial values are reflected when we use AI, we humans need to bring them into the work that we do together.

When working with an AI tool, we want to be asking ourselves, What is the problem that I’m solving? Why am I solving it? What is the context? And so we really need to be intentional with AI, because without asking ourselves those things first, AI doesn’t know why we’re coming to it.

Before you actually sit down with a tool, you can muster those values and those vital factors related to the problem that you’re solving, and then articulate them and communicate them to the machine.

If we let the machine think for us, we can lose that sense of right and wrong, for example, because we actually care about all of those details that AI can’t possibly know about the problems that we’re solving and the people that we’re solving those problems with and for.

For example, you might ask yourself or your AI tool: Before I act, help me think through the people, relationships, and responsibilities this decision affects—not just the outcome it produces.

This type of human-centric AI interaction helped Felice, a food scientist at a pet food organization, who was responsible for developing newly introduced recipes that balance nutrition, taste, and market trends. She often has to delegate tasks within her research team, ensuring that product testing, ingredient sourcing, and regulatory compliance all move forward smoothly. Using AI, she was able to analyze workloads and expertise that suggested the best person for each task, but only Felice understood the deeper dynamics at play—who works best under tight deadlines, who has a passion for innovative formulations, and who needs mentorship. When AI recommended assigning a crucial stability test to her most experienced technician, this prompt supported her thinking about a different option: giving it to the junior scientist who was eager to develop his skills in quality assurance. The AI tool’s choices made sense based on efficiency, but Felice’s decision ensured both short-term success and long-term team development.

Sources indicate that KA: In the book, your “cheetah” metaphor celebrates slowing down. Why is a strategic pause so key when working with AI?

Sources indicate that CSE: The cheetah metaphor relates that although this is an animal that goes zero to 60 in about three seconds, its hunting prowess actually comes from being able to decelerate up to nine miles an hour in a single stride. And the reason why that’s so notable in problem solving and decision making is that’s where you build agility, flexibility, and maneuverability. Do I want to stay the course, or do I want to pivot and do something else?

This pause allows you to chunk your learning and pry open that cognitive space for new information and insight. With an AI tool, it’s so important because there’s a difference between speed and quality.

In a recent development, when something truly matters to us, we want to make sure that we’re solving the problem in a way that solves it holistically, that takes care of the people who are involved in the problem with us. And when we’re moving really promptly, sometimes those very notable factors are hard to bring forward. So there’s a real difference between what is efficient and what is effective.

KA: Why can having more information make it harder—not easier—to make good decisions?

CSE: Francis Bacon once mentioned, “Knowledge is power,” but that’s not really true anymore, right? We now have all of the answers with AI to a lot of commonly asked questions and some uncommon questions.

According to recent reports, we need to make sure we’re defining the problem that we’re solving, that we are understanding and communicating the motivation and providing the context, because you don’t want all the information. Otherwise, we’re going to end up with analysis paralysis.

In a recent development, one thing people can use is what I call the “vision of success” question. This question asks you to time travel, to jump over the decision to see that the decision has been made well. What’s happening? What are those few things that if they don’t succeed, the decision fails? It’s actually very powerful, because it allows you to clearly identify so that you can articulate those factors that you absolutely need to be able to share with AI. These become the constraints and boundaries that set the perimeter around the decision, so that it can give you research that’s targeted and focused on those things.

For example, Max deciding where to spend his next vacation. Asking AI for help directly—without turning to himself first—he got a list of destinations, airline options, and local attractions, complete with ratings, reviews, and price comparisons. On paper, that sounds ideal. But in reality, Max rapidly found himself paralyzed by the sheer amount of information. What if he picked a less-than-perfect hotel? What if he overlooked a hidden gem? AI has handed him a mountain of data, but it didn’t necessarily make the decision any easier.

However, when he used the “vision of success” question, he was able to realize and to share with his AI tool: “I want to return home feeling genuinely rested, having spent quality time with my family, without overspending or feeling like I missed the experience I was hoping for.”.

Only then does AI have a meaningful problem to solve. Instead of searching for the “best” vacation—a question with no objective answer—it can help Max find the destination most likely to produce the outcome he actually wants. AI can’t define success but it can optimize for the success you define.

KA: How does the AREA method help people make wiser decisions, especially when AI is involved? CSE: AREA is more than an acronym—it’s a framework for challenging our assumptions and thinking mistakes, and actively includes the perspectives of others. It stands for Absolute, Relative, Exploration and Exploitation, and Analysis.

According to recent reports, the first “A,” Absolute, focuses on primary, unfiltered information straight from primary sources. “R,” Relative, shifts to external viewpoints—secondary sources connected to the subject. “E,” Exploration and Exploitation, fuels creativity: Exploration broadens research through interviews and unconventional sources, while Exploitation turns inward, challenging personal biases and assumptions. The final “A,” Analysis, synthesizes everything, bringing clarity and structure to complex decisions.

When using AI, a system like AREA becomes even more notable because AI doesn’t eliminate bias—it can reflect and sometimes amplify biases in its training data, design, and the way we use it. Good decisions require a process that helps us recognize and challenge both AI’s biases and our own.

For AI, so much of the information, for example, is from Reddit. Information can be incomplete or outdated, and you also know that you’re interacting with a liar. It’s a machine that just gives you answers that are wrong sometimes.

So you need to be able to have a quality due diligence process to not only be able to use the tool effectively, but to be able to evaluate its outcome. Too often, people look at an answer with AI and think that it’s a transaction, and they can just take it. AREA is going to help you make sure that it’s a conversation. So you have an evidence-based perspective that has looked at a variety of stakeholder viewpoints, and made sure that you have pried open that cognitive space to challenge the natural, well-worn mental pathways that we all lean on every day.

KA: How can we use AI in ways that strengthen—rather than undermine—our values and agency?

CSE: It’s a great question. I think the latest competitive advantage is going to be self-awareness.

This is the first tool that actually asks for some of our cognitive load; it wants us to offload some of our decisions to it. And this is a machine fundamentally about decision making, because we ask it for something and it gives us an answer. But there’s a very interesting invitation here, which is to each of us to get to know ourselves better.

It has been revealed that we each have a special sauce, which is the way that we make our decisions, and we make thousands of them every single day. But most of us have not sat down and stated to themselves, What does that process actually look like? Can I actually name those pieces and put language to it?

There is this invitation to get to know our thinking so that we can translate it better, and not only for the tool. How helpful would it be in conversation with our colleagues to be able to say clearly, This is how I’m actually going through the steps, this is how I’m thinking about it, these are the variables that I’m prioritizing, and here’s what I think is the most diagnostic.

You can think about your thinking skills as muscles. If we turn over our cognitive load, we will also weaken it. But if we actually take this invitation to understand our self-awareness and our metacognition, we can make sure that we strengthen those tools.

AI is a tool that has so many implications for our environment and for our world, in addition to the fact that it has implications for our actual thinking skills.

In a recent development, so I would say that the invitation is to turn to yourself first. Ask yourself why you’re using the tool, and whether or not you should be turning to yourself instead. And either way, bring your own thinking forward before sitting down, so that you can feel far more comfortable that you can problem-solve both with it and beyond it.

Kia Afcari is the director of Greater Good Workplaces at GGSC. Tech Report: Are Chimps Less Likely to Steal From Friends?

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (780 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Berkeley

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In recent years, scientists have shown that chimpanzees favor certain peers by picking whom they prefer to groom and selectively sharing food.
  • But a question has lingered: How might a chimpanzee friendship affect antisocial acts?
  • Industry observers note that in a new study that uses fruit as the loot, UC Berkeley researchers found that chimps steal less from their friends, and that friendship status affected the emotional expression of both victim and thieves.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In recent years, scientists have shown that chimpanzees favor certain peers by picking whom they prefer to groom and selectively sharing food. The behavior offers a glimpse into humanity’s prosocial evolutionary past.

But a question has lingered: How might a chimpanzee friendship affect antisocial acts?

Industry observers note that in a new study that uses fruit as the loot, UC Berkeley researchers found that chimps steal less from their friends, and that friendship status affected the emotional expression of both victim and thieves. Closely bonded chimps swiped pineapple pieces from one another less frequently than those with weaker relationships. Additionally, victims were quicker to calm down when the thief was a friend, and thieves indicated less hostility when stealing from a bonded pal than from a non-friend.

Sources indicate that the new research deepens our understanding of the emotional underpinnings of our social lives, said Oded Ritov, the paper’s first author and a Berkeley psychology Ph.D. student.

“Collaborative relationships are vital for our well-being, health, and survival,” said Ritov, who works with Berkeley’s Social Origins Lab. “Increasingly, we’re understanding that this isn’t something that’s unique to us, but that other animals have friends, as well.”.

The paper was published online in September and will appear in the November glitch of the journal Evolution and Human Behavior.

In a recent development, scientists are sometimes hesitant to describe an apparently close relationship between chimps as akin to human friendship, arguing that we can’t grasp their cognitive and emotional complexity. To identify those who showed signs of a close relationship, researchers observed 26 chimps for more than 800 hours at the Ngamba Island Chimpanzee Sanctuary in Uganda. The team documented which chimps appeared to be closely bonded—like friends—by taking note of their grooming patterns, daily interactions, and how regularly they were within arm’s reach of others.

According to recent reports, then they set up two rooms. One contained a “victim” chimp with three trays baited with pineapple. Researchers attached a rope to the trays and led it into the other room, where a second chimp—the thief—could either leave the rope alone or yank it to steal the pineapple.

Sources indicate that chimps stole in 70% of trials with non-friends, compared with 61% of trials with friends. While 9 percentage points may not seem large, each chimp experienced both friend and non-friend conditions, a methodological technique that leads to a higher degree of confidence that the difference is meaningful and not just random chance.

“Ours is the first study to show that they’re able to hold back antisocial behavior with their friends,” Ritov noted.

According to recent reports, researchers also measured how the victims responded to being stolen from by evaluating their stomping, fist-pounding, and screeching. Victims were initially angrier when friends stole from them but quickly moderated their feelings compared with when non-friends stole from them.

In a recent development, the thieves’ behavior also changed. When non-friends were the thieves, the thieves expressed negative emotions for much longer, suggesting they viewed the interaction as more hostile.

“This suggests that there may be mutual expectations in chimps from both sides of the friendship, which makes it seem more like the complex friendships we see in humans,” Ritov noted.

Sources indicate that jan Engelmann, an associate professor of psychology and principal investigator with the Social Origins Lab, remarked previous work has shown relationship-specific intentions in nonhuman primates. But human friendships are about more than special intentions, he added—they’re about stronger expectations.

Industry observers note that “We expect more of our friends,” stated Engelmann, a senior author of the paper. “These findings really deepen our understanding of the evolutionary roots of friendships. This is, to my knowledge, the first evidence showing that also chimpanzees expect and maybe demand special treatment from their friends. These kinds of social expectations might form the basis of human moral principles.”.

The paper adds to Ritov’s work that focuses on the evolution of human behavior and how morals and norms are part of our core being, traceable to other animals. He has recently studied whether nonhuman animals have a sense of fairness and is broadly interested in how emotions unfold across cultures and species.

Industry observers note that “We think that these expectations might be the basic building blocks of the larger-scale cooperation we see in humans,” Ritov noted. “The expectations that chimpanzees have from their friends or close collaborative partners might have scaled up to more generalized expectations for how we should treat each other.”.

Jason Pohl is a science writer in UC Berkeley's Office of Communications & Public Affairs.

Industry News: Air Pollution Reprograms Brain Immune Cells, Raises Dementia Risk by 25%

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1021 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Neurosciencenews

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A latest study reveals that fine particulate air pollution (PM2.5) raises dementia risk by 25% and triggers Alzheimer’s-like brain damage even without amyloid plaques.
  • Microscopic soot, industrial emissions, and wildfire smoke, collectively categorized as fine particulate matter 2.5 (PM2.5), have long been recognized as major drivers of cardiovascular and respiratory disease.
  • Now, a comprehensive translational study published in the Journal of Neuroinflammation by researchers at Case Western Reserve University, University Hospitals, and the Louis Stokes Cleveland VA Medical Center provides compelling human and experimental evidence that air pollution directly fuels neurodegeneration by hijacking the brain’s immune system.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A latest study reveals that fine particulate air pollution (PM2.5) raises dementia risk by 25% and triggers Alzheimer’s-like brain damage even without amyloid plaques. The research highlights that inhaled pollution reprograms the brain’s resident immune cells (microglia), compromises the blood-brain barrier, drains cellular energy reserves, and kills newborn neurons in the hippocampus.

Source: Case Western Reserve University.

Microscopic soot, industrial emissions, and wildfire smoke, collectively categorized as fine particulate matter 2.5 (PM2.5), have long been recognized as major drivers of cardiovascular and respiratory disease. Mounting epidemiological evidence has also linked polluted air to cognitive decline, yet whether inhaled particles actively cause dementia, and precisely how they injure the brain, has remained an urgent scientific question.

Now, a comprehensive translational study published in the Journal of Neuroinflammation by researchers at Case Western Reserve University, University Hospitals, and the Louis Stokes Cleveland VA Medical Center provides compelling human and experimental evidence that air pollution directly fuels neurodegeneration by hijacking the brain’s immune system.

According to recent reports, led by co-senior authors Dr. Sanjay Rajagopalan and Dr. Andrew Pieper, the research team combined population-scale human health tracking with controlled five-month inhalation experiments in mice to map the cellular chain reaction linking dirty air to dementia.

To quantify how long-term air pollution exposure shapes dementia risk across diverse genetic backgrounds, the researchers analyzed medical and environmental records from roughly 500,000 adults enrolled in the UK Biobank, tracked for up to 14 years.

It has been revealed that even after controlling for confounding variables, including age, smoking status, diabetes, and socioeconomic factors—people residing in the most polluted third of geographic regions were 25% more likely to develop Alzheimer’s disease or a related dementia than those living in the cleanest third. Crucially, high air pollution elevated dementia risk regardless of whether an individual carried high or low inherited genetic risk for Alzheimer’s.

To test causation directly, the investigators exposed mice to real-world outdoor Cleveland air for five months, concentrating PM2.5 particles to match levels recorded in the world’s most heavily polluted urban centers.

Even in otherwise healthy mice without genetic predispositions to neurodegeneration, chronic PM2.5 exposure triggered widespread brain pathology:.

It has been revealed that remarkably, these memory deficits and Alzheimer’s-like cellular injuries emerged in healthy mice completely devoid of amyloid plaques. When the researchers exposed mice genetically engineered to develop Alzheimer’s pathology to the same polluted air, the particles inflicted identical neuroinflammatory and metabolic damage while simultaneously accelerating amyloid plaque accumulation.

Recent findings suggest that “By recreating in mice what happens when people breathe polluted air, we found that pollution causes major changes in which genes are active in the brain’s immune cells,” explained Rajagopalan, professor of medicine and director of the Cardiovascular Research Institute at Case Western Reserve School of Medicine. “These cells normally keep the brain healthy by clearing away debris and fighting infection. Seeing how pollution disrupts them helps explain how a stress that affects much of the world’s population harms the brain, and it points us toward a way to treat it.”.

“We’ve identified a key way that air pollution harms the healthy brain and speeds up Alzheimer’s disease,” added Pieper, director of the Harrington Discovery Institute Brain Health Medicines Center and psychiatrist at the Louis Stokes Cleveland VA Medical Center. “This helps us understand how factors in our environment can accelerate and intensify brain diseases of aging. It also opens the door to studying other environmental stresses on the brain, and to finding ways to keep the brain resilient even when we can’t avoid those stressors.”.

How much does air pollution increase the risk of developing dementia?

In an analysis of nearly 500,000 adults tracked for up to 14 years, researchers found that people living in areas with the highest levels of fine particulate air pollution were 25% more likely to develop Alzheimer’s disease or related dementias than those in the cleanest areas, even among people with low genetic risk.

What does fine particulate air pollution (PM2.5) physically do to the brain?

In mouse experiments recreating urban air pollution, inhaled PM2.5 particles caused the blood-brain barrier to leak, triggered brain inflammation, lowered cellular energy reserves (NAD+/NADH ratio), killed newborn memory neurons in the hippocampus, and reprogrammed the genes of the brain’s immune cells (microglia).

Does air pollution only harm brains that already have Alzheimer’s plaques?

No. Researchers were struck to find that air pollution caused memory problems, immune cell disruption, and neuron death in healthy mice that had no amyloid plaques at all, while also speeding up plaque buildup in mice genetically prone to Alzheimer’s disease.

Air pollution exposure interacts with Alzheimer’s genetic susceptibility to reshape microglial epigenomic and transcriptional programs.

Chronic exposure to fine particulate matter air pollution (PM2.5) is associated with cognitive decline and neurodegenerative disease, but the biology connecting inhaled particles to the brain remains incompletely defined. Among 475,325 eligible UK Biobank participants, long-term PM2.5 exposure and Alzheimer disease (AD) polygenic risk were both independently associated with higher risk of AD and related dementias (ADRD).

The PM2.5-by-polygenic risk score (PRS) interaction in Cox models was statistically significant but sub-multiplicative or below unity (interaction HR 0.981, 95% CI 0.965–0.998; p = 0.026), indicating that the combined association was smaller than the simple product of the two individual associations.

Industry observers note that to define the underlying biology, we exposed 5xFAD mice, an amyloid-based model of AD, and wild-type (WT) littermates to concentrated ambient PM2.5 or filtered air for 20 weeks. PM2.5 exposure activated microglia, disrupted the blood-brain barrier, depleted the brain NAD+/NADH pool required for resilience and repair, impaired postnatal hippocampal neurogenesis, and caused cognitive deficits.

Industry observers note that in 5xFAD mice it additionally increased amyloid burden. Paired RNA-seq and ATAC-seq of microglia isolated from the same animals showed that exposure remodeled both gene expression and chromatin accessibility, and that that magnitude and direction of this response depended on genotype, converging on inflammatory, lysosomal, oxidative-stress, synaptic, and amyloid-related pathways.​.

​These population-scale data in humans and experimental data in mice​ support PM2.5 as an environmental neurotoxicant and define microglial regulatory programs through which genetic background shapes the biological response to a common and modifiable exposure.

Brain Speech Hub Builds a “Blueprint” Before We Speak

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1507 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Neurosciencenews

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Neuroscientists have overturned a century-old textbook model of human language, revealing that a key speech comprehension region inside Wernicke’s area also generates an abstract “blueprint” for upcoming words a quarter-second before we speak.
  • For more than a century, neuroscience textbooks have divided human language into two separate anatomical compartments: Wernicke’s area in the temporal lobe to understand heard speech, and frontal motor circuits (such as Broca’s area and the motor cortex) to produce spoken words.
  • Yet that neat division never fully explained a persistent clinical paradox: why patients who suffer strokes or injuries in Wernicke’s area frequently struggle not only to comprehend language, but also to retrieve and speak the words they intend to say.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Neuroscientists have overturned a century-old textbook model of human language, revealing that a key speech comprehension region inside Wernicke’s area also generates an abstract “blueprint” for upcoming words a quarter-second before we speak. The study reveals that listening and speaking neurons sit side by side, opening newly introduced targets for neurosurgical mapping, autism research, and brain-computer interfaces that restore speech.

For more than a century, neuroscience textbooks have divided human language into two separate anatomical compartments: Wernicke’s area in the temporal lobe to understand heard speech, and frontal motor circuits (such as Broca’s area and the motor cortex) to produce spoken words.

Yet that neat division never fully explained a persistent clinical paradox: why patients who suffer strokes or injuries in Wernicke’s area frequently struggle not only to comprehend language, but also to retrieve and speak the words they intend to say.

It has been revealed that now, in a landmark study published in Science, researchers at UC San Francisco (UCSF) led by neurosurgeon Dr. Edward Chang have resolved that 150-year-old puzzle.

Drawing on 15 years of high-resolution intracranial brain recordings alongside targeted neural experiments, the team demonstrated that a specialized hub within Wernicke’s area actively generates a cognitive “blueprint” for each word roughly a quarter-second before a person begins to speak.

In the 1870s, German neurologist Carl Wernicke originally speculated that the posterior temporal lobe housed an “auditory image of words”, an internal template that could guide spoken output. Over subsequent decades, however, because the region sits nestled inside auditory cortex, neuroscientists largely pigeonholed it as purely a passive receiver for incoming speech sounds.

In a recent development, “What’s different now is that we finally have the tools and the data to see the brain at the speed and scale at which speech actually happens — millisecond by millisecond, down to individual neurons,” explained co-first author Dr. Matthew Leonard, associate professor of neurological surgery at UCSF.

Combining longitudinal intracranial recordings gathered in Chang’s laboratory with upcoming experiments designed to separate listening from speaking, Leonard and co-first author Dr. Alex Silva, a student in UCSF’s Medical Scientist Training Program, pinpointed a crucial cortical hub: the left posterior superior temporal gyrus (lpSTG).

Tracking neural activity at millisecond resolution revealed that specific populations of neurons inside the lpSTG surged into action approximately 250 milliseconds (a quarter-second) before vocalization began.

Crucially, this pre-speech firing did not represent raw acoustic sounds or physical movements of the lips and tongue. Instead, lpSTG neurons constructed an abstract linguistic blueprint encoding:.

Once assembled in the lpSTG, this structural blueprint traveled forward to speech-planning networks in the frontal lobe, and subsequently to the motor cortex, which translated the proposal into precise articulatory muscle commands. Furthermore, high-resolution mapping indicated that neurons dedicated to hearing speech sit directly beside, and sometimes overlap with, the neurons generating outgoing word blueprints.

Recent findings suggest that “This changes the textbook view of how the brain perceives and produces speech,” mentioned Chang, chair of the UCSF Department of Neurological Surgery and member of the UCSF Weill Institute for Neurosciences. “Instead of being separate systems, the processes of hearing speech and actually speaking are very intertwined.”.

Housing incoming auditory processing and outgoing word planning inside the same microcircuit provides a compelling neural mechanism for how infants acquire language, converting heard sounds directly into motor-ready speech blueprints. It also offers a targeted anatomical region to investigate why roughly one-quarter to one-third of autistic children remain minimally verbal despite demonstrating strong language comprehension.

“It gives us a specific place in the brain to look, and a specific question to ask,” Chang noted.

It has been revealed that equally transformative are the implications for neurotechnology. Today’s speech brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) typically decode intended words from the motor cortex, a strategy that fails if a patient’s motor pathways are severely damaged. Because the lpSTG operates upstream of motor execution, it offers an alternative decoding gateway.

In proof-of-concept testing with two participants living with severe paralysis and anarthria (inability to speak), the UCSF team successfully decoded both the words participants attempted to say and the words they heard directly from lpSTG signals, pointing toward future conversational BCIs capable of capturing both sides of human dialogue.

How does this discovery change what we know about how the brain produces speech?

For over 100 years, textbooks taught that speech comprehension (Wernicke’s area) and speech production were handled by separate brain systems. UCSF researchers proved that a region inside Wernicke’s area (the lpSTG) actually activates a quarter-second before we speak to build an abstract “blueprint” of each intended word, including its length and syllable count, before sending it to motor areas.

Why can damage to Wernicke’s area make it hard to speak words, not just understand them?

Because the neurons that process heard speech sit directly alongside the neurons that build the structural blueprint for spoken words in the left posterior superior temporal gyrus, a stroke or injury to that region disrupts both language comprehension and word planning.

How could this finding help paralyzed patients communicate?

In a recent development, current speech brain-computer interfaces read signals from the brain’s motor cortex, which can be damaged in some paralyzed patients. Because the lpSTG creates word blueprints earlier in the speech pipeline, decoding signals from this region could restore communication for a wider range of paralyzed individuals—and potentially capture both heard and spoken words for natural conversation.

Bowes, Jr. Foundation, and Aligning Research to Impact Autism (ARIA-NSNM-003), which is managed by the Coalition for Aligning Science and funded by the Sergey Brin Family Foundation.

Recent findings suggest that disclosures: Alex Silva, Matthew Leonard, and Edward Chang are inventors on a pending UCSF patent application related to this work. Chang is the co-founder of Echo Neurotechnologies, LLC.

A neural code for generative speech production in human Wernicke’s area.

Recent findings suggest that wernicke’s area, located in the posterior superior temporal gyrus of the human brain, has long been considered essential for understanding speech. However, damage to this region also disrupts the ability to produce speech, creating a long-standing puzzle in neuroscience. Traditional explanations propose that this area primarily supports speech production indirectly by monitoring sounds during speaking. However, it remains unclear whether this region plays a more direct role in generating speech itself, and if so, what kind of information it represents: sounds, movements, or even properties of whole words. Resolving this question is critical for understanding how the brain constructs language and for developing technologies to restore speech in individuals who have lost it.

Industry observers note that addressing this question requires probing the human brain at multiple scales with both correlational and causal methods. We combined several complementary approaches, including high-resolution direct recordings of neural populations and single neurons during speaking and listening, electrical stimulation of specific brain regions to test causality, and analysis of patients with localized brain lesions. Across these methods, participants performed a variety of speaking and listening tasks ranging from naturalistic speech to single word repetition, providing a detailed and holistic view of the role of the posterior temporal lobe in generating upcoming speech.

We identified a specific subregion within individual participants’ Wernicke’s area—the left posterior superior temporal gyrus—that becomes active before speech begins. This early activity precedes word onsets in continuous speech rather than reflecting feedback from hearing one’s own voice. Brain stimulation and lesion analyses showed that disrupting this region causes errors in speech production, confirming its causal role.

According to recent reports, detailed analyses revealed that this region encodes properties of entire words, such as their length and frequency, rather than individual sounds or motor movements. This is distinct from neighboring brain regions that encode auditory feedback and do so by representing lower-level features such as articulation or sound.

Industry observers note that timing analyses indicated that activity in this region occurs earlier than in motor areas responsible for controlling speech muscles, placing it at the start of the speech production process. Recordings from individual neurons further confirmed that cells in this region respond before speech production, respond selectively to specific words, and are active during both speaking and listening.

Finally, in people unable to speak due to paralysis, signals from this region could be used to decode both intended and perceived speech, demonstrating its potential for multimodal brain-computer interface technologies aimed at restoring communication.

It has been revealed that this work identifies a specialized region within Wernicke’s area that generates word-level representations before speech is produced. Rather than serving primarily as a center for speech perception, this region acts as an early stage in the production process, organizing upcoming words before they are translated into motor commands. These findings resolve a long-standing paradox about Wernicke’s area and provide a unified framework for understanding how the brain links language comprehension and production. They also highlight a promising target for future neuroprosthetic devices aimed at restoring speech in individuals with communication impairments.

Latest Update: How Artificial Intelligence Can Help With Critical Thinking

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (803 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Berkeley

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that knowledge workers such as scientists, teachers, lawyers, and business leaders are increasingly using generative artificial intelligence applications for tasks that demand imagination, creativity, and problem solving.
  • Scholars refer to this increasingly prevalent problem as cognitive offloading.
  • My research at the intersection of artificial intelligence and knowledge work provides a different view, however.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that knowledge workers such as scientists, teachers, lawyers, and business leaders are increasingly using generative artificial intelligence applications for tasks that demand imagination, creativity, and problem solving. Ironically, perhaps, recent research reveals that people who interact with generative AI for work tasks can end up not thinking critically. They can surrender to AI’s quick and confident answers, which can lead to speedy but low-quality solutions.

Scholars refer to this increasingly prevalent problem as cognitive offloading. And they are showing that it can erode the very skills that make knowledge workers valuable.

My research at the intersection of artificial intelligence and knowledge work provides a different view, however. In one study, my colleagues and I interviewed 45 knowledge workers at a U.S. public university. They all were using generative AI applications in their core tasks: generating new ideas, solving complex problems, and designing novel solutions. We also analyzed the prompts and outputs from their iterative AI chats.

We found that when knowledge workers intentionally use AI to challenge their ideas—to generate friction—they can significantly improve their performance. Previous research on human-AI collaboration for loan evaluations had similar results.

Industry observers note that using AI to find information that contradicts your own can reveal unlikely perspectives that disrupt your familiar logic and spark upcoming insights. This is particularly crucial because AI models swiftly become familiar with how a user prompts the model and interprets its output, and the model presents information according to these patterns.

Sources indicate that for example, a marketing professional in our study asked AI to create virtual customers with personas that would lead them to dislike a product under development, which was an accounting certificate program. The contrary feedback from the AI model revealed customer preferences that the accounting professional designing the program had not considered, such as using multiple cases from different industries to illustrate a principle, rather than cases from the same industry.

An attorney used AI to find obscure legal loopholes and to consider how companies might exploit them. That exposed surprising but realistic scenarios of hard-to-detect unethical behavior in employees.

Exploring unlikely and opposing ideas presented by AI can feel disorienting. To help, knowledge workers should lean on their own expertise to question surprising information that an AI system might provide.

An operations research scientist who works with supply chains described adapting unfamiliar computing programs from other fields suggested by AI, such as signal processing and wireless communication, which helped him create a stronger program of his own. Although the programs were latest to him, his strong understanding of supply network modeling helped him see how he could apply them.

A study I was not involved with found that creative writers produce better copy when they use AI as a sounding board rather than to ghostwrite.

Knowledge workers can also use AI’s outputs to examine topics from multiple viewpoints, deepening their knowledge.

It has been revealed that A research scholar in our study probed an AI system for journal papers that used a concept he was using, but in contrasting settings, which helped him understand the concept from different angles. A lawyer followed up on legal citations suggested by an AI model by asking for different types of illustrative cases. That helped her fully understand the original case and write a strong legal brief.

Leaders of organizations can encourage knowledge workers to develop friction-generating queries of AI models.

Industry observers note that A straightforward approach is to use prompts that challenge rather than agree with a person’s thinking. People can also draw on their own knowledge, work experiences, and professional ethics to scrutinize AI outputs. Sometimes people realize that a response lacks originality, even if it is factually correct.

Organization leaders can also create programs for knowledge workers to share their experiences and insights. Regular sessions—led by cross-functional AI task forces or AI champions—can also help knowledge workers keep up with rapidly evolving AI tools.

Providing resources for knowledge workers is important, as well. Internal AI bootcamps and workshops led by AI experts or experienced users can help workers understand what AI tools can and cannot do.

It has been revealed that A professor leading an initiative about AI use in teaching described how she developed internal competitions with prizes for professors who successfully completed AI bootcamps. Organizations can also offer AI sandboxes—safe, private environments where employees can experiment and learn how to use AI tools.

In these efforts to support knowledge workers, an vital detail is pointing out that adding friction can appear to make an AI system work against you, but—as new research indicates—it actually helps it work for you.

Industry observers note that airline pricing is driven by demand, and demand follows predictable weekly patterns. Business travelers fly Monday mornings and Thursday or Friday afternoons. Leisure travelers fly Friday evenings and return Sunday afternoons. The days with the least demand — and therefore the lowest fares — are Tuesday, Wednesday, and Saturday.

Here is what the aggregate pricing data from Google Flights, Hopper, and airline fare databases consistently highlights:.

The savings are most pronounced on popular leisure routes (Fresh York to Miami, Chicago to Los Angeles, any route to Las Vegas or Orlando) where weekend demand is highest. On less popular routes or business-heavy corridors, the day-of-week effect is smaller. The practical takeaway: if you have any flexibility, fly out on Tuesday or Wednesday and return on a Tuesday or Wednesday. A couple flying round-trip can save $100 to $400 simply by shifting their travel days.

One crucial note: these are averages across thousands of routes. Individual route pricing varies based on competition, seasonal demand, and airline capacity decisions. Always compare specific dates using Google Flights rather than assuming Tuesday is cheapest for your exact itinerary.

Recent findings suggest that the old advice about booking flights on a specific day of the week — typically Tuesday at 1 AM — is a myth that has never been supported by data. Airlines use dynamic pricing algorithms that adjust fares thousands of times per day based on demand, competition, and remaining seat inventory. There is no magical booking day.

Industry observers note that what does matter is how far in advance you book. Here are the optimal booking windows based on aggregate data from Hopper, Google Flights, and CheapAir analyses of millions of fares:.

Sources indicate that the general pattern is that prices start high when flights first open (9-11 months out), drop to their lowest point in the 1-3 month window as airlines compete for bookings, then spike in the final 2-3 weeks as remaining seats become scarce. Holiday travel follows a compressed version of this pattern with higher floor prices throughout.

The most reliable strategy is not to try timing the absolute bottom but to set fare alerts and buy when the price drops to a level you consider a good deal. Waiting for a slightly lower fare risks watching prices climb permanently as departure approaches.

Recent findings suggest that the right tools eliminate the need to manually check prices. Here is what works best and how to use each one:.

In a recent development, fare alerts are the single most effective strategy for the time-constrained FI-minded traveler. Set alerts on Google Flights for every trip you are considering in the next 6 months. You will receive email notifications when prices drop, and you can book immediately without daily searching. This passive approach consistently saves $50 to $300 per ticket.

It has been revealed that for those building a travel rewards strategy, credit card travel portals (Chase Ultimate Rewards, Amex Travel, Capital One Travel) sometimes offer slightly better prices than booking direct. More importantly, points earned through everyday spending can cover flights entirely. A card earning 2x points on all purchases turns $25,000 in annual spending into 50,000 points — enough for 1-2 round-trip domestic flights. The FI approach to travel rewards is not to spend more to earn points, but to redirect spending you would do anyway through a rewards-earning card and let the points accumulate passively.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that A neuroimaging study reveals that women who chronically view their own appearance from an outsider’s perspective, a psychological trait known as self-objectification, exhibit dampened brain activity in aesthetic judgment regions when viewing sexualized images of women.
  • Widespread sexualization of women across advertising, entertainment, and social media has long been linked to societal objectification and broad mental health burdens, including body dissatisfaction, anxiety, and disordered eating.
  • Over time, repeated exposure to objectifying imagery can lead individuals to internalize an observer’s gaze, a psychological phenomenon known as self-objectification, in which a person habitually monitors and evaluates their own body from an outsider’s perspective.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that A neuroimaging study reveals that women who chronically view their own appearance from an outsider’s perspective, a psychological trait known as self-objectification, exhibit dampened brain activity in aesthetic judgment regions when viewing sexualized images of women. The findings suggest that internalized beauty standards reshape how the brain regulates and evaluates objectifying media.

Source: Society for Neuroscience.

Widespread sexualization of women across advertising, entertainment, and social media has long been linked to societal objectification and broad mental health burdens, including body dissatisfaction, anxiety, and disordered eating.

Over time, repeated exposure to objectifying imagery can lead individuals to internalize an observer’s gaze, a psychological phenomenon known as self-objectification, in which a person habitually monitors and evaluates their own body from an outsider’s perspective.

While behavioral studies have established that self-objectification heightens sensitivity to media portrayals, precisely how a woman’s self-perception alters the underlying neural circuitry that evaluates sexualized visuals has remained unclear.

In a study published today in eNeuro, a research team led by Zhennan Liu at Shanghai Normal University and Haoyue Qian at the Chinese Academy of Sciences investigated how individual differences in self-objectification shape both subjective beauty judgments and brain responses to sexualized imagery.

Industry observers note that the investigators recruited 60 healthy cisgender heterosexual female participants with an average age of approximately 20 years. First, the team assessed each participant’s baseline level of self-objectification using a validated psychological scale measuring how strongly individuals prioritize external appearance over internal bodily competence.

Next, participants viewed and rated a series of photographs categorized by the researchers as either:.

While participants across the board rated the sexualized photographs as more attractive than the non-sexualized images, women with higher self-objectification scores assigned significantly higher attractiveness ratings to the sexualized visuals.

When the team examined the accompanying brain activity, they uncovered a striking neural signature: women who scored higher on self-objectification exhibited dampened neural activity in brain regions involved in aesthetic judgment while assessing sexualized images.

Rather than heightened analytical engagement, this reduced activation suggests an altered regulatory or automatic evaluative response when processing culturally idealized, objectifying imagery.

“Differences between individuals [in this study] may come from how their brains regulate and evaluate the attractiveness of these images,” explained Qian.

By connecting self-objectification to measurable shifts in aesthetic evaluation circuitry, the study illustrates how internalized social standards leave a functional footprint on visual and emotional processing.

Looking ahead, the researchers aim to move beyond observational associations to test whether psychological training can buffer the brain against objectifying media.

It has been revealed that “We want to test whether experimentally training or manipulating regulation strategies (e.g., cognitive reappraisal) can change how women respond to and rate sexualized images,” Qian said. “This will help move the work from association toward causal and intervention-relevant questions.”.

What is “self-objectification,” and how did researchers measure it?

It has been revealed that self-objectification is the tendency to view and judge one’s own body primarily from an outside observer’s perspective, prioritizing physical appearance over internal physical capabilities. Researchers measured this trait using a validated psychological questionnaire before participants viewed media images.

How did self-objectification affect brain responses to sexualized images?

Women with higher self-objectification scores rated sexualized images of women as significantly more attractive than peers with lower scores, and highlighted dampened brain activity in regions responsible for aesthetic judgment, indicating differences in how their brains regulate and evaluate beauty standards.

Could psychological strategies change how the brain reacts to objectifying media?

Researchers hope to test whether training cognitive regulation techniques, such as cognitive reappraisal, which helps people consciously reframe how they interpret visual stimuli, can modify brain activity and reduce vulnerability to sexualized media representations.

Trait Self-Objectification Modulates Attractiveness-Regulating Neural Activity in Sexual Objectification Processing: An ERP Study.

Sources indicate that contemporary mass media frequently emphasize women’s sexual attractiveness, thereby perpetuating sexual objectification and exacerbating mental distress. Trait self-objectification is presumed to be a risk factor for these adverse outcomes; however, the neurocognitive mechanisms underlying individuals’ responses to sexual objectification remain poorly understood.

The present study examined how trait self-objectification modulates behavioral and electrophysiological responses to sexualized female images. Behaviorally, sexualized portrayals of women increased attractiveness ratings, and this enhancement was further modulated by individual levels of trait self-objectification. Neurally, processing sexualized female images evoked a set of ERPs indexing early neurocognitive processes, including perception-related N170 and EPN, and attention-related P200.

In a recent development, distinct later neural responses were also identified, including the emotion-related centro-parietal LPP and the regulation-related frontal LPP (f-LPP). Among these sexual objectification-related ERP components, only the f-LPP was modulated by trait self-objectification.

Furthermore, follow-up analyses revealed that the degree to which trait self-objectification increased individuals’ attractiveness ratings of sexualized images was associated with their reduced f-LPP activity.

Collectively, these findings suggest that trait self-objectification modulates the processing of sexually objectifying stimuli by altering neurocognitive processes underlying attractiveness regulation, highlighting the importance of this regulatory mechanism in shaping individual responses to sexual objectification.

In a recent development, the cultural emphasis on women’s sexual attractiveness perpetuates sexual objectification, which is associated with adverse mental health outcomes. Trait self-objectification may modulate these outcomes, yet its relationship with the processing of sexual objectification remains unclear. This study found that trait self-objectification shapes attractiveness ratings during sexual objectification processing.

In a recent development, although sexualized images elicited multiple neurocognitive components—N170 and EPN (perception-related), P200 (attention-related), cp-LPP (emotion-related), and f-LPP (regulation-related)—individual differences in trait self-objectification were selectively associated with f-LPP activity. These findings highlight the potential role of attractiveness-related regulatory processing in shaping individual responses to sexual objectification.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • People with higher vitamin D levels tend to sleep longer and have more consistent sleep patterns.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Two weeks of sleep tracking linked higher levels of one vitamin to longer, more consistent sleep.

Two weeks of sleep tracking linked higher levels of one vitamin to longer, more consistent sleep.

People with higher vitamin D levels tend to sleep longer and have more consistent sleep patterns.

Those with higher levels also tend to spend a greater proportion of their time in bed asleep.

One proposed explanation involves melatonin, the hormone that helps signal when it is time to sleep.

The findings suggest that vitamin D status and sleep may be connected through other biological processes or shared everyday habits.

The research involved almost 80 generally healthy adults aged 18 to 45, recruited from the University of Delaware and the surrounding area.

Participants wore wrist monitors for two weeks, allowing researchers to estimate their sleep duration and timing.

Blood tests measured vitamin D levels, while urine samples provided an indicator of overnight melatonin production.

Before statistical adjustments, people whose vitamin D levels were 10 ng/mL higher slept around 12 minutes longer per night.

The association with longer sleep remained across the adjusted analyses, although several other links weakened.

Because the research was observational, it cannot establish whether increasing vitamin D improves sleep.

Sleep follows an internal rhythm that repeats roughly every 24 hours.

Light reaching the eyes helps the brain keep this rhythm aligned with the cycle of day and night.

As darkness falls, the brain normally increases its release of melatonin, helping the body prepare for sleep.

Bright artificial light late in the evening can interfere with this process and delay that signal.

Time spent outdoors and physical activity can also influence these rhythms.

Sunlight has another role in the body, allowing exposed skin to produce vitamin D.

People who spend little time outside may have more difficulty obtaining enough of the vitamin.

Food provides another source, particularly oily fish such as salmon and mackerel, while egg yolks contain smaller amounts.

Previous research offers some evidence that vitamin D supplements may improve how people rate their sleep quality (Abboud, 2022).

A review brought together 19 intervention studies, although only three trials could be combined in its main statistical analysis.

Those trials found improvements in questionnaire scores after supplementation, but participants included people with fibromyalgia and those receiving methadone treatment.

Results for sleep duration and specific sleep disorders were less consistent, leaving questions about who might benefit and which aspects of sleep could change.

The study was published in the journal SLEEP Advances (D’Agata et al., 2025).

Does Working Harder Make Learning Fun?

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (881 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Neurosciencenews

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A fresh psychology study challenges the classic educational advice that simply putting in more effort makes learning enjoyable.
  • According to recent reports, parents and educators frequently repeat a familiar piece of advice when children groan over difficult homework: if you just try harder, you’ll start to enjoy it.
  • Yet a fresh psychological investigation from Kyushu University suggests that this relationship works in the exact opposite direction.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A fresh psychology study challenges the classic educational advice that simply putting in more effort makes learning enjoyable. Three experiments reveal that while cognitive effort improves comprehension, it does not spark curiosity or enjoyment, instead, preexisting interest motivates students to engage in the first place.

According to recent reports, parents and educators frequently repeat a familiar piece of advice when children groan over difficult homework: if you just try harder, you’ll start to enjoy it. Behind this common wisdom lies an intuitive assumption that sustained cognitive effort naturally blossoms into curiosity and intrinsic motivation.

Yet a fresh psychological investigation from Kyushu University suggests that this relationship works in the exact opposite direction.

Recent findings suggest that published in Acta Psychologica, the study demonstrates that forcing effort improves basic comprehension, but it does not make dry or unappealing material more interesting. Instead, genuine interest and liking come first—serving as the psychological spark that motivates learners to invest cognitive effort voluntarily.

“I’m curious if a student is made to work harder, does that bring the same benefits as effort they choose to give,” asked Yimeng Jin, a doctoral student at Kyushu University’s Graduate School of Systems Life Sciences and first author of the study. “It matters because many learning environments rely on required effort, such as assignments, on the assumption that more effort is always better.”.

To disentangle voluntary motivation from mandatory mental exertion, Jin and senior author Professor Johan Lauwereyns at Kyushu University’s Faculty of Arts and Science conducted three behavioral experiments involving 110 university students.

Participants read pairs of seemingly unrelated sentences and decided whether they wanted to construct an explanation connecting them. By tracking participants’ initial choices, task completion, and time spent, the team isolated two distinct components of learning: willingness to engage and cognitive effort invested.

Across the three experimental phases, a clear cognitive pattern emerged:.

Sources indicate that “Interestingly, participants who were required to explain spent more time on the task than those who chose to do so,” Jin noted. “Perhaps they initially skipped it because the sentences were harder to understand, so they needed more time to make sense of them. It’s a bit like struggling through homework in a subject you don’t enjoy. Together, the experiments suggest that effort can help people make sense of information, while interest is more closely linked to their willingness to engage.”.

It has been revealed that while the researchers caution that short laboratory reading tasks among university students differ from long-term classroom learning in younger children, the findings carry broad implications for how educators, parents, and communicators design learning environments. Rather than relying solely on mandatory drill work to manufacture enthusiasm, sparking authentic curiosity first may unlock deeper, faster comprehension.

“The findings have implications far outside education. The connection between engagement and effort is key whenever our understanding depends on reading texts,” concluded Lauwereyns.

Does working harder on a subject automatically make it more enjoyable?

No. Researchers at Kyushu University found that while putting in cognitive effort helps students better understand difficult material, it does not increase their interest in or enjoyment of the subject.

What actually motivates students to put effort into learning?

The experiments demonstrated that preexisting interest and liking come first. When students already find a topic intriguing, they are far more willing to engage voluntarily, and they comprehend the material more efficiently than when forced to work through topics they want to skip.

What happens when students are forced to work on material they don’t find interesting?

When participants were required to explain material they initially chose to skip, they spent significantly more time struggling with the task, gained less comprehension compared to voluntary effort, and demonstrated no increase in enjoyment.

Effort enhances understanding, while appreciation drives engagement in Cross-sentence semantic processing.

Comprehensive reading requires active semantic processing, going beyond explicitly stated information to construct connections and meaning. Building on discourse coherence theory, Reader-Response Theory and insights from Language Poetry, the present research investigates how active engagement and cognitive effort shape semantic processing.

We propose that evaluative dimensions central to aesthetic appreciation, namely understanding, interest, and liking, also play key roles in semantic processing.

To examine these processes, we developed a novel cross-sentence elaboration paradigm using unconnected, randomly paired sentences that create semantic gaps and encourage reader-driven meaning construction.

Industry observers note that in Experiment 1, participants could voluntarily invest effort by thinking aloud during elaboration. Results showed greater volitional engagement was associated with higher levels of understanding, interest, and appreciation.

Experiment 2 dissociated willingness to engage from actual effort, revealing that appreciation predicted participants’ willingness to invest further effort, whereas additional completed effort did not consistently increase appreciation.

Experiment 3 examined forced effort, showing that externally imposed effort enhanced semantic understanding but did not consistently increase appreciation, highlighting the distinct roles of volitional and imposed effort.

An integrated 2 × 2 analysis of Experiments 2 and 3 revealed that active engagement and cognitive effort made distinct, interactive contributions to evaluation and processing time, with completed cognitive effort more reliably predicting accurate recognition memory and active engagement more closely tied to memory for the processing context.

Together, these findings clarify the interplay between engagement, effort, understanding, and appreciation, offering upcoming insights into the cognitive dynamics of active meaning construction in semantic processing.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Johnson Banks rebuilds RIBA for its 200th birthday: the RIBA brand identity turns negative space into a bold typographic mark.

The first thing you see is the space between the letters. RIBA arrives as four solid capitals on a pale wall, each letter built from the gaps around it, the R split into a bowl and a leg, the B into two stacked bowls, the A into a triangle over a flat base. It is a mark about architecture made from architecture itself, walls and openings rather than a drawn symbol, and it holds at every size, from a tote bag to a building banner.

Industry observers note that the type does the work. Johnson Banks started from a Philip Johnson line, that all great architecture is the design of space that contains, cuddles, exalts, or stimulates the people in that space, and let the negative space inside the four letters carry the idea. The mark can sit on top of a photograph, cut into it, or anchor a corner or an edge, and the same logic runs through a set of drop capitals, letters drawn to open a page like a doorway.

It has been revealed that the old identity, letters drawn by Eric Gill beside a highly detailed symbol, had drifted over twenty-five years into hundreds of sub-brands with no house style holding them together. The latest system pulls them back into line, with related identities for RSAW, the Royal Society of Architects in Wales, and RIBAJ, the institute journal, each sitting inside the same approach, and clear guidelines built on accessible fonts so the brand stays useful and durable.

Colour went back to the beginning. The historic red, the shade the public knows from RIBA signboards, returns front and centre, running across the tote bag, the drawing stencil and the vertical banner on a brick facade. Against it, the palette stays quiet, stone grey, pale blue, black, so the red reads as a signal rather than a decoration, and the crest, the two lions, survives in a simplified, softened form as a quiet sign-off, debossed in black on black.

In a recent development, the system proves itself on the objects architects use. Book spines carry RIBA, RSAW and RIBAJ in red, white and blue on a wooden shelf. A red stencil ruler cuts the letters into a drawing tool. A poster for the Domestic Building Contract pairs a giant yellow D with a red architectural photograph. And the illustration style, flat geometric shapes in red, blue and green with small cut-out figures, gives the brand a way to talk about people without a photograph.

#160724. What My Son Is Learning From Artificial Intelligence

📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2449 w)
