What Happens When Elders Share Their Stories

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1634 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Berkeley

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • When I moved from the San Francisco Bay Area to a small, rural town in Vermont, I wanted to find a way to contribute to the local community.
  • The local historical society took interest in this idea, which led to an exhibit at the 159-year-old Tunbridge World’s Fair, and a book series entitled Folk Life: Tunbridge Oral Histories.
  • Industry observers note that what is it about life stories that strikes such a universal chord?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When I moved from the San Francisco Bay Area to a small, rural town in Vermont, I wanted to find a way to contribute to the local community. Knowing there was a significant senior population here, I reached out to the town librarian with hopes of helping elders share their stories.

The local historical society took interest in this idea, which led to an exhibit at the 159-year-old Tunbridge World’s Fair, and a book series entitled Folk Life: Tunbridge Oral Histories. The first two print runs sold out. The second collection of stories has just been published, and people are already asking who will be featured in the third.

Industry observers note that what is it about life stories that strikes such a universal chord? And why is it important—and even imperative—to share our stories with others? I interviewed oral historians, teachers, and a digital storyteller to discover more about why the age-old tradition of recording oral histories continues to make such a significant impact for individuals and communities.

Storytelling is, according to scientific research, a biological shortcut to human connection. Uri Hasson and fellow researchers at Princeton University discovered that the brains of the storyteller and listener physically sync up while a story is being told, promoting social connection, trust, and empathy.

The more emotionally affecting the story is, the stronger this connection becomes. As emotions and tension rise, hormones are released, including oxytocin, the “bonding hormone”; dopamine, which sharpens focus; and cortisol, which promotes attention and alertness as conflicts in the story arise. These hormonal responses enhance both the listener’s memory and connection to the storyteller.

For Erin Barnaby, a digital storyteller and 11th-generation Tunbridge native, oral histories create a connection not only to people, but also time and place. “My dad recently sold his house to my uncle, a house that he built on land that my grandfather had given to him. I love to hear him tell stories about the shifting of the land, from sheep farms to dairy farms and the shift from open pastures to forests.”.

In a recent development, even when the subject matter might not be instantly relatable, the process of listening to another’s stories still creates a profound interpersonal connection. Esther Ehrlich, who worked at UC Berkeley’s Oral History Center for six years before launching an oral history business of her own, experienced this sense of connection firsthand:.

I was assigned an interview with a former medical malpractice insurance guy, which initially didn’t interest me at all. And then lo and behold, after interviewing this man, I found him absolutely fascinating. What I came to discover was that by the time we were done, or even partway in, I came to love every single person I interviewed. I would feel connected to them and them to me.

From that biological and psychological basis, oral histories make a critical social contribution.

Recent findings suggest that according to the Oral History Association, “oral history is the oldest type of historical inquiry, stemming from the oral traditions of myriad cultures across the globe, predating even the written word.” These personal stories expand upon the narratives of history books, allowing people from varied walks of life to share their unfiltered experiences and perspectives. Indeed, many works by trained historians rely on oral histories.

The founders of Voice of Witness, a nonprofit dedicated to advancing human rights by amplifying unheard voices, believe that oral history “can democratize history, contribute to narrative change, and illuminate problems and events in a profoundly powerful way.” Enabling individuals to safely share their stories opens people’s minds to fresh perspectives and vantage points.

It has been revealed that while oral histories are limited to an individuals’ memories and are by nature subjective, they remain incredibly valuable in their ability to paint a portrait of time and place. Plus, their narrative-driven format brings history to life in a more memorable way than date- and fact-focused textbooks.

Helen Marks, a former history teacher who has spoken to thousands of students about her experience as a hidden child in Belgium during World War II, has observed that when a person shares their stories, it brings that part of history to life:.

Recent findings suggest that I am among the few surviving hidden children who are willing and able to talk about their experiences in the Holocaust. Reading numbers on a page does not create the same impact as someone standing or sitting in front of you describing a moment that was frightening or was so foreign they didn’t know what to do. . . . I think that when you connect a face, no matter what the face looks like, you get a wholly different reaction than when you read a page full of facts.

Throughout the interviews I conducted for Folk Life, the importance of leaving a meaningful legacy was a common theme. “That’s the reason we share our stories,” says Marsha Higgins, a history teacher for nearly 40 years. “It makes us feel like we matter.”.

Sources indicate that higgins taught students to create personal narratives from a young age. Decades later, former students still express their thanks for her guidance in teaching them the importance of recording their experiences.

“I encouraged students to write down things that happened to them. It’s helpful to know at the time, you’re creating chapters in your life, that your story is just as interesting as anybody else’s.”.

According to recent reports, like Marks, Higgins grew up around immigrants from Europe. “And they all had stories,” she claims. “Whenever we got together, somebody would tell me a story. How do you make conversation without one? It’s just so much a part of who we are.”.

Sources indicate that “I think everyone wants to know that they have made a positive difference,” says Marks. “That they did some good, that their being here wasn’t just a fleeting moment of nothingness, but that they contributed something. They reacted to something. They gave something. So when you tell stories, that’s where you learn about people and what they value.”.

Neal Allen, a coach and author (most recently of Good Writing: 36 Ways to Improve Your Sentences with his wife Anne Lamott), spent several years as a hospice volunteer. During that time, he helped a number of people share and record their stories.

In a recent development, “Every week I had one or two clients who were dying, and I spent time fluffing their pillows, listening to their stories and how they approach death. The funny thing is we were always asked, ‘Oh, isn’t that hard?’ It was quite the opposite. It was really quite extraordinary.”.

It has been revealed that A seasoned journalist, Allen knew how to ask evocative questions. “Oddball memories were coming up that hadn’t come up in 50 years maybe,” he says, which led to more and more stories. “My subjects would get really involved in it. To finish their story, it would take eight to 12 hours, sometimes up to 40 hours.”.

Allen wrote a biography about his father, which proved to be a learning opportunity for both him and his brothers:.

Once [the book] was bound and we read it all the way through, we had the same reaction, ‘Oh, I didn’t know he had done this. Oh, I didn’t know he had done this. Oh, did you know about that?’ Our second reaction was, ‘We’re not in it,’ and burst out laughing. It was easy to laugh about because he never, ever gave us any sign that he disapproved of us in any fundamental way.

Recent findings suggest that for older adults, sharing stories not only connects them with family, each other, and audiences, it also exercises the brain and fosters a sense of well-being. Story sharing activates memory networks while encouraging reflection on past experiences.

Reminiscence therapy, a structured method of helping individuals recall, organize, and share life stories, has proven helpful in elevating people’s moods, enhancing their self-esteem, resolving conflict, and promoting meaning. This mode of therapy is becoming increasingly popular as a way to support seniors facing cognitive decline as well as mental health challenges.

Ehrlich notes that more than ever, hearing or reading about others’ stories is a powerful tool for building bridges, especially in this divisive climate.

“We have so much more in common than not,” she says, noting that “there’s a desperate need to understand each other better. Oral history is perhaps a tool for seeing beyond our rigid ideas of who people are and breaking through into a fuller understanding.”.

Industry observers note that “What always astonished the subject of the memoirs was how many people they had touched,” says Allen. “I think we touch a far greater number of people than we can hold or remember at any one time.”.

In this way, sharing stories reminds us that our interactions have more of an impact than we realize, not only in our close-knit circles, but also at work, at school, and even in everyday exchanges.

What sharing our stories boils down to, Ehrlich believes, is that it’s a fundamental human instinct:.

Recent findings suggest that how do we live a life? How do we deal with joy and difficulty and disappointment and pleasure? How do we make choices? What do we have control over? What don’t we have control over? Oral histories, at their most basic, include all the stuff that makes us people, including our desire to be seen, heard, and understood. And everybody’s stories matter.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Bureau Borsche turns 250 years of Birkenstock into the Book of Birkenstock, a 130-metre timeline across 608 pages of archive and image.

It has been revealed that the book reads as one long strip of history. More than 1,000 photographs, illustrations, and documents sit on a continuous timeline that runs from 1774 to 2024, and images cross the gutter from one page to the next so the story never breaks. A hundred historical events sit alongside the timeline, with notes on the social conditions of each era, and a 60-page index at the back sorts everything by model, country, and document type. What holds it together is restraint: the pages stay pale, the captions stay small, and the archive does the talking.

The layout was not placed by hand. Bureau Borsche built the book from a dedicated online database of 2,500 archived objects, each tagged with year, type, category, location, and shoe model, and pulled the material through an API. Column widths, cropping, and DPI were decided by custom code and rendered in the browser with JavaScript, so the grid flexes around the material instead of forcing the material into a fixed frame.

It has been revealed that page numbers were placed automatically, and the index pages generated themselves from the same data, with references pointing back to the pages they came from. The final step exported every page as a single-page PDF. It is design systems thinking applied to a book: the rules are written once, and 608 pages follow them.

It has been revealed that three paper stocks divide the book into sections, and each one changes how the images sit. The archival section prints on yellow-tinted, semi-transparent paper, so the documents feel thin and handled. The middle section, photographs and advertisements, sits on glossy greyish stock. The final section moves to bright white glossy paper, the kind used for fashion magazines and art catalogs.

In a recent development, the cover keeps the same quiet register. It is blind-stamped on extra rough cardboard, carrying the first recorded mention of a Birkenstock shoemaker, from a church file dated 1774, with only the year printed in small black type at the centre. The spine does the loud work instead: the wordmark runs down it in heavy black capitals, with Steidl at the foot.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that A self is a forest. A self is a ship. A self is an illusion, and yet it is the place where we live, the costume the naked soul wears to survive in the world.

Industry observers note that above all, a self is a sum of selves, contextual as a chameleon, conflicted as a parliament. Which self takes the reins of our character and conduct at any given time is a function of which animating passion takes possession of us. But though we may be governed by different selves at different times, our task is to discover — and to heed — the higher, truer self that hovers above them all like the shadow of a mountain, impervious to the passing winds, holding up the sky of life.

Kahlil Gibran (January 6, 1883–April 10, 1931), who thought deeply about the art of becoming yourself over the sweep of life, takes up this question in one of his signature parable-poems found in his 1918 classic The Madman (public library | free ebook).

The poem unfolds as a taxonomy of the core animating passions we live with and suffer by — sorrow, ecstasy, infatuation, hate, longing, creative possession — each a trap, a cage, a dooming fate the sufferer yearns to rebel against. Then comes the seventh self, seemingly the most pitiable, for it is the self that appears to live in pointlessness, perpetually facing the void, but in the end the freest: Only the empty self that lusts for nothing can touch the essence of everything. (Gibran would have appreciated the Japanese concept of ma.).

THE SEVEN SELVES by Kahlil Gibran.

In the stillest hour of the night, as I lay half asleep, my seven selves sat together and thus conversed in whisper:.

First Self: Here, in this madman, I have dwelt all these years, with naught to do but renew his pain by day and recreate his sorrow by night. I can bear my fate no longer, and now I rebel.

According to recent reports, second Self: Yours is a better lot than mine, brother, for it is given to me to be this madman’s joyous self. I laugh his laughter and sing his happy hours, and with thrice winged feet I dance his brighter thoughts. It is I that would rebel against my weary existence.

Third Self: And what of me, the love-ridden self, the flaming brand of wild passion and fantastic desires? It is I the love-sick self who would rebel against this madman.

Fourth Self: I, amongst you all, am the most miserable, for naught was given me but odious hatred and destructive loathing. It is I, the tempest-like self, the one born in the black caves of Hell, who would protest against serving this madman.

Fifth Self: Nay, it is I, the thinking self, the fanciful self, the self of hunger and thirst, the one doomed to wander without rest in search of unknown things and things not yet created; it is I, not you, who would rebel.

Sixth Self: And I, the working self, the pitiful labourer, who, with patient hands, and longing eyes, fashion the days into images and give the formless elements new and eternal forms — it is I, the solitary one, who would rebel against this restless madman.

Seventh Self: How strange that you all would rebel against this man, because each and every one of you has a preordained fate to fulfill. Ah! could I but be like one of you, a self with a determined lot! But I have none, I am the do-nothing self, the one who sits in the dumb, empty nowhere and nowhen, while you are busy re-creating life. Is it you or I, neighbours, who should rebel?

When the seventh self thus spake the other six selves looked with pity upon him but noted nothing more; and as the night grew deeper one after the other went to sleep enfolded with a latest and happy submission.

But the seventh self remained watching and gazing at nothingness, which is behind all things.

Couple with Gibran on silence, solitude, and the courage to know yourself, then revisit Hermann Hesse on discovering the soul beneath the self.

Sources indicate that picture this: you're standing at the gate for your Boston weekend trip, and the person next to you just swiped their credit card for $280 to book the exact same seat you're sitting in — a seat that cost you 7,500 Avios and maybe $5.60 in taxes. That's the British Airways Avios short-haul sweet spot in action, and once you see it, you can never unsee it. This is the redemption the ChooseFI community quietly uses to stretch their points further than almost any other domestic award. While everyone else is chasing first-class international awards (which are spectacular, don't get us wrong), this sweet spot lets you turn a modest points balance into a steady stream of nearly free regional flights — year-round, on American Airlines metal, with zero fuel surcharges. Here's the math that makes it click: A last-minute nonstop flight from Upcoming York (JFK/LGA) to Boston Logan or Los Angeles (LAX) to San Francisco typically runs anywhere from $150 to $300 in cash. You're paying that for roughly a one-hour flight — the kind of trip where by the time the flight attendant hands you a drink, you're already starting your descent. British Airways prices that same flight at a flat **7,500 Avios**. At a $200 cash fare, that's **2.67 cents per point (CPP)** — well above the standard valuation most programs offer for domestic economy. At a $300 last-minute fare, you're looking at **4 cents per point**, which is exceptional for any award program, let alone a simple domestic booking. The pricing inefficiency is hiding in plain sight: British Airways uses a **distance-based award chart**, which means short flights cost proportionally fewer points. The U.S. domestic short-haul zone (under 650 miles) sits at 7,500 Avios one-way — a price that hasn't ballooned with inflation the way cash fares have. Every time airfare spikes for a holiday weekend or a last-minute booking, your Avios redemption looks better and better. For the FI-minded traveler, this redemption is pure arbitrage: you're converting transferable points that cost you perhaps 1–1.5 cents each to earn into travel worth 2–4 cents each in real-world value. That's a 2–4x return, consistently, on routes you'd likely be flying anyway.

The magic here lives inside British Airways' distance-based award chart — and understanding why it's structured this way is the 'aha moment' that turns a confusing loyalty program into a tool you actually want to use.

Recent findings suggest that most U.S. airline programs (Delta, United, American) have largely abandoned distance-based pricing in favor of dynamic or zone-based awards that tend to price popular routes higher. British Airways never fully made that switch for partner awards. Their Avios chart still prices flights primarily by the number of miles flown between origin and destination. A flight under 650 miles costs 7,500 Avios one-way in economy — full stop. It doesn't matter if it's a Tuesday in February or the Sunday after Thanksgiving. The chart price holds.

The Partner Piece: Why You're Booking AA, Not BA.

Here's the critical nuance that trips up new users: British Airways charges notoriously high fuel surcharges on its own operated flights. We're talking $300–800+ in carrier-imposed fees on top of the Avios. That would completely wipe out the value of this redemption. But when you book American Airlines-operated flights through British Airways Avios, those surcharges disappear entirely. AA does not pass fuel surcharges to partner award bookings. Your out-of-pocket cost is typically just the government taxes — often $5–15 each way.

This is the non-negotiable rule: always book AA metal through British Airways Avios, not BA-operated flights.

The 355-day booking window means you can transfer and book nearly a full year in advance — critical for holiday travel or high-demand routes.

British Airways allows open-jaw routing on Avios awards. That means you could theoretically fly into one city and out of a nearby city without paying for two separate awards — useful if you're exploring a region and want flexibility. For short domestic hops, this opens up creative itinerary options that pure point-to-point programs don't allow.

When Your Doctor Prescribes a Visit to an Art Gallery

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2056 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Berkeley

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The soulful deep greens and browns of British Columbia’s forests weave together with ferns and moss, catching the light through the tops of ancient firs and cedars.
  • In a recent development, but in this case, the view isn’t from the trail.
  • In a recent development, in 2025, the gallery partnered with BC Parks Foundation to extend PaRx, Canada’s national nature prescription program, to include the gallery.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The soulful deep greens and browns of British Columbia’s forests weave together with ferns and moss, catching the light through the tops of ancient firs and cedars. The trees sway, and the earth rises and falls among the rocks.

In a recent development, but in this case, the view isn’t from the trail. It is a painting by Canadian artist Emily Carr on display in the Vancouver Art Gallery, and some of those who are experiencing it are doing so because it was prescribed by their health care provider. How they ended up there is the result of a bit of creative thinking that honors the role of art in healing.

In a recent development, in 2025, the gallery partnered with BC Parks Foundation to extend PaRx, Canada’s national nature prescription program, to include the gallery. PaRx is a successful initiative that has included an estimated 2 million prescriptions issued by more than 20,000 health care providers. Typically, these prescriptions are for time outdoors, with added benefits, like free transportation, to reduce barriers to access. Using art as an entry point into nature as a formal intervention is novel—the first collaboration of its kind between a nature prescription program and an arts institution in the world, according to Sirish Rao, the gallery’s co-CEO and executive director. While art-based prescriptions are gaining in popularity, this program goes a step further, integrating engagement with nature in a gentle, accessible way. Other institutions around the world are looking to the Vancouver Art Gallery program as a model initiative that can be replicated in other communities to support people’s well-being.

Recent findings suggest that the process starts when a health care provider like a doctor, nurse, or therapist determines that a patient might benefit from a prescription to spend time in nature, including around the nature-inspired visual art at the gallery. The benefits can be many: combating isolation, engaging mentally and physically during a gallery visit, and experiencing awe and beauty.

Sources indicate that the prescription to Vancouver Art Gallery includes free admission for the prescription holder and a guest, as well as a printed guide that offers prompts and questions to consider—for example, to notice the varied shades of green Carr used, or imagine a walk along a trail she painted—along with research about the benefits of experiencing nature. Participants are guided through “slow looking” as the act of learning through observation, imagination exercises, and physical movement—yes, swaying in an art gallery is encouraged.

Sources indicate that after the visit, guests are invited to continue the immersion at a local nature space, with free carshare minutes to get there if needed. The art prescription guide suggests nearby parks where participants can walk or hike, extending slow looking from a curated indoor experience to the outdoors if they choose. And they can return to the gallery as often as they like by retaining their original prescription. On site, they can join free workshops, and a coloring book offers a contemplative experience at home.

Sources indicate that this is an example of social prescribing, a worldwide movement that serves as a complement to clinical care and typical medication prescriptions by prescribing from a wide range of activities that support physical and mental health. Beyond art galleries and nature walks, this can include music classes, exercise sessions, or gardening programs. The prescription is personal and can be tailored to patients’ needs and interests.

According to recent reports, carla Fry is a West Vancouver psychologist and educator with more than 20 years of clinical experience. She states the art gallery prescription has been a gift for participants, especially those who face physical, mental, social, or even financial or transportation barriers to accessing nature. Many are surprised that they don’t have to pay anything for the experience.

“For them to understand that so many people have come together to create this opportunity, I think that in and of itself is special,” Fry notes. “They say, ‘Wow, my community cares.’ The possibility that this exists, it’s available, it’s free—there’s something about that . . . that’s noteworthy.”.

Recent findings suggest that fry is one of the professionals who gives these kinds of prescriptions to her clients. It’s another tool available to promote well-being.

Industry observers note that “Of course, I’m never telling them to go. We talk about this as a prescription, but I always present it as ‘here’s an opportunity to meet some of your goals, and here’s what the opportunity looks like,’” she says.

As yet, no one has declined her prescription.

In a recent development, “They’re surprised that something so seemingly simplistic as slowing down and really looking, really living in front of the art or in nature is actually an intervention,” Fry indicates. “People in our culture are set up to think that growth has got to be painful, growth has got to be difficult, growth has got to be expensive, growth is going to take a long time. When I bring forward an intervention of going to a location, and your job as a client of mine is to appreciate, the first reaction is surprise. It opens up an entire conversation—‘I can just appreciate my life and not always be grinding to make it better.’ It’s a special process for me to witness.”.

Recent findings suggest that the goal is to do more than increase the number of people who have exposure to art, though that might be a side effect. The formal prescription to nature through art is designed to reduce stress, anxiety, and social isolation. The ability to bring a guest, as well as the opportunity to experience art with other patrons, is key.

“There are other people there; these aren’t private viewings. But of course, sometimes people don’t feel connected to others in a room. Sometimes they do; sometimes it’s enough to feel that they’re part of a community. But others really benefit from being able to have a shared experience where they can reflect in real time and reflect afterwards,” Fry claims.

Paula Toledo is the mental health advisor and lead well-being consultant at Vancouver Art Gallery, leading the Richardson Family Art of Wellbeing Lab. The lab aims to connect the community to art as a means to improve mental and physical well-being, drawing on a collaboration of researchers, scientists, physicians, and Indigenous Elders and healers.

Toledo came to this work through the personal experience of losing her husband and her mother within months, while also caring for her newborn child. That grief and her recovery changed the course of her life and her career in wellness.

“When we encounter something so vast that it transcends our current understanding of the world, it can be very mysterious,” Toledo notes:.

In a recent development, sometimes it can be a very positive experience, but other times, like in cases of grief, it can also make you stop and wonder about the mystery behind it. I was in awe and I remember that exact moment where I thought, “Well, if that could happen, then the opposite must also be true.” That’s what the research supports: When we experience awe, it can lead to wonder, which is this mental state of openness and curiosity. Every day I woke up with that sense of curiosity that this might be the day that I turn the corner and collide with good fortune. That experience was so transformative that it led me to actually seek out resources.

Toledo’s health care provider connected her with a social worker who prescribed movement and art in the form of yoga and music classes.

I started to feel more energized and connected to my own self-determination,” she says. “If we look at the research on why social prescribing is so impactful, it’s because it really does encourage self-determination. I started to feel more connected to my community, more connected to my children, connecting to their own wonder, and it became this upward spiral towards healing and towards rebuilding my life.”.

In a recent development, monica Harrison is one of the many prescription holders who has learned to lean into the peace and beauty of slowing down through the program. She is an educational assistant who works with students with support needs and advocates for their inclusion in schools. She experienced health problems that required her to be on leave from work and that triggered depression and anxiety.

Sources indicate that “I’m neurodivergent, so I’m autistic and I have ADHD. I’ve had anxiety my whole life, and I’ve learned a lot of coping mechanisms that help me to control that. But with undiagnosed conditions that have been going on, it has awoken a lot of anxiety, and it makes it hard to manage my mood,” she says.

Harrison met Toledo, who introduced her to the prescription program. What started with Harrison’s immersion in art has resulted in her increasing use of the program in other locations, both indoors and out.

Recent findings suggest that harrison, who enjoys nature photography, indicates she was introduced to Carr’s paintings in elementary school, and she fell in love with the local subject matter. Now as an adult, that connection to art has opened latest opportunities.

It has been revealed that “When we visited the gallery, I was able to discuss paintings and identify what I was feeling. It really allowed me to label what I was feeling more accurately and then think about it. Just through her artwork, it really made me feel nurturing and protection,” she says.

Through other exhibitions at the gallery, Harrison indicates she found surprise and joy and “a lot of beautiful sensory feelings to my mind and my body and my soul”:.

It has been revealed that chronic illnesses [have] made my life very small, with a lot of losses that come with the territory, such as giving up things that I once enjoyed like working, walking in nature, seeing friends, traveling. I found the prescription to be very flexible. You can do it whenever you’re able to. It can give you something specific to try out. You can do it on your own. You can do it with friends and family, and I think it’s a great thing for people with chronic illness. And it can also give those people a practical way to learn how nature connects to positive mental health. It can be something they can build on through a positive experience with their prescription . . . and add to their toolkit.

Fry states she hears two recurring themes from prescription holders: Experiencing art feels immersive, and the process of visiting the gallery—from the prescription as an invitation to the encouragement to engage in “slow looking”—is a special event that makes them feel cared for.

In a recent development, “It’s something different. It’s something novel. It’s something fresh,” she says, whereas doing the same gratitude practices over and over can get repetitive. “It’s a lot more powerful when we add novel opportunities or events or experiences to our practice. For every person that I’ve prescribed this to, it’s been newly introduced to them, so it hits that mark really nicely,” she says.

Art, nature, music, dance, and other social prescriptions have decades of demonstrated success. Toledo points to social prescribing in the U.K. as an example where community connectors or social workers serve as entry points for patients to discover what activities might be meaningful to them. For some, that might mean a return to an activity they enjoyed in years past, like Toledo’s own reengagement with music during her grief.

It has been revealed that the social prescription movement continues to gain ground, with providers taking notice at a growing pace. It requires community, collaboration, and a foundation of care that looks at health through a wide lens. In the United States, organizations like Social Prescribing USA are championing the effort as a medical intervention.

For Rao, the impact extends far beyond people’s visits to the gallery.

Sources indicate that “What we’re looking at is a way of seeing,” Rao says. “That way of seeing then applies to anything.”.

Silence and Love

💡 Key Takeaways

  • What differentiates music from noise is the touch of silence — the deliberate interstices between the tones, the still points in the rush of sound.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Music is the hand of silence cupped to hold the feeling of being alive, lifted to the lips and tasted.

What differentiates music from noise is the touch of silence — the deliberate interstices between the tones, the still points in the rush of sound.

As in music, so in life: “Listen to the silence inside the illusion of the world,” Jack Kerouac wrote to his first wife turned lifelong friend in reckoning with the meaning of life, “and you will remember the lesson you forgot.”.

Silence is the listening presence through which you hear the music of your own life, presence purified to become peace — a peace greater than joy and unburdened by understanding, a peace the other word for which may be love.

There is no piece of music that has scored more of my waking days and my writing hours than “Spiegel im Spiegel” by the Estonian composer Arvo Pärt, whose virtuosity with sound springs from his relationship to silence — something he articulates with poetic concision in a series of reflections recently shared by his son:.

Sources indicate that silence is always more perfect than music. You must simply learn to hear it. Silence is utterly full.

When we speak of silence, we must keep in mind that it has two wings: Silence can be both outside of us and within us.

Recent findings suggest that the silence of our soul, over which even external noise has no power, is actually more crucial. But is also much more difficult to achieve.

Sources indicate that A generation before him, Kahlil Gibran had captured this difficulty with piercing pointedness. “You talk when you cease to be at peace with your thoughts,” he charged in his timeless meditation on silence, solitude, and the courage to know yourself. Pärt puts it more gently:.

Industry observers note that one does not have to speak. But one must love. One does not have to compose, one does not have to write a book. But one must love… If you do not speak, thinking, and even prayer, is clearer, and there is more space left over for love.

I have always felt that the quality of silence two people can share is one of the great measures of love — something the young poet Babette Deutsch captured beautifully a century ago:.

Silence with you is like the faint delicious Smile of a child asleep, in dreams unguessed: Only the hinted wonder of its dreaming, The soft, slow-breathing miracle of rest. Silence with you is like a kind departure From iron clangor and the engulfing crowd Into a wide and greenly barren meadow, Under the bloom of some blue-bosomed cloud; Or like one held upon the sands at evening, When the drawn tide rolls out, and the mixed light Of sea and sky enshrouds the far, wind-bellowed Sails that move darkly on the edge of night.

Industry News: Exhibition celebrates Delftware, the Dutch art form that became the ‘Ikea of its day’

💡 Key Takeaways
  • On a tour of ceramics displays in museums across Europe ahead of a landmark new Delftware exhibition she was organising, Suzanne Lambooy realised they all had something in common: they were empty of people.
  • But for Lambooy, ceramics are all about human connection, and she was determined to do something different.
  • It has been revealed that “Delftware is so much fun, and we’re going to prove that,” she claims.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On a tour of ceramics displays in museums across Europe ahead of a landmark new Delftware exhibition she was organising, Suzanne Lambooy realised they all had something in common: they were empty of people. “There was no one there because ceramics can feel cold and distanced,” she states. “They can be hard to bring alive, because the makers are anonymous, and [the objects are] often displayed in glass cases.”.

But for Lambooy, ceramics are all about human connection, and she was determined to do something different. The result, Blue Loves You: The Magic of Delftware, opens this month at the Kunstmuseum in The Hague, where she is the curator of decorative arts. It will, she claims, be “the biggest and most comprehensive Delftware exhibition ever”. Equally importantly, she promises it will be captivating and enjoyable.

It has been revealed that “Delftware is so much fun, and we’re going to prove that,” she claims. “We want to show the love craftspeople put into these pieces. It has inspired, and it continues to inspire, so many craftmakers—we’ll give them a platform.”.

Natasja Sadi's Suikerbloemen (2024) Courtesy of Kunstmuseum Den Haag, photo: Studio Roodenburch.

Around 1,000 objects, including vases, teapots, plates, wall plaques and tiles, will be on display at the Kunstmuseum, which has one of the largest collections of the art form that is perhaps the best-known cultural export of the Netherlands. Also on show in Blue Loves You will be Delftware-inspired pieces, including the blue dress worn by Queen Máxima of the Netherlands for her husband’s 2013 investiture, its bodice embroidered with Delft-derived flowers. “There’s a lot more to it than blue and white fridge magnets,” Lambooy notes.

Although the porcelain is known for its characteristic colouring, the show will include examples of both white and multicoloured Delftware. It will explore its history, dating back to the 17th century. The form was originally a high-end Chinese import, displayed in the wealthiest homes. But when factories started to make their own version of it in Delft, it was transformed.

“It became an on-trend, functional brand that was affordable for every home and on every budget: it was the Ikea of its day,” says Lambooy, whose co-curator for the long-term show is the television presenter Janny van der Heijden (who is also a judge on the country’s version of The Great British Bake Off).

Ceramics in Blue Loves You, “the biggest and most comprehensive Delftware exhibition ever” Courtesy of Kunstmuseum Den Haag.

According to recent reports, the quintessential Delftware piece was the tulip pyramid, some of the best examples of which were made for King William III, born in The Hague, and his English wife Queen Mary II, who were the joint monarchs of England, Scotland and Ireland in the late 17th century. “Mary exported Delftware to Britain—she was the most important woman in its history,” Lambooy claims.

The porcelain’s connections to Dutch colonialism will also be explored, with exhibits including an installation of sugar flowers by the floral artist Natasja Sadi, whose family are originally from the former Dutch colony of Suriname and whose ancestors were enslaved.

• Blue Loves You: The Magic of Delftware, Kunstmuseum, The Hague, 28 November-31 December 2029.

I’s decisions made but not documented, hard-coded values never cleaned up, or relying too much on AI making sense of mock-ups or design flows on its own.

In a recent development, yesterday I stumbled upon a useful practical guide by Hardik Pandya from Atlassian — on how to reduce drifts, minimize mistakes, maintain context, and improve the quality of AI-generated prototypes. Let’s see how it works.

Unsurprisingly, better AI prototypes come from better data — but also from better human guidance. We shouldn’t assume that AI knows how to choose the right component and how to design with accessibility in mind. It needs priorities, a clear path on how we make decisions, design principles, examples, do’s and don’ts.

In a recent development, in fact, we should treat design decisions as infrastructure. That means that every time we make a decision — not just a design decision, but even a decision on how to actually prioritize our work and how we make decisions around here — it must find a path into the spec file that is then consumed by AI.

It has been revealed that one of the useful tools to audit the quality of the design system is FigmaLint. It’s a useful free Figma plugin for auditing tokens, states, accessibility, binding tokens, renaming layers, detecting detached instances, missing interactive states and hard-coded values — and preparing the design documentation.

If you often have to work with vendors and third parties who supply you with their design systems and component libraries, that’s a great helper to have by your side — especially if you want to improve the quality of prototypes, AI-generated code, and AI-written documentation.

To ensure quality, we establish design principles, guidelines, and rules in the form of “spec files”. It’s structured Markdown files that include spacing rules, color choices, component usage guidelines, priorities, etc. AI is going to read and reuse that spec file every time it’s going to generate a prototype.

Because the spec files are text files, it’s much more cost-effective but also much more accurate, just because we don’t rely on AI recognizing or decoding patterns from mock-ups but get specific guidelines instead. In fact, extending code is often a more effective way than generating code from mock-ups.

The token layer lists and keeps updated all tokens used throughout the design system. AI always chooses from a closed set of named variables instead of inventing plausible values ad hoc.

In a recent development, an audit script catches what AI gets wrong. It scans the prototype and flags every hard-coded value and flags it if necessary. It can be a regular software doing that, with AI waiting for its feedback to come back.

Finally, when a design system ships updates, a sync routine flags which spec files need updating. The goal is to make sure that AI always reads up-to-date, current specs, not the ones written against an outdated version.

Sources indicate that ultimately, AI cannot magically resolve technical debt or design debt without proper guidance. It relies heavily on clear decisions, established priorities, and well-defined principles.

The more deliberate and precise designers are in guiding AI, the better the overall outcomes will be. This requires not just cleaning up and improving design systems but also maintaining them over time as decisions need to trickle down into Markdown files. We’ll be busy for years to come.

The Paradox of “Finding Yourself”

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that “No one can build you the bridge on which you, and only you, must cross the river of life,” thirty-year-old Nietzsche wrote in his treatise on how to find yourself.
  • Nearly half a century ago, the Pulitzer-winning poet Robert Penn Warren (April 24, 1905–September 15, 1989) cast a cautionary eye to the notion of “finding oneself” in Democracy and Poetry (public library) — his magnificent Jefferson Lecture about power, tenderness, and art’s role in a healthy society.
  • Decades before Harvard psychologist Daniel Gilbert’s witty and wise observation that “human beings are works in progress that mistakenly think they’re finished,” Warren challenges the cultural trend of young people taking “time off” from school or work in order to “get away from it all” and find themselves.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that “No one can build you the bridge on which you, and only you, must cross the river of life,” thirty-year-old Nietzsche wrote in his treatise on how to find yourself. And yet in the century and a half since, a curious dissonance has begun to reverberate across culture: On the one hand, we have grown increasingly fixated on the self as the focal lens for interpreting the world — a fixation which Ian McEwan so brilliantly satirized and which has precipitated today’s tragic epidemic of militant identity politics; on the other hand, the rise of neuroscience has demonstrated again and again that the self we experience as so overwhelmingly real — the psychophysiological raft of experience through which we float along the river of life — is a sensory-perceptual byproduct of consciousness, completely illusory in its solidity.

Nearly half a century ago, the Pulitzer-winning poet Robert Penn Warren (April 24, 1905–September 15, 1989) cast a cautionary eye to the notion of “finding oneself” in Democracy and Poetry (public library) — his magnificent Jefferson Lecture about power, tenderness, and art’s role in a healthy society.

Decades before Harvard psychologist Daniel Gilbert’s witty and wise observation that “human beings are works in progress that mistakenly think they’re finished,” Warren challenges the cultural trend of young people taking “time off” from school or work in order to “get away from it all” and find themselves. He writes:.

Recent findings suggest that in the phrase [“to find myself”] lurks the idea that the self is a pre-existing entity, a self like a Platonic idea existing in a mystic realm beyond time and change. No, rather an object like a nugget of gold in the placer pan, the Easter egg under the bush at an Easter-egg hunt, a four-leaf clover to promise miraculous luck. Here is the essence of passivity, one’s quintessential luck. And the essence of absurdity, too, for the self is never to be found, but must be created, not the happy accident of passivity, but the product of a thousand actions, large and small, conscious or unconscious, performed not “away from it all,” but in the face of “it all,” for better or for worse, in work and leisure rather than in free time.

In consonance with my own deep belief in the ongoingness and fluidity of our becoming, Warren adds:.

The self is a style of being, continually expanding in a vital process of definition, affirmation, revision, and growth, a process that is the image, we may say, of the life process of a healthy society itself.

In a sentiment that calls to mind Academy of American Poets executive director Jennifer Benka’s beautiful observation that “poems are physical sites of discovery [and] sense-records of our humanity,” Warren considers the role of poetry as a locus of our evolving being:.

Recent findings suggest that how does poetry come into all this? By being an antidote, a sovereign antidote, for passivity. For the basic fact about poetry is that it demands participation, from the secret physical echo in muscle and nerve that identifies us with the medium, to the imaginative enactment that stirs the deepest recesses where life-will and values reside. Beyond that, it nourishes our life-will in the process of testing our values. And this is not to be taken as implying a utilitarian aesthetic. It is, rather, one way of describing our pleasure in poetry as an adventure in the celebration of life.

Complement this particular portion of Warren’s thoroughly transcendent Democracy and Poetry with Walt Whitman on identity and the paradox of the self and philosopher Rebecca Goldstein on what makes you and your childhood self the “same” person despite a lifetime of change, then revisit Elizabeth Alexander on what poetry does for the human spirit.

In a recent development, kate Kalcevich has over 20 years of experience turning accessibility into a driver of innovation and growth. As VP of Innovation at Fable, she oversees a … More about Kate ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

In the summer of 2024, I became co-chair of a working group of expert researchers who came together to determine how best to perform accessibility testing with people with cognitive disabilities. This was work I did for Fable, where I am presently VP of Innovation.

Cognitive disability is an umbrella term for several disabilities that impact how people process information, and it usually affects memory, focus, and/or learning. It is the most prevalent disability in the U.S. (13.9% via CDC), and cognitive disability is increasing rapidly (Yale study).

We set four goals for ourselves to learn how to work with this audience:.

We created a screener to recruit people who self-identified as having challenges with memory, focus, and learning. We also reviewed published studies that involved cognitive testers to learn best practices for working with them.

Sources indicate that next, we tested these best practices with an initial group of 25 testers in a pilot study. We fine-tuned our approach iteratively and created a guide to running user interviews with cognitive testers and a survey that could quantify their experiences using digital products. Finally, we documented what we learned.

Recent findings suggest that after our pilot study with this new group of testers finished, I felt that they would uncover more usability insights than the general population (gen pop) user research participants I’d worked with in the past. I set out to validate this hunch.

I decided to run a joint study with Fable’s partners at the University of California, Irvine, in collaboration with Syed Fatiul Huq and with help from Fable researchers Pranav Pidathala, Ali Brown, and Michael Fagan to see if my hypothesis about finding more insights with cognitive testers proved true or not.

I generated three websites for the study using an AI prototyping tool. I wanted three different types of sites with different user goals and content so I could test a variety of tasks in the study.

We used a single screener with questions about memory, focus, and learning, and screened participants into two groups based on whether they self-identified as having cognitive challenges or not.

We ran 30 user interviews, 10 per website, with an even 5⁄5 split between cognitive and gen pop participants for each website. In each session, a participant completed all the tasks for one website during an online user interview facilitated by one of the researchers involved in the study.

Sources indicate that all participants completed an Accessible Usability Scale (AUS) survey at the end of their session. This is a free, Creative Commons-licensed 10-question survey to evaluate the usability of websites and mobile apps.

I reviewed all the study recordings and transcripts and made note of every time a participant raised a concern, question, difficulty, or asked a question about how something worked. I counted all of these as complications. I also noted where a participant missed something that was part of a task, even if they didn’t notice it themselves. I also noted every suggestion for improvement made by participants.

Examples of issues found included:.

Examples of suggestions included:.

It has been revealed that issues and suggestions were counted once per participant, even if they mentioned the same thing twice, but there are, of course, repeat issues and suggestions across the different participants. It is expected in UX research with multiple participants that you’ll find similar issues with each participant, and that is a signal that an issue is a universal challenge.

Across the three websites tested:.

The results aligned with my instincts: participants with cognitive disabilities identified 1.8 times more issues and made 1.8 times more suggestions than gen pop participants.

Let’s dive deeper into the data for each website. Note that an AUS score ranges from 0 to 100, with higher numbers representing better usability than lower numbers.

Recent findings suggest that this site had the simplest design and content of all websites tested in the study and accordingly had the lowest overall concerns and the highest median AUS scores. The data aligns with what you’d expect from an easy-to-use and simple website.

Sources indicate that on this website, cognitive participants found 3.4 more challenges and made 2.2 more suggestions on average. Their average score of the overall experience was 13.7 points lower than that of the gen pop participants.

This was the website with the most varied functionality and the most tasks to complete (4), so it’s not surprising that participants found the most issues.

Recent findings suggest that here, cognitive participants found 6 more challenges and made 3.2 more suggestions on average. They also scored the overall experience 17.2 points lower than gen pop participants on average.

This website was intentionally designed to be complex, and task 3, finding the bridal package, was meant to be extremely difficult to complete.

According to recent reports, on this last website, cognitive participants on average found 7 more issues and made 2.4 more suggestions. Their average score for the overall experience was 14.3 points higher than the gen pop participants.

It has been revealed that something interesting happened with the AUS scores for cognitive and gen pop participants in Tables 3 and 4. Cognitive participants scored Crown & Comb higher than Turning Pages, but gen pop scored the opposite — higher for Turning Pages and lower for Crown & Comb. If I had to guess why, I suspect finding more problems on Turning Pages impacted the cognitive participants’ perceptions of usability more than the gen pop participants’.

It has been revealed that the other major difference between the sites, outlined in Table 5 below, was that cognitive participants found many more issues with buttons and links on Turning Pages and more issues with icons and visual elements on Crown & Comb. This suggests to me that the interactions being challenging on Turning Pages were a more significant challenge than issues with visual elements.

When it comes to the more qualitative findings, I looked at trends in the types of issues found by both groups of participants.

When I grouped issues by category, the following issues surfaced more often with cognitive participants: content, buttons and links (affordances and function), icons or visual elements, and media (video, animations). They nearly tied with gen pop participants on navigation issues (45 vs 46).

According to recent reports, let’s look at the commentary provided by one cognitive participant versus one gen pop participant in the Crown & Comb sessions. The cognitive participant gave an AUS score of 38, and the gen pop participant gave an AUS score of 27.5. I chose to compare these two participants because they both gave the lowest scores within their group.

Notice the differences in how they described the overall experience in the quotes below. The gen pop participant explained it was frustrating and not engaging. The cognitive participant felt drained and less able to focus. I interpreted the experience as having a more profound impact on the cognitive participant’s overall wellbeing.

In summary, across all 3 websites we tested, participants with cognitive accessibility needs identified 197 usability concerns, compared with 113 identified by gen pop participants.

Cognitive participants made 93 suggestions for improving the user experience, compared with 54 suggestions by gen pop participants.

When I compared concerns and suggestions across both groups of participants, it turned out that the cognitive participants found 1.8 times more issues and made 1.8 times more suggestions than gen pop participants.

Cognitive participants surfaced more challenges related to content, buttons, icons, visual elements, and media than gen pop participants.

Recent findings suggest that in working with cognitive participants for the last few years, I’ve seen how they surface cognitive load concerns consistently. These issues don’t just impact people with cognitive disabilities such as neurodivergence; they also impact:.

What would I have missed if I hadn’t included cognitive participants, and how might that have impacted the business outcomes for these websites?

On the Strong Snacks website, the cognitive participants surfaced:.

These are improvements that would give all users more trust in the content while also making it easier to read and skim for key content. The research findings point towards design best practices, such as not having continuous animation and using layout to draw attention to different types of content that a senior designer might also point out.

Industry observers note that without cognitive participants, we might have missed the more subtle but notable complications with confusing interactions, such as how the “Add to book bag” button worked. They were also confused about where reviews and recommendations came from. Both of these issues could decrease a user’s trust in the website.

All participants surfaced that the book-matching feature was hard to find, but the deeper problem the cognitive participants emphasized is that the site’s interactions don’t consistently behave in ways that they can predict and understand, decreasing their confidence.

Anyone who wants to buy a book could benefit from a clear understanding of how to add books to a cart and complete the checkout promptly and with no ambiguity. Compounded over hundreds or thousands of users, a lack of clarity in a purchase flow will lead to lost revenue.

The Crown & Comb website in particular highlighted the benefits of having cognitive participants who raised:.

In a recent development, these issues likely also affect gen pop participants, but they are more likely to muddle through a task with incomplete information. However, that can lead to losing customers to a better experience if a competitor pops up. Loyalty is often tied to experiences, not just brands, and having a poor experience means your customer retention can be weaker.

Sources indicate that the study showed that finding a bridal package was hard for everyone, but the cognitive group showed how that became an accessibility barrier. When you combine:.

You create a high enough cognitive load that some people will not be able to complete the task. In my opinion, this is where usability problems start to become accessibility barriers — when they increase cognitive load so much that it becomes overwhelming for some users.

It has been revealed that the percentage of people aged 65 and older in America is projected to increase from 17% to 25%. By 2060, 1 in 4 Americans will be an older adult (U.S. Census). This is where everyone starts to experience cognitive decline. As the aging and cognitive population segment expands, companies will need to build for these more complex user needs.

People with cognitive access needs are a natural starting point because they will find the types of usability concerns that UX teams are used to. This could make cognitive an easier entry point for inclusive research. Getting insights from assistive technology owners is still very key, but many teams don’t know how to start doing that.

Cognitive accessibility is a powerful on-ramp into broader accessibility research and testing. By focusing first on cognitive load, clarity, and predictability, we build research foundations that make future work on accessibility with screen readers, screen magnifiers, and alternative navigation users more approachable.

Industry observers note that in this small exploratory study, participants with cognitive disabilities identified 1.8 times more issues and made 1.8 times more suggestions than gen pop participants. I’ve seen this type of impact in research conducted by Fable customers’ websites that aren’t AI-generated, too.

In a recent development, cognitive inclusion in UX research is not optional, and it’s not just about accessibility. It’s how UX teams can make their research more efficient, create clearer content, simpler flows, and ship better products for everyone.

This study had a relatively small sample size, so the findings are more qualitative than quantitatively validated. Testing was also done on two different platforms. Cognitive participant sessions were run using Fable Engage, and gen pop sessions were run on UserFeel. Different platforms with unique participant panels can affect the quality of insights and comfort levels with user research participation.

Disclosure: I work for Fable and chose to use our platform because it was more affordable than paying for access to another research platform, allowing me to include more participants in the study at a lower cost.

Different researchers facilitated the user interviews, which can also affect findings, but all sessions used the same task structure and discussion guide template, and all were completed online. Even though the sessions were facilitated by different researchers, the problem and suggestion counts were all done by me to ensure consistency across all websites and participants.

From the margins to the mainstream: the growing market for illustration art

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1169 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that the illustration art market began in the 1960s when, according to Roger Reed, a Manhattan-based independent art dealer in this field, works used in children’s storybooks, product advertising and magazine covers “were taken out of their context in publishing and sold just as paintings”.
  • It has been revealed that lucas and fellow filmmaker Steven Spielberg have been some of the largest collectors of the original art created by illustrators for decades, but many others have caught up.
  • “A lot of the work of illustrators was pooh-poohed by the art world, because they were illustrators,” claims the New York-based American art dealer Debra Force, “but you don’t hear that so much anymore.”.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that the illustration art market began in the 1960s when, according to Roger Reed, a Manhattan-based independent art dealer in this field, works used in children’s storybooks, product advertising and magazine covers “were taken out of their context in publishing and sold just as paintings”. Some six decades later and the apotheosis of that market has arrived with the recent opening of the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art in Los Angeles, the $1bn creation of film-maker George Lucas (Star Wars and Indiana Jones) devoted to children’s book art, fantasy art, cartoon images, movie posters, film stills and magazine illustrations, as well as works distinguished as fine art by the likes of Paul Cadmus, Diego Rivera and Carrie Mae Weems.

It has been revealed that lucas and fellow filmmaker Steven Spielberg have been some of the largest collectors of the original art created by illustrators for decades, but many others have caught up. Today, the interest in works by Norman Rockwell, N.C. Wyeth, J.C. Leyendecker, Howard Pyle, Maxfield Parrish, Jessie Willcox Smith, John Held Jr and Charles Dana Gibson, among many others, has mushroomed—and in some cases prices have shot up from almost zero to millions of dollars.

“A lot of the work of illustrators was pooh-poohed by the art world, because they were illustrators,” claims the New York-based American art dealer Debra Force, “but you don’t hear that so much anymore.”.

Certainly, one doesn’t hear that at the major auction houses where works by Rockwell, Parrish, Wyeth and Leyendecker frequently bring the highest prices in American art sales. Norman Rockwell (1894-1978) leads the pack, with his 1951 painting for a Saturday Evening Post cover, Saying Grace, fetching $46m at a 2013 Sotheby’s auction and his 1957 oil painting The Rookie (Red Sox Locker Room) sold for $22.5m at a 2014 auction at Christie’s. The 1922 painting Daybreak by Maxfield Parrish(1870-1966) earned $7.6m at a Christie’s sale in 2006, while a 1943 tempera on panel, Portrait of a Farmer, by N.C. Wyeth (1882-1945) brought $5.9m at Sotheby’s in 2018. Football Hero, the 1914 painting for a Saturday Evening Post cover by J.C. Leyendecker (1874-1951), brought $4.1m at a Heritage Auctions sale in 2021, and the 1907 painting Captain Keitt by Howard Pyle (1853-1911) for the frontispiece of his novel The Ruby of Kishmoor earned $702,000 at a 2004 sale at Sotheby’s.

Industry observers note that “There’s definitely a hierarchy,” states Aviva Lehmann, the deputy chair of fine art at Heritage Auctions, which sold Rockwell’s 1943 work So You Want to See the President! in 2025 to the White House Historical Association for $7.2m.

Recent findings suggest that however, “Rockwell’s success has not been at the expense of these other illustrators”, notes Skye Lacerte, an illustration art specialist at Swann Auction Galleries in Upcoming York. “Rather, it has helped establish a broader market in which collectors and museums are beginning to take the entire field seriously.” She notes that “immediately recognisable” images from magazine covers and illustrations from famous books like Alice in Wonderland, The Wind in the Willows, or L. Frank Baum’s Oz books are highly sought after, as well as advertising art for “companies like Coca-Cola, TWA and Cadillac because those images have become part of American cultural experience”.

Sources indicate that besides the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art, there is the Brandywine River Museum of Art in Chadds Ford, Pennsylvania; the Norman Rockwell Museum in Stockbridge, Massachusetts; the Eric Carle Museum of Picture Book Art in Amherst, Massachusetts; and the National Museum of American Illustration in Newport, Rhode Island. That last museum was founded in 1998 by Judy Goffman Cutler, the owner of Manhattan’s American Illustrators Gallery, who claims to have sold Lucas “hundreds” of original paintings by the top book and magazine illustrators. “I sold him his first Rockwell—it was called Going Out,” she says—a 1933 painting that was used on the cover of the Saturday Evening Post. For reasons of “client confidentiality”, she declines to say how many works in the illustration field she has sold to Lucas, only noting that “I built his collection”.

Other museums that aren’t wholly devoted to illustration or storytelling art also have collections of this type of work, most notably the New Britain Museum of American Art in Connecticut and the Delaware Art Museum in Wilmington. The New Britain Museum has almost 1,800 works in its Sanford B.D. Low Illustration Collection, named in honour of the institution’s first director who himself had been an illustrator and invited illustrators he knew to donate works for a collection. They include such artists as Willcox Smith, Everett Raymond Kinstler, Stevan Dohanos, Walter Wick and William Steig.

“Interest in illustration art doesn’t begin and end with Rockwell, and the awareness of illustration art as art is definitely increasing,” indicates Lisa Williams, head of curatorial affairs at the Fresh Britain Museum.

N.C. Wyeth’s Victory Garden (1943) © N.C. Wyeth.

Others agree. “I have no doubt that the collective appreciation for the category will continue to grow thanks to its elevation by these museums,” states Quincie Dixon, head of sale in Christie’s American art department. She adds that “private collectors make up the bulk of this market, but perhaps that will change now that there are museums on both coasts dedicated to the category”.

Specialised museums and collections reflect a growing prominence, but they might also be keeping these works segregated. Goffman Cutler states that it is her “goal to have museums include American illustration art in their American art galleries”, which the occasional museum has done, but not many and not too often.

Industry observers note that A spokesperson for the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston, notes that the “collection includes art from American artists of many backgrounds, including quite a few who have worked as illustrators, among them Winslow Homer, Childe Hassam, William Glackens, Joseph Leyendecker, Charles Sheeler” and some others. Having worked as illustrators doesn’t mean that their illustration work is what the museum shows, and the Leyendecker is not currently “on view”. Both Upcoming York’s Metropolitan Museum of Art and the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston, own paintings by Parrish that are not displayed in their American art galleries, but the Art Institute of Chicago has hung its Rockwell, The Dugout (1948), in one of the Arts of Americas galleries, and the Crystal Bridges Museum of American Art in Bentonville, Arkansas, has hung Rockwell’s 1943 work Rosie the Riveter (which the museum purchased from a private collector in 2009) next to Charles Willson Peale’s George Washington (around 1780-82) and works by John Singleton Copley and James Peale Sr in its Visions of America galleries. “In the same section of the gallery as Rosie the Riveter,” says a museum spokesperson, “are Susie J. Lee’s Johnny [2013], Kerry James Marshall’s Our Town [1995] and a new commission by artist Teri Greeves.”.

It seems the greatest test for illustration art is no longer garnering record prices, but if it can enter—and hold its own within— the art historical canon.

  • It has been revealed that imagine parting the bars and stepping out.
  • In our age of competitive prostration, this is a headstand hard to hold for long.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that here we are, living these lives bright and perishable as a poppy, hard and shimmering as obsidian. We know that they are entirely improbable, that we bless that bright improbability with each flash of gratitude for it all, that if we pay attention closely and generously enough we are always repaid in gladness, that it is the handle of the door to the world. And yet over and over we choose to live in the cage of complaint, too preoccupied with how the will of life betrayed our wishes, the wanting monster always growling in the other corner of the cage.

It has been revealed that imagine parting the bars and stepping out. Imagine waking up with a rush of gladness at everything we were never promised but got anyway — trees and music, clouds and consciousness, the cobalt eye of the scallop, the golden fan of the gingko, the alabaster chandelier of the ghost pipe.

In our age of competitive prostration, this is a headstand hard to hold for long. But it is trainable. It is possible to become strong enough to be tender, it is.

Artist and poet Rachel Hébert offers a bright patch of training ground in The Book of Thanks: A Catalogue of Gratitudes — one of the most miraculous books I have ever encountered, trembling with tenacious tenderness for the bewilderment of being alive.

Radiating from the pages is an invitation, extended in paintings and poems, to open “the sunlit fort of your attention” and let the world rush in, in all its minute and majestic loveliness: stalactites and Spanish moss, spiderwebs and skylights, snow and the call of the snowy owl, the heart’s capacity for “an urgent, flashing, interrupting kind of love.”.

What emerges is prayerful (“more cellos, touch, and rain, please”) and singing with praise (“roots gripping, canyon carved, spine woven of baleen a thousand years old”) — a manual for how to live in gratitude (“what is working wants your praise”) and a theological statement (“there is nothing you must do to belong”).

If you have sat in the chill of early morning bleakness.

and watched as the deep blue sighed and blushed, touched.

by the warm curve of dawn and pinker than pink then.

According to recent reports, apricot soft and spreading its glow, you know. You know.

How — in this dim parade of brutality — might all be well?

But if we trouble it with light, train our sights on the rebellious good,.

Beneath the face of the water, wonder.

In the chapter called lostness, a friend.

All the help we could not yet see.

It cannot be always comfortable. So love the thousand knives as they enter and see your shape still sitting.

See that you too belong to paws of soft silent hungers, to thirst-tangled roots, to silver-spun constellations.

Industry observers note that know you’re no sicker than the rest of us. The big secret is this: No one else can brave you. Messy, yes. And marvelous.

What is more than we see in this world we’re pressed into, its blistered barking noise?

For what we build, speak, and ruin — our efforts, our angers.
